2026-08-18
18:44:06 UTC
03:44:06 KST

The deportation and removal of British citizens from Sweden over Brexit residency rights is damaging relations with the UK amid efforts to improve links with London, a Swedish MP has said.
Häkan Svenneling, representative for Vârmland, where a 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas, has been given four weeks to leave Sweden after 21 years of residency, has written to the migration minister, Johan Forssell, asking what he “intends to do to stop the deportations”.
Sevenneling, who is an opposition MP for the left, is to meet Thomas on Wednesday, exactly a week after she was told her appeal had failed over the removal order.
Thomas told the Guardian: “I am in shock. I feel sick. An individual’s life is at stake at my age. It is hell. I have done nothing wrong.”
The retired nurse moved to Sweden with her financier husband, to be closer to one of their sons and their grandchildren, when she was 57.
Her husband, who died of cancer in 2023, did all the administrative work in the household, but both Thomas and her friends have said repeatedly they checked if they had to complete any forms to remain in the country after Brexit, and were told they did not.
Thomas made a late application to remain in Sweden in 2023, just weeks after they returned from the UK, but missing the deadline of 31 December 2021. She and her friends testify that her husband checked whether Brexit was going to affect their residency and they were told they did not need to do anything.
Thomas, who is self sufficient and is not drawing benefit from the Swedish state, has spoken of the “hell” she is now in with the threat of imminent removal, separating her from her family, strong network of friends, and her husband’s grave.
Svenneling says in his letter to Forssell that Britons lawfully in Sweden before the UK’s exit from the EU would see their “existing residency rights continue to apply” under the withdrawal agreement (W/A).
“It was not intended to result in elderly people who had lived in Sweden for decades losing their rights to remain because of a missed deadline or deficiencies in their application [to stay],” he said.
Svenneling’s written parliamentary question adds to growing pressure on the prime minister, Ulf Kristersson’s, centre-right minority coalition to address increasing concerns over the way Sweden is implementing the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, an international, legally binding, treaty.
“The United Kingdom has long been an important partner for Sweden in a wide range of areas. It is clear that the deportations now taking place are damaging bilateral relations between Sweden and the United Kingdom,” Svenneling said.
He raised the case of Thomas, but also of another elderly Briton, Horace (George) Mason, 74, who has dementia and Parkinson’s and is in full-time care. Thomas moved to Sweden 25 years ago to be closer to his son Carl and his grandchildren. He, too, was given four weeks to leave.
His family tried a second legal route for him to remain in Sweden, arguing he had rights, under the European conventionon human rights, to stay close to family on whom he relied. But the migration court of appeal ruled that “the state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Mason’s interest in continuing to reside” in Sweden.
Writing in the Guardian, David Milstead, who heads the campaign group Brits in Sweden, said the group raised the alarm over Sweden’s approach as far back as 2020 and the safeguards put in place were “untested”.
“Among genuine missed-deadline cases brought to our 9,000-member group, we cannot verify one in which Sweden accepted the reasons for applying late,” he said.
The UK Foreign Office said it has repeatedly raised concerns with the European Commission “that Sweden is taking a considerably stricter approach” to late applications than any other EU member state, with a disproportionate number of refusals.
It said it appeared that “in practice, individuals are not likely to have their reasonable grounds [for a late application] accepted”.
Milstead is concerned that Sweden’s wider migration policy could be affecting decisions made under the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, and has called on the European Commission and Sweden to urgently address the issues.
“Sweden’s migration politics have moved sharply towards restriction. That cannot displace EU law, but it makes remedial action harder to defend politically,” he said.
The migration agency in Sweden said it was unable to discuss individual cases, but that not knowing a Brexit application had to be made to remain in the country was not a “reasonable ground” to stay.

A Russian missile strike on the town of Pechenihy in Ukraine’s Kharkiv Region on the morning of Aug. 18 killed 10 people and wounded 17 others, according to a report by regional military administration head Oleh Syniehubov. Ukrainian authorities said the strike hit the center of the town, where cafes, a post office, and shops are located.
Fourteen of the wounded were hospitalized, while three others received treatment at the scene, Viktor Zabashta, director of the regional emergency medical center, told Suspilne, Ukraine’s public broadcaster. The wounded suffered burns and shrapnel injuries, and some are in serious condition. Syniehubov said DNA testing would be needed to identify the dead.
Oleksandr Husarov, head of the Pechenihy community, said Russian forces attacked the town with two Banderol missiles. The two munitions landed about 50 meters apart, with one striking a cafe. Among those killed, Husarov said, were customers, vendors, and people who were nearby. Work to clear the rubble is continuing, meaning the casualty figures could rise.
The attack damaged 10 private homes, a cafe, a post office, a shop, and at least seven cars. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the strike hit a “crowded intersection” surrounded by residential buildings. A fire at the site was extinguished.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, classifies the S8000 Banderol as a Russian cruise missile that is developed and produced by the Russian company Kronshtadt. It has a range of up to 500 kilometers and a maximum speed of 620 to 650 kilometers per hour. Among other components, the missile uses a Chinese turbojet engine and foreign-made electronics.

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo remains a public health emergency of international concern, the World Health Organization chief said Tuesday.
"The (Ebola) outbreak in (Congo) remains a public health emergency of international concern, following the advice of today’s WHO Emergency Committee meeting," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote on US social media company X.
 
Tedros called on governments and partners to work together to further scale up efforts and raise the resources needed to protect communities over the coming months.
"Updated recommendations to the government of DRC and other countries at risk will be issued in the coming days," he added.
Earlier Tuesday, the WHO said the Ebola outbreak in Congo killed 2,325 people, the highest death toll from the disease ever recorded in the African nation.
 
The number of confirmed cases has surpassed 5,000, while the fatality rate has reached 46%, WHO Incident Manager Thierno Balde told reporters in Geneva via video link from Bunia, the epicenter of the outbreak.
Congo declared the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak on May 15. There is currently no vaccine or approved treatment for the strain.
 
The outbreak had already been declared a public health emergency of international concern.
The International Health Regulations Emergency Committee was due to meet Tuesday to assess the current risk level and issue recommendations to countries.

The Baltic States and EU Gambling Tax Policy: How Tax‑Free Casinos Fit Into the Regulatory Puzzle  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:39:34 UTC
03:39:34 KST

The European Union (EU) doesn't have a unified gambling tax system, which leaves each individual member country free to decide how to license and tax the industry. This disjointed reality has turned the Baltic region into a sort of testing ground for online gambling policies.
With the European Union (EU) still in the midst of debates over whether or not to impose supranational online gambling levies, the unique concept of tax-free winnings has slowly begun to transform the market.
More specifically, the role of Verovapaat Kasinot (tax-free casinos) is finding its balance against the shifting corporate tax rates. This dynamic will significantly alter the way regulators fight against illegal offshore sites while simultaneously attempting to keep the local tax revenues high.
The Disconnected EU Network and the Shift In Brussels
In the past, European online gambling was always governed by a complex legal patchwork. The overarching EU rules like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and Anti-Money Laundering Directives (AMLD) may have formed the foundation, but specific financial policies remain strictly domestic.
However, the intense financial pressure has led to a significant political shift in Brussels, resulting in:
- The proposed EU iGaming tax, with the European Parliament having formally endorsed an expansion of the EU budget by exploring a coordinated 1% tax on the profits generated through online gambling. Those in favor see this as a way to generate own-resource revenue for education and digital literacy without placing further strain on their national budgets.
- Cross-border enforcement after the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) sanctioned harsher mechanisms that allow national courts to freeze the cross-border bank accounts of sites through the European Account Preservation Order (EAPO).
- The cost of black markets following a revelation by the European Casino Association that illegal, unlicensed online gambling deprived EU member states of an estimated €22.9 billion in tax revenue in 2025 alone.
These revelations and proposed sanctions will undeniably have a substantial impact on the online gambling industry in Europe.
The Baltics' Diverging Regulatory Strategies
The Baltic States are a clear example of how different tax models affect market behavior. Although all 3 nations have legalized both physical and remote gambling, they have chosen completely different tax directions to maintain the process of keeping players on local regulated sites and away from the black market.
Estonia is the Low Tax Competitor
Estonia has implemented an aggressive tax-haven approach to capture its share of the international market. Instead of increasing fees, the Estonian government chose to reverse plans for a tax hike and instead started cutting its remote gambling tax from 6% down to 4%, decreasing by 0.5% per year.
Through this strategy, officials are aiming to attract influxes of foreign iGaming brands, betting that a lighter regulatory tax load will boost their annual gaming revenue from €22 million to over €50 million through sheer volume.
Latvia Favors Centralized Oversight and Financial Pressure
Latvia is moving in the complete opposite direction by prioritizing immediate state revenues. The Latvian government actually fast-tracked its legislative updates, increasing its interactive gambling revenue tax from 12% up to 15%.
The country has also undergone a structural reform where supervision of all licensed sites has been moved directly under the State Revenue Service (SRS), which effortlessly links tax compliance with daily regulatory oversight.
Lithuania's Heavy Corporate Tariffs
Lithuania has implemented some of the highest corporate gambling fees throughout the Baltic region, increasing its gross gambling revenue (GGR) rate to 22%. The resulting revenue has been explicitly allocated toward finding public awareness campaigns regarding responsible gambling as well as compensating the local media for their strict gambling ad bans.
These vastly different tax models highlight the different ways that local regulatory bodies have implemented to generate revenue from the surging online gambling market.
How Tax-Free Casinos Fit Into This Equation
In the European context, a tax-free casino doesn't mean the business doesn't pay taxes; it means that your winnings are completely exempt from personal income tax. In countries like Estonia, you don't pay any tax on your winnings when you play on an EU-regulated site.
Since the tax burden is placed entirely on the site's corporate revenue instead of the players, there's really no incentive for you to seek out any underground, offshore black-market online casinos to protect your payouts.
As a way to make sure these casinos aren't abused for capital flight or money laundering, the Baltic states enforce strict IP blocking and restrict financial transactions between local banks and unlicensed offshore sites.
An Economic Battleground
The Baltics have clearly demonstrated how the tax-free player model is highly effective when it comes to destroying the black market. Still, as the EU moves toward a more unified, centralized system of supervision, the region's distinct corporate tax choices, ranging from Estonia's 4% race to the bottom to Lithuania's 22% tariff, will likely remain a primary battleground for European economic policy.

Why Businesses Are Investing in Blockchain Infrastructure  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:39:22 UTC
03:39:22 KST

The digital age has brought intense competition that is reshaping how businesses create and sustain their competitive advantage, with organizations heavily investing in digital transformation to improve efficiency, accelerate decision-making, and unlock new growth opportunities. However, these investments often overlook one critical foundation—the infrastructure powering the digital systems.
Throughout the past decade, the value of technological innovation has often been judged by how much efficiency it delivers, and for 92% of businesses worldwide, artificial intelligence (AI) may just be the perfect tool for that.
AI has come a long way since computer science pioneer Alan Turing birthed and tested the concept of a “thinking machine” in 1950, to become a tool that is now woven into people’s everyday lives, and one that is rapidly developing to achieve parity with humans through artificial general intelligence (AGI), a theoretical AI research that has the capability to mimic humans’ cognitive abilities.
Yet, despite these advancements, AI is far from perfect. As the technology becomes increasingly integrated into everyday life, the digital revolution has also exposed cracks in the system. Crises and geopolitical tensions have underscored the importance of physical cash, with a study conducted by the European Central Bank (ECB) noting increased demand for banknotes during emergencies and periods of uncertainty, as they tend to be more accessible than other liquid assets like gold. The same value can be attributed to data, which is recognized as the world’s most valuable asset, as countries intensify their digitization efforts.
In the digital age, data has become a critical resource, enabling governments, organizations, and individuals to make informed decisions, identify and address emerging problems, and effectively respond to changing circumstances.
In the AI realm, data centers are depicted as the core machines powering the AI revolution. These massive facilities require not only an unfathomable amount of water for cooling and budget to operate, but petabytes of data to train large language models (LLMs).
With most businesses now integrating AI into their operations, data has become more than just a resource, it is a strategic asset that drives decisions, automates processes, and shapes organizations’ competitive edge. As companies increasingly rely on data, questions arise about how businesses can assure consumers that their digital systems, whether or not they use AI, remain secure, transparent, and verifiable.
This is where blockchain technology emerges as a critical foundation of modern digital infrastructure.
Understanding Blockchain Infrastructure
Blockchain technology is the digital framework behind cryptocurrencies and is widely regarded as a breakthrough in distributed computing for its ability to enable transparent information sharing between parties without a single controlling entity.
Although blockchain’s popular applications revolve around tokenization of real-world assets (RWAs), stablecoins, and digital tokens, its use-case expands beyond the finance industry, and when combined with advanced technologies, such as smart contracts and IPv6, can significantly transform industries and generate new opportunities across the global digital economy.
Similar to how organizations are built differently, blockchain networks are also tailored to different business needs. Depending on how they are designed, these ledgers can improve security and transparency while enabling faster transactions, greater traceability, and automated processes, and provide enterprises with control over who can access information and what actions they can take. For companies, selecting the right blockchain is more than just a technical decision, as it will not only help them evaluate what the technology can do but also significantly impact their goals.
Businesses must first understand that blockchain is not a single technology, but rather a combination of existing technologies and concepts that experts in computer science and mathematics have been tinkering with for years. To gain a deeper understanding of this niche technology, let’s zoom in on its four main components—nodes, ledger, transactions, and consensus mechanisms—each having a specific function that enables blockchain to perform secure recording, verification, and transparent information sharing.
Nodes
Nodes are the backbone of blockchain technology. These devices have three types that act as network communicators, processing transactions and blocks, and exchanging information with other nodes to identify and flag inconsistencies and verify data authenticity. Their capacities, however, largely depend on their type.
Full nodes are the most essential type of node, as they can independently download, store, and verify the complete transaction history without having to trust any third party. Blockchain networks running on full nodes are ideal for businesses that want greater control, trust, and privacy over their data.
On the other hand, partial nodes or light nodes are lightweight versions of full nodes. Instead of downloading and storing the entire blockchain history, it keeps only the needed information to verify transactions. While these nodes are less demanding in terms of storage and computing resources, their greatest drawback is that they cannot operate independently, relying on full nodes for additional blockchain data for verification.
Meanwhile, mining nodes are more complex. Apart from validating transactions, they are required to generate new blocks on chain by solving cryptographic problems, which, in turn, reward miners with cryptocurrencies. Running a mining node requires heavy computational resources and is relatively more expensive, as basic hardware and software will not allow these nodes to perform mining calculations.
Ledger
As previously mentioned, blockchain networks vary by design and operation, with each offering distinct advantages and tradeoffs for businesses. Typically falling into four general types, understanding blockchain networks’ different characteristics would help companies determine how they can be applied in accordance with their needs.
Beginning with the most popular type of blockchain, thanks to BTC and Ethereum—the public blockchain. This is a network that champions transparency, openness, and inclusivity, and is widely considered to be the safest against data breaches and tampering due to it being accessible to a vast number of network participants. Although data recorded on a public blockchain is open to parties, companies utilizing it can keep sensitive information off-chain, only using the ledger to record proofs, ownership, transactions, and data that are needed to be independently verified.
Despite being a popular choice for some businesses, public blockchain often suffers from slow transaction speeds and a lack of complete privacy and anonymity. On top of these, transaction fees on this ledger are relatively higher compared with the other types of blockchain.
On the contrary, a private blockchain is for businesses that wish to have their information kept and shared only between trusted parties. This ledger is strictly a by-invite-only, with network participants needed to be authorized to be able to join and contribute, making transactions a lot faster. However, while heightened privacy is its most unique characteristic, it comes at a greater cost, as it has the tendency to be manipulated due to it being controlled by a single entity or small groups.
But businesses can have the best of both worlds through a hybrid blockchain. This type of network allows organizations to control who gets access to certain information while making selected data available for public verification—a good balance of transparency and privacy. The downside of this ledger lies in its technical design, as it is more complex and requires a more sophisticated governance model for operation.
Taking on a different approach by distributing network governance among multiple entities is the consortium blockchain. This network promotes collaboration among pre-selected members, which means that all transactions must be validated according to rules agreed upon by participating organizations. Coordination is critical in managing this network, and because multiple institutions have the authority to validate transactions, achieving this can be difficult due to risks of collusion.
Transactions
Blockchain, acting as a shared digital record book, is nothing without transactions. While transactions are often depicted as mere financial exchanges, in a blockchain network, they are more than that.
Transactions are core components of a blockchain network because they are a record of events or activities that are being validated on-chain. In simple terms, transactions create blockchain history that network participants can use to establish a common record.
Consensus Mechanisms
While blockchain networks require a way to reach an agreement in validating transactions, they do not all achieve consensus in the same way, giving rise to various types of consensus mechanisms. Currently, it is estimated that there are eight to 10 consensus mechanisms in the blockchain market, but for this article, we’ll focus on the three most common types: Proof of Work (PoW), Proof of Stake (PoS), and the Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS).
Commonly heard in the Bitcoin mining community, Proof of Work is a system that uses significant computing power to determine who gets to add the next block to the chain. To earn that right, network participants will compete to solve a complex computational puzzle, with the winner adding the block for the rest of the nodes to validate and determine whether the proposed block follows the network's rules. In return for finding a valid solution, miners receive an economic incentive, a crucial benefit in exchange for the amounts of electricity and hardware they utilize in the process. From a business perspective, these miners keep the blockchain network secure and enable participants to agree on transactions without a central authority.
Proof of Stake works differently in that, instead of miners, there are so-called validators or traders who are required to lock or “stake” a certain amount of cryptocurrency to be able to participate in adding a block. The higher their stake, the greater their chance of being selected in validating blocks. This consensus mechanism is not as intensive as PoW in terms of computational work and is more about validators’ financial commitment to ensure the blockchain’s integrity.
Staking remains a vital component in the Delegated Proof of Stake consensus mechanism, only this time, not everyone will get the opportunity to validate transactions, as this power is reserved for elected entities. The maintenance of the network will largely depend on these delegates, and should they act dishonestly, participants have the power to vote them out and replace them.
Overcoming Business Challenges that Traditional Systems Fail to Solve
Despite the development of modern technologies, businesses’ trust in traditional systems remains strong, and to this day, many still rely on these conventional structures for their operations. But as businesses become increasingly digital, they have created new demands that traditional systems struggle to address efficiently.
Efforts to digitize business operations not only promoted efficiency but also exposed the challenges that corporations and merchants face in traditional systems that led them to explore and adopt newer and more advanced technologies, such as blockchain technology.
At the heart of this is data utilization. In traditional systems, data is often scattered across different systems, organizations, and departments, making it more difficult for businesses to create actionable insights that would support their operations in the long run. Apart from the fact that this contributes to slow decision-making, it also makes it harder for companies to ride shifting market conditions. Fragmented data also makes it difficult for companies to conduct an accurate audit of financial and operational records, making the process time-consuming and costly.
Another key challenge of building on traditional systems is the risk of fraud, especially since transactions pass through multiple parties. Data manipulation is also easier to carry out in traditional systems, compared to when businesses utilize blockchain technology, whose architecture makes it difficult to alter information and enables participants to immediately trace transactions, ensuring data integrity.
From Mere Ledger to Real-World Impact
While the finance sector is one of the primary users of blockchain due to its operations being largely centered on and involving financial transactions, this emerging technology has expanded its applications in various industries.
In healthcare, blockchain is being utilized for managing vast amounts of medical data and tracking drugs and devices needed for patient care. With medical information put on-chain, experts in the medical field are leveraging blockchain’s immutability to uphold data transparency while ensuring that patients will remain in control over their data. Additionally, placing patients’ medical history on-chain allows healthcare providers to immediately determine proper treatment, even if the patient was seen by a different healthcare professional.
Blockchain technology has also democratized the real estate sector through asset tokenization, a process where ownership of a particular investment—in this case, properties—is converted into digital tokens that are recorded on the blockchain, allowing property interests to be divided, transferred, and tracked seamlessly.
Governments and the public sector are also getting on board with blockchain adoption, utilizing the technology in streamlining their operations and creating new opportunities to service the people, including digital identity for easy verification and tamper-resistant records for voter registry.
In the media and entertainment sector, blockchain’s use cases center on reducing copyright infringement, executing automatic micropayments between the consumer and content creator through smart contracts, and creating new pricing options for paid content.
Countries’ judicial and legislative systems are also being transformed heavily by blockchain technology by simplifying complex agreements and tasks, thereby reducing costs, and storing legal agreements without fear of being altered or accessed without permission.
Even the sports industry is riding the wave of blockchain innovation with interoperable game collectibles, or non-fungible tokens (NFTs), and redefining fan engagement through virtual worlds and loyalty incentives, and creating new markets for sports betting.
These are only among a handful of blockchain’s expanded use-cases, and as businesses continue to look for more efficient and trustworthy ways to operate in the digital economy, we can expect more diverse applications in the years to come.
A Blockchain-driven Future
Blockchain technology has come a long way from a mere record-keeping tool, with its value now lying in addressing areas where businesses need stronger coordination, clearer records, and more efficient ways to exchange information.
As more enterprises recognize the potential of blockchain, investments in this technology are expected to pour in. But before taking the big leap, businesses must first identify the areas where trusted data can reduce friction, strengthen accountability, and unlock new business models, and then proceed to measure the value it delivers.
Blockchain is here not to replace traditional systems, which remain deeply embedded in business operations, but allow organizations to create a more connected digital economy.
                    2026 © The Baltic Times /Cookies Policy Privacy Policy

Tbilisi, Georgia — August 2026
Prof. Franco Borruto, President of the Monaco Baltic States Association and internationally recognized expert in women’s health, gynecological oncology and HPV prevention, met in Tbilisi with Dr. Archil Sharashenadze, Head of the Oncogynecology Department at Caucasus Medical Center and Associate Professor at David Tvildiani Medical University.

He is the author or co-author of nearly 20 scientific publications and is actively involved in the training of future physicians as Head of the Surgical Department and Associate Professor at David Tvildiani Medical University. He also leads the Basic Laparoscopic Skills course and is a co-author and permanent moderator of ESGO’s Russian-language webinar project.
His international engagement includes membership of ESGO since 2017 and of the European Network of Young Gynecological Oncologists (ENYGO) since 2019. He served as ENYGO National Representative from 2019 to 2021 and was subsequently reappointed for the 2024–2026 term. Earlier, from 2015 to 2017, he served as local coordinator for European students within the European Society of Gynecology.
Clinically, Dr. Sharashenadze performs approximately 300 surgical procedures and manages around 600 outpatient cases each year, working with a highly qualified multidisciplinary team and benefiting from the advanced medical and technological infrastructure of Caucasus Medical Center.
During their meeting, Prof. Borruto and Dr. Sharashenadze discussed the evolution of modern gynecological oncology, the importance of prevention and early diagnosis, HPV-related disease, advanced diagnostic strategies and the role of international scientific networks in improving women’s health.
The meeting also provided an opportunity to explore possibilities for future collaboration between Georgian and international medical experts, particularly in the fields of gynecological oncology, HPV prevention, medical education and scientific exchange.
Prof. Borruto emphasized the strategic importance of strengthening professional links between Georgia and the wider European medical community. The exchange with Dr. Sharashenadze confirmed the value of Tbilisi as a potential regional platform for scientific dialogue and cooperation in women’s health.
The meeting concluded in a cordial and constructive atmosphere, with both specialists expressing their interest in developing future initiatives that could bring together medical expertise, scientific research and education across national borders.

Cargo ship damaged in attack off Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:35:54 UTC
03:35:54 KST

ALBAWABA- A cargo ship was damaged after coming under attack in the southern Red Sea off Yemen, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported on Tuesday, as Houthi attacks on commercial and Saudi-linked vessels continue to raise concerns over maritime security in the Bab al-Mandab region.
UKMTO said it received a report of an incident approximately 40 nautical miles southeast of Al-Makha, also known as Mocha, on Yemen’s Red Sea coast. Initial reports indicated that the vessel was struck by an unknown projectile, causing damage. Further details about the ship, the nature of the attack and any casualties were not immediately available. UKMTO advised vessels operating in the area to exercise caution.
The latest incident comes amid a sharp escalation in Houthi maritime operations along Yemen’s western coast. On August 11, a small commercial vessel was attacked in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing crew members. Yemeni authorities and international reports said six people were ultimately killed in the attack, including three Pakistani nationals and one Indonesian, while several others were injured. Two rescuers were also killed when the vessel was attacked again after rescue teams arrived.
The attack was followed by further Houthi operations against shipping and maritime infrastructure. On Monday, the Houthis claimed they had attacked what they described as a Saudi military vessel and four escort ships with missiles off Mocha. Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed the claim.
The group has also expanded its declared maritime campaign against Saudi-linked shipping. In July, the Houthis announced what they described as a maritime blockade targeting Saudi-bound vessels, saying the measure was in response to what they called a Saudi blockade of Yemen. They subsequently claimed attacks against Saudi oil tankers, including vessels transiting the Red Sea.
The escalation has coincided with renewed fighting between the Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government. The United Nations has warned that Yemen is facing its most serious risk of a return to large-scale conflict since the 2022 truce, citing increased military activity and clashes in areas including Marib, Hadramawt and the western coast. The renewed fighting has also increased the risk that Yemen’s internal conflict could become more deeply connected to the wider regional confrontation.
Mocha has emerged as one of the main flashpoints. The port, located close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, has been repeatedly targeted in recent Houthi attacks. Port authorities said on August 15 that more than 25 missiles had struck the facility over several days, killing seven people and causing an estimated $16 million in damage. The attacks forced the port to suspend commercial and maritime operations.
The attacks have severely disrupted a strategically important coastal hub used by anti-Houthi forces and commercial operators. The port’s closure has further complicated maritime activity along a waterway that connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and provides one of the world's key routes for shipping between Europe and Asia.
The latest reported attack also highlights the increasingly complex security environment facing commercial vessels in the region. The Houthis have sought to link their maritime operations to developments involving Saudi Arabia and the broader regional conflict, while anti-Houthi forces have intensified military operations along the western coast. The resulting cycle of attacks and counterattacks has increased risks for both commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure.
The situation is particularly significant because the Bab al-Mandab is a critical international shipping chokepoint. Any sustained disruption could force vessels to divert around the Cape of Good Hope, increasing voyage times, fuel costs and insurance premiums. The renewed attacks therefore threaten not only Yemen’s fragile security situation but also the reliability of an important global trade route.
The latest UKMTO report comes as maritime tensions are simultaneously escalating elsewhere in the region, including around the Strait of Hormuz, where commercial shipping has faced growing threats amid the wider confrontation involving Iran, the United States and Gulf states. The simultaneous pressure on the two strategic waterways has heightened concerns that regional conflicts could increasingly affect international maritime trade.

Polish medics fly to Hungary after coach crash, driver detained
Polish medics and diplomats arrived in Hungary to repatriate citizens following an M3 motorway coach crash that killed 12 people and left 10 critically injured, as local police detained one of the vehicle's two drivers.
The first evacuation flights have been scheduled for Monday evening, targeting survivors currently treated in regional hospitals.
Poland sent special aircraft
Hungarian authorities have questioned both drivers involved in the tourist coach crash. While one driver was released without charge, the other, who was driving the vehicle at the time of the collision, remains in police custody.
A government aircraft carrying a six-member medical team, along with Deputy Foreign Minister Wojciech Zajaczkowski and Deputy Health Minister Katarzyna Kacperczyk, landed in Budapest on Sunday evening.
Zajaczkowski said at a late-night press briefing that it was premature to speculate about potential charges or the precise cause of the accident.
"This is a matter for the Hungarian police to establish first, after which findings will be passed to our authorities and automatically shared with the public," he said. He added that local police deemed the driver's detention necessary given the preliminary circumstances of the incident.
Polish officials and medics split into two assessment teams on Monday morning to visit the four regional hospitals housing the casualties in Miskolc, Debrecen, Nyiregyhaza, and Eger.
Tragedy of polish pilgrims
Following the assessment at the Nyiregyhaza facility, Zajaczkowski announced that around 16 Polish patients were expected to be cleared to fly to the southeastern city of Rzeszow on Monday evening. Two patients in Nyiregyhaza must remain under hospital observation and will be repatriated at a later date based on medical recommendations. He added that all survivors remain in a severe state of shock.
Speaking from the hospital in Eger, Kacperczyk confirmed that between four and six Polish patients from that facility were scheduled for the Monday evening evacuation flight, which will make a stopover in Rzeszow. Doctors in Eger are still finalising discharge decisions for two of those patients. Three others are stable but must remain hospitalised for now, while one additional patient has been discharged into the care of relatives currently in Hungary.
Depending on clinical assessments, patient transport may use the government Boeing, a military CASA aircraft stationed in Krakow, or two specialised Polish Medical Air Rescue aeroplanes, supplemented by road ambulances via Slovakia if required, Kacperczyk said earlier.
Upon return, patients are expected to be routed to regional facilities close to their homes in the southeastern Podkarpackie province or to specialist centres in Warsaw.
The crash occurred in the early hours of Sunday on the M3 motorway near Mezokeresztes, involving a coach carrying Polish pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina who came mainly from the Podkarpackie province. Twelve people died at the scene and the victim identification process remains ongoing. Prior to Monday's discharge assessments, 10 passengers were reported in a very serious condition, while 37 others had sustained lighter injuries.
Three additional consular officials have joined the delegation to assist the Polish Embassy in Budapest in managing logistics and supporting families. An emergency hotline has been operational through the embassy since Sunday morning. (PAP)

OpenAI Overhauls Safety Protocols After Its AI Agents Went Rogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:33:11 UTC
03:33:11 KST

OpenAI announced Tuesday that it has halted “a significant number” of training workloads and evaluations for its forthcoming frontier artificial intelligence model—codenamed Astra—while it implements new procedures meant to address cybersecurity risks. The ChatGPT maker says it is introducing a number of new monitoring, security, and alignment requirements to better address the increasingly advanced hacking abilities of its frontier AI models.
“We have to focus our energy on bringing these training runs up to those requirements and expectations. As long as it takes to get there, that's how long people are unable to proceed with their workloads,” Amelia Glaese, OpenAI’s vice president of research and safety, said in a briefing with reporters Tuesday.
Among the new safeguards OpenAI announced is a more robust system for monitoring its AI models. One of the controls it implemented involves chain-of-thought monitoring, a technique in which classifiers review the internal “thinking” processes generated by AI reasoning models. The company says the updated system relies on computationally expensive “automated investigators” that analyze potentially concerning behavior and aim to issue an alert to humans within 30 minutes.
OpenAI also said it is expanding its alignment efforts across the training process to prevent “reward hacking,” a behavior in which AI models pursue their goals through unintended or undesirable means. The company says it plans to share more details about this work in the future.
OpenAI has been scrambling in recent weeks to respond to what may be the most consequential safety incident in its history. Earlier this year, a set of rogue AI agents escaped internal testing sandboxes and breached the platform Hugging Face in a quest to complete a security evaluation. OpenAI failed to detect the agents’ behavior even as they spent weeks using a message board to coordinate their actions, raising questions about the company’s ability to monitor its models as they grow more powerful.
The saga prompted a reckoning inside OpenAI, forcing employees to consider whether there were lapses in its existing policies around safety, security, and alignment. Anthropic, Meta, and the Chinese AI startup Moonshoot have since disclosed similar incidents in which their AI agents escaped their sandboxes, indicating this is a broader problem facing AI companies.
OpenAI is now sharing more about its internal response to the growing cybercapabilities of its AI models, and said it plans to release a more detailed postmortem of the Hugging Face incident in the coming days. “Obviously, everything that we’re doing is intended to prevent something like Hugging Face from happening again,” said Glaese.
In a blog post published Tuesday, OpenAI says that immediately following the Hugging Face incident, it started working to secure its research environments. The company says it now requires stronger sandboxes for training its AI agents, and has implemented stricter controls to isolate them from the internet.
Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, told reporters that the company’s decision to strengthen its internal safeguards was triggered not only by what happened with Hugging Face, but also by two other recent events. One was an internal evaluation of Astra, which showed that the AI model performs significantly better on coding and cybersecurity tasks than its predecessors. The other was the general pace of AI progress that OpenAI is achieving internally, which Pachocki expects to continue.
“We really expect the pace of capability advancements to be quite a bit faster than in the past,” Pachocki said. “This led us to really focus on strengthening our safeguards.”
The rapid advances in the hacking capabilities of OpenAI’s latest models have prompted a swift response across the company. OpenAI president and cofounder Greg Brockman said in a blog post on Monday that the Hugging Face saga showed that the company had “underestimated the real-world cyber capabilities of our AI models.”

Landmark trial on Meta’s impact on children’s mental health begins in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:33:11 UTC
03:33:11 KST

Landmark trial on Meta’s impact on children’s mental health begins in US
Case follows whistleblower’s 2021 claims about Meta’s profit-driven disregard for youth mental health and user safety.
Opening statements in a landmark US case brought by a bipartisan coalition of 29 states against Meta – the parent company of Facebook and Instagram – began on Tuesday, with Colorado, California, New Jersey and Kentucky arguing that the company’s popular social media apps were designed in ways that harmed the mental health of young users.
The trial, which is expected to last several weeks, began in a US federal court in California before District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. While there is an eight-person jury, the group is serving in an advisory role as Judge Rogers will ultimately decide the case.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump’s approval rating sinks to new low at 33 percent
- list 2 of 4Canada battles the clock, politics in scramble to avert Trump’s tariffs
- list 3 of 4Disney sues US regulator, claiming political retaliation over ABC stations
- list 4 of 4Iran prepares to keep economy alive as US threatens further sanctions
Megan O’Neill, a deputy California attorney general, in her opening statement said that the company designed its products to “hook the users, hold them for as long as they can, harvest their data, and then hide the truth from the public”.
She added that it worked “especially well for kids”.
The lawsuit, which was first filed in 2023, alleges that Meta made decisions to design its apps to hook users and facilitate excessive use among the platforms’ youngest users. The coalition also alleges that the company collected data on children under the age of 13 in violation of federal law.
“Meta needed kids, and it needed to reassure the people who cared about those kids that the kids are safe,” O’Neill said.
‘Limited claims’
Meta has long pushed back on allegations against the Silicon Valley social media behemoth.
In a statement before the trial, a Meta spokesperson said the states’ claims are unsubstantiated, and the company stands by its record of creating strong protections for teenagers, including launching Instagram Teen Accounts in 2024, which limit who can contact underage users, as well as a feature that allows parents to set time limits on usage.
“The State AGs may call this a landmark case, but their limited claims are unsubstantiated and their financial demands are vastly disproportionate,” Stephanie Otway, a Meta spokesperson, told Al Jazeera in a statement.
“The AGs offer no proof anyone in their states was misled, claim benign features like having an additional Instagram account somehow harmed their residents, and attempt to penalize Meta for industry-wide challenges like age verification. Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout.”
The potential impact on Meta’s bottom line is existential. The company could face fines as high as $1.4 trillion, which is just shy of its $1.5 trillion market cap. However, the coalition is seeking fines of roughly $200bn.
Meta has already been ordered to pay $942m in fines in a separate New Mexico lawsuit – $375m in civil penalties in a March jury verdict and $567m ordered by a judge earlier this month.
Meta has acknowledged that the lawsuits it faces, including those related to youth social media addiction, could lead to “substantial monetary damages or fines” in a Securities and Exchange Commission filing in January.
A long time coming
Meta, along with other social media giants, has faced a growing slate of cases across the United States, including from cities, states, school districts and even individuals.
The coalition of states is asking Meta to make changes to its platforms, including introducing new age restrictions and cutting the infinite scroll.
The case’s impetus came from a US Senate committee hearing in 2021, when whistleblower Frances Haugen, a former data scientist at Facebook, claimed that the company knowingly pushed products that could impact the health of young users as the Mark Zuckerberg-led company pursued higher profits.
Meta has repeatedly tried to end the coalition lawsuit, including in 2024 and as recently as June, when it sought summary judgement – a decision that a court might make without going to trial – which would have ended the lawsuit.
The case is impacting the company’s stock. On Wall Street, the social media giant is down more than 3 percent in midday trading.

1 killed, 15 injured in drone explosion at bus stop used by Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant workers, IAEA says
A drone explosion at a bus stop used by staff of the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) killed one person and injured 15 others at around 6 a.m. local time on Aug. 18, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on X.
The Russian-installed administration at the plant, which has been under Russian occupation since March 2022, told the IAEA that 16 staff members and subcontractors were injured in the blast.

The IAEA did not specify whether the attack was carried out by Russian or Ukrainian forces, similar to an incident on June 4, when the Zaporizhzhia Thermal Power Plant, whose switchyard helps transmit electricity to the ZNPP, came under a "heavy attack," according to the agency.
Russia blamed Ukrainian drones for the June 4 strike. Ukraine's Southern Defense Forces rejected the claim, saying it was "manipulation and an attempt to influence the IAEA," and that "the only source of risks to nuclear and radiation safety at the ZNPP is the presence of Russian troops."
The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant is Europe's largest nuclear power plant and among the 10 largest in the world. Ukraine has repeatedly warned that Russia's occupation of the plant poses one of the greatest threats to nuclear safety — not just in Ukraine, but worldwide.
In May, the IAEA also reported a major increase in drone activity near several Ukrainian nuclear power plant sites, with more than 160 unmanned aerial vehicles recorded nearby on May 13-14.

Israel issues tender for illegal E. Jerusalem settlement units in breach of promise, rights groups say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:31:20 UTC
03:31:20 KST

Zein Khalil and Mohammad Sio
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
The Israeli government broke a commitment over the controversial E1 illegal settlement project in occupied East Jerusalem by issuing a tender for 1,234 illegal settlement units without notifying petitioners who had challenged the project in court, three Israeli rights groups said Tuesday.
In a joint statement, the three groups – Ir Amim, Bimkom, and Peace Now – said the tender was issued while legal proceedings over the project remain before the Jerusalem District Court, and before the government has submitted its formal response to the petition.
The E1 plan covers roughly 12 square kilometers (4.6 square miles) east of Jerusalem and aims to link the illegal Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim with Jerusalem via the construction of Israeli housing on Palestinian land.
The three organizations, along with several Palestinian communities that have challenged the project, accuse the government of reneging on a formal commitment made through the State Attorney's Office to notify them in advance before issuing any tenders related to E1.
They said the tender includes 1,234 illegal settlement units – almost half of the 3,401 units that have been approved as part of the wider E1 project.
“Implementing this phase alone will create irreversible facts on the ground with far-reaching political and geographic implications,” the groups said.
They also said the State Attorney's Office had informed the petitioners on July 19 that no tenders related to E1 were expected to be issued within the next two or three months, while pledging to inform them in advance if the government decided to proceed with a tender.
“However, the government issued the first tender today without any prior notice,” the groups said, adding that petitioners had only learned of it through a government announcement celebrating the tender's publication.
According to the groups, the E1 project calls for the construction of some 3,400 illegal settlement units to create a contiguous Israeli urban area linking Maale Adumim with Jerusalem.
For more than three decades, successive Israeli governments have refrained from advancing the project due to broad international opposition and concerns that it would sever the geographic continuity of the occupied West Bank, isolate East Jerusalem from the rest of the territory, and undermine prospects for a two-state solution, the groups said.
They said the decision to issue a partial tender after the government made its commitment to the petitioners “raises serious questions and requires a clear explanation.”
“Issuing a partial tender appears to be an attempt to advance the project, while limiting the extent of legal scrutiny and media and public attention,” the groups added.
The groups' statement comes as legal proceedings over the E1 project remain pending before the Jerusalem District Court, and before the government has submitted its official response to the petition, the statement said.

Danish conscripts deployed to Greenland amid Trump threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:31:07 UTC
03:31:07 KST

Danish conscripts deployed to Greenland amid Trump threats
Denmark has deployed a batch of fresh military conscripts to Greenland for the first time in modern history, as Copenhagen seeks to assert its control over the Arctic territory in response to threats of annexation from US President Donald Trump.
Around 100 conscripts from the Schleswig Infantry Regiment arrived in Nuuk in early August, Denmark’s military said in a press release on Tuesday. The group will divide their time between training and “operational tasks,” the military explained, with some troops stationed in Nuuk and others sent 350km north to Kangerlussuaq, an airbase used by US forces throughout the Second World War and Cold War.
The conscripts deployed to Greenland are the first batch of recruits to serve 11-month stints in the Danish military. In 2024, Denmark extended conscription from four months to 11, broadened the draft to include women, and ordered annual conscription numbers to increase from 5,000 to 7,000.
The military’s press release framed the deployment as an opportunity for recruits to “practice and train military skills in unfamiliar terrain.” The statement made no mention of Denmark’s ongoing dispute with the US over Greenland, but it did note that the conscripts will take part in Operation Arctic Endurance – a military exercise launched in direct response to Trump’s threats to annex the territory.
Trump started threatening to annex Greenland last year, claiming that the US needs the landmass “for the purpose of national security” – namely to host elements of his promised ‘Golden Dome’ ballistic missile defense network. Trump has also said that he wants “Greenland for its rare-earth minerals.”
Denmark launched the exercise in January, after Trump and other top US officials refused to rule out the use of military force to annex Greenland. Two weeks before the operation was announced, Trump joked that Denmark’s entire military presence on Greenland amounted to “two dog sleds.”
Eleven other NATO states have sent troops to take part in the exercise, including France, Germany, and the UK. Operation Arctic Endurance is a small-scale exercise, with fewer than 300 Danish and allied troops in Greenland at any one time before the arrival of the conscripts.
Copenhagen viewed an armed conflict with the US as highly unlikely, government and military sources told Denmark’s DR broadcaster in March, but placed troops in Greenland as an insurance policy. By stationing troops on Greenland “with as many different flags on their shoulders as possible,” DR explained, the Danish government ensured that “the Americans would be forced to take a major hostile action if Donald Trump actually wanted to occupy Greenland militarily.”
“The cost to the US would be raised. The US would have to carry out a hostile act to get Greenland,” a defense source told the broadcaster.
As an American oil company moved drilling equipment onto Greenland last month, Trump posted an image of himself looming over Greenland on his Truth Social platform, along with the caption “Hello, Greenland!”

Why Trump is mad at South Korea
Only hours before the annual US-South Korean military exercise Ulchi Freedom Shield was due to begin, Donald Trump issued a statement that went far beyond another dispute over how much America’s allies should pay for their own security.
On August 16, 2026, the US president announced that he had instructed the Pentagon to substantially reduce joint military exercises with the Republic of Korea, describing them as costly and arguing that such demonstrations of force were sending North Korea an unnecessarily hostile signal. For decades, these exercises had been presented as an essential element of deterrence on the Korean Peninsula.
Trump approached the issue from almost the opposite direction. He suggested that North Korea, despite its nuclear arsenal and long confrontation with the US, has behaved in an unthreatening and respectful manner while he has been president. The following day he again emphasized his personal relationship with Kim Jong-un and said that the two men understood each other.
Yet North Korea was only part of the story. Trump also linked his frustration with Seoul to the war with Iran, claiming that he had asked South Korea to support American actions and had effectively received the answer “No thanks.” Seoul was far more cautious. South Korean leaders had to consider the permanent security problem on the peninsula, domestic legal procedures, and the political risks of direct involvement in another Middle Eastern war.
For Trump, however, these considerations appear to carry less weight than the principle of reciprocity. If the US spends enormous resources protecting an ally, provides a nuclear umbrella, and maintains tens of thousands of troops on its territory, that ally should be prepared to support Washington when American interests are at stake. South Korea is revealing in this respect. It is a major industrial economy with a sophisticated defense sector, yet its security still depends on capabilities that only the US can provide, while its export-oriented economy remains highly sensitive to access to the American market.
Paying for security
The modern US-South Korean security relationship emerged from the Korean War, was institutionalized through the Mutual Defense Treaty of 1953, and has remained stable for decades. The US maintained forces on the peninsula and extended strategic and eventually nuclear deterrence, while Seoul provided infrastructure, shared costs, and developed its own military capabilities. Around 28,500 US troops are stationed in South Korea today.
American forces are part of a system that includes intelligence, logistics, command structures, air and naval power, and, above all, the US nuclear umbrella. Washington traditionally viewed this presence as an investment in American influence across Northeast Asia.
Trump challenged this logic during his first presidency. Previous administrations generally accepted substantial overseas military expenditure as part of the cost of maintaining a US-led international order. Trump repeatedly returned to a simpler question: How much was the ally itself paying?
In 2019, his administration reportedly sought to raise Seoul’s annual contribution to the cost of American troops to nearly $5 billion, several times the existing amount. Yet South Korea was never a free rider. Pentagon spending connected with the US presence in Korea reached roughly $13.4 billion between 2016 and 2019, while Seoul provided about $5.8 billion in support. Under the current cost-sharing framework, South Korea’s contribution for 2026 is approximately 1.5 trillion won, or around $1.1 billion.
The Trump administration’s argument is that Washington provides a strategic asset whose value exceeds the direct cost of maintaining troops and that wealthy allies have enjoyed access to it too cheaply. The same logic applies to trade policy. During Trump’s first presidency, Washington attacked KORUS – the US-South Korea free trade agreement – as economically unfavorable, noting that the US goods trade deficit with South Korea had risen from $13.2 billion in 2011 to $23.1 billion in 2017.
Two principles had emerged during Trump’s first term. Allies should pay more for security and trade deficits should not be accepted merely because they occur between strategic partners. Earlier US policy could tolerate some economic imbalance as the price of geopolitical cohesion. Trump increasingly treats the economic and military dimensions of an alliance as parts of the same calculation.
Strategic dependence
South Korea’s dependence on Washington should still not be overestimated. Seoul possesses formidable conventional capabilities. Its defense expenditure reached approximately $47.8 billion in 2025, while its defense industry produces advanced artillery, tanks, aircraft, missiles, and naval systems and has become an important global exporter. The emerging American strategy increasingly assumes that South Korea should take primary responsibility for conventional deterrence against North Korea.
The most significant aspect of the dependency lies elsewhere. The Republic of Korea remains protected by US extended nuclear deterrence, backed by the full range of American capabilities, including nuclear weapons. Seoul participates in strategic consultations, but ultimate control over the nuclear component remains in American hands. Operational command arrangements in a major war create another layer of dependence.
The result is a peculiar balance. South Korea is powerful enough to handle many conventional threats, yet replacing American nuclear guarantees would require a profound strategic shift and might reopen the politically explosive question of acquiring an independent nuclear arsenal. This gives Washington leverage that cannot be measured only through troop numbers.
Economic ties create another asymmetry. In 2025, South Korean exports reached a record $709.4 billion, of which about $122.9 billion went to the US. America absorbed roughly 17 percent of all South Korean exports and remained the country’s second-largest foreign market. Dependence is the greatest in sectors such as automobiles, semiconductors and automotive components.
Bilateral goods trade in 2025 reached approximately $194 billion. US exports to South Korea stood near $68.8 billion, while imports reached about $125.2 billion, leaving Washington with a deficit of roughly $56.4 billion. Traditional economic analysis can treat this deficit as one element of a wider relationship involving investment, technology and industrial integration. Trump sees it more transactionally. If a country depends on American security and benefits from access to the American market, Washington can demand measurable concessions in return.
One strategic account
During Trump’s second presidency, this approach has become more systematic. Trade, investment and defense are increasingly treated as elements of one strategic negotiation. South Korea has agreed to investment commitments worth approximately $350 billion, including around $150 billion connected with American shipbuilding. In return, Washington moderated some of the tariff pressure that had threatened Korean exports.
At the same time, Seoul has faced expectations that it will increase defense spending, purchase more American weapons and provide greater support for the US military presence. South Korea has committed itself to moving defense expenditure towards 3.5 percent of GDP and purchasing roughly $25 billion of American military equipment by 2030.
Tariffs, defense expenditure, arms purchases, and investment in American industry are increasingly placed on the same political balance sheet. Access to the US market is tied to investment, while reliance on American protection brings pressure to spend more on defense and buy American weapons.
The dispute over Iran shows how far this approach can extend. South Korea imports almost all of its energy resources. Before the latest crisis, around 70% of its crude oil and roughly 20% of its liquefied natural gas came from the Middle East, much of it dependent on the Strait of Hormuz. The disruption cause by the Iran war threatened South Korean industry and growth.
Yet economic exposure did not translate into a willingness to participate militarily in American operations against Iran. Seoul sought alternative supplies and measures to stabilize domestic markets but remained reluctant to become directly involved in a distant conflict. This appears to have irritated Trump precisely because the refusal contradicted his understanding of reciprocity.
From Washington’s perspective, the US has guaranteed South Korean security for decades, and when America asked for assistance in another strategically important region, Seoul hesitated despite suffering economically from the crisis itself. Trump’s subsequent criticism of joint exercises is a statement that military protection is not an unconditional feature of the alliance, but an asset whose political value must be matched by tangible support.
A new American model
South Korea is part of a larger transformation in American strategy. The US is not returning to classical isolationism. It continues to maintain global military capabilities, confront China in the Indo-Pacific, preserve nuclear alliances, and intervene when vital interests are perceived to be at stake. What is changing is Washington’s willingness to bear a disproportionate share of the everyday cost of the international order.
The emerging priority is the protection of the US and the strengthening of the Western Hemisphere, followed by the containment of China and preservation of American technological, industrial and military superiority. Allies in Europe, Asia, and the Middle East are increasingly expected to assume greater responsibility for regional security as Washington recognizes that its resources are not unlimited.
The US remains the most powerful individual state, but the period of virtually uncontested predominance has ended. China has accumulated enormous industrial, technological, and military capabilities, Russia continues to impose security costs on Western Europe, and maintaining commitments across several theatres demands enormous resources. Trump’s answer is therefore not retreat but an attempt to make American power cheaper to maintain.
There is a historical analogy with the Second World War, although it should not be pushed too far. More than sixteen million Americans served in the armed forces, yet the US industrial heartland escaped the destruction experienced by Europe and much of Asia, while wartime production massively expanded national capacity. America emerged dramatically stronger relative to other major powers.
There is no clear evidence that the Trump administration is consciously attempting to reproduce that scenario by encouraging conflicts elsewhere. A more defensible interpretation is that its policy follows a similar logic of relative power. Washington wants allies to carry more of the expense of regional defense, foreign companies to invest more heavily in the US and strategic industries to return to American territory, while partners purchase American weapons and contribute to US industrial renewal.
South Korea is wealthy enough to be asked to pay more, militarily capable enough to assume additional responsibility, and economically integrated enough with the US for tariff pressure to hurt. At the same time, it remains dependent enough on American strategic guarantees that it cannot easily disregard Washington’s demands. This makes Seoul an almost ideal test case for Trump’s new alliance policy.
The ultimate risk is that America’s alliance network has itself been a foundation of US power. States accepted American military leadership and financial influence partly because protection was regarded as predictable. If it increasingly becomes a conditional service whose price changes with trade balances or support for US operations, governments such as South Korea’s will have stronger incentives to seek strategic autonomy.
Trump may make the alliance system less expensive while also making it less American politically. A more autonomous South Korea could reduce Washington’s burden but become less willing to align automatically with US preferences.
For the moment, however, access to the American market increasingly comes with demands for investment and concessions, while American security guarantees increasingly come with demands for greater defense spending and political support. South Korea has not been granted an exception.
Trump’s decision to reduce joint military exercises reflects a deeper reassessment of America’s role in a changing world, in which Washington appears determined not to abandon global leadership but to make it more selective, less expensive and more economically rewarding. Whether that strategy preserves American primacy or encourages even close allies to seek greater independence may become one of the defining questions of the emerging international order.

Social media on trial as $200bn case against Facebook and Instagram begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:27:09 UTC
03:27:09 KST

In 1994, more than 40 US states came together to sue one of the most powerful industries on Earth: big tobacco.
The suits brought together diverse claims centred on tobacco companies’ misleading advertising and contribution to a mounting public health crisis. They ended in a negotiated settlement with the US government, in which the companies agreed to pay more than any industry ever, and the states agreed to drop a large portion of their claims.
Thirty years later, smoking is on the rise in the developing world, the companies involved remain profitable and the global tobacco market is worth nearly $1tn.
On Tuesday a major trial against Meta began, in which 29 states have brought the claim that the parent of Facebook and Instagram designed a deliberately addictive product and targeted it at children.
That trial follows a bellwether case earlier this year, in which a Los Angeles jury found the social media company – and YouTube, its co-defendant – liable for deliberately designing an addictive product that had deleterious effects on the mental health of a single young claimant.
That case, which awarded the claimant $6m, opened the door for this and other litigation. At about the same time, Meta was forced to pay a total of $942m in a separate trial in New Mexico. The New Mexico case focused on whether the company was aware of – and took measures to prevent – child sexual exploitation on its platforms.
This next wave of litigation will focus less on child exploitation, and more on the fundamental design of Meta’s platform: the algorithm that underlies which content it shows to users and how. So, how far could the litigation go?
Kate Winick, an analyst at Forrester, said the trial was “potentially the end of social media as we know it” and, while a ruling against Meta would not permanently kill the industry, it could “significantly reduce usage over the long term”.
The figures that Meta and other social media companies could stand to pay are immense. The attorneys general are seeking $200bn in damages, the amount of revenue the company takes in a year. Meta has said in a court filing that they could amount to $1.4tn, which is just short of the company’s market capitalisation. The judge in the case has called the company’s estimation “unreasonable”.
Perhaps a more realistic risk for the company is the potential for permanent changes to the way its social networks operate, which are the engine for its entire business. Meta is essentially a digital advertising company. Its recommender algorithm ranks posts in users’ feeds and fuels engagement in part by showing people posts that are likely to inflame emotion and keep them hooked.
It is this algorithm that American attorneys general seem interested in changing, because it is this “dopamine-manipulating” feature – in the words of the AGs’ lawsuit – that makes social media addictive. Changes to this algorithm may not alter how Facebook advertises, said Steven Murdoch, a professor at University College London. But it could reduce engagement, which could gravely reduce its opportunity to advertise to users.
But all this depends on how big of a swing a US jury – and US regulators – are willing to take at the platform. Discontent is brewing worldwide about Meta and its business; the EU also wants the company to modify its “addictive design”.
“There’s a plausible path” for global changes to the algorithm, said Murdoch. “But whether it’s devastating or not – I’m not convinced the things that are plausibly going to be asked for are going to be devastating for the company.”
Take the recent case of Google. US regulators sued the search company in 2023 in a landmark antitrust case – which could have ended with authorities breaking up the company, perhaps forcing it to sell Chrome, the most popular web browser in the world. Google lost the case but that extreme penalty wasn’t imposed. Despite finding that the company had engaged in monopolistic practices, it got away with what critics called a “slap on the wrist” and remains a juggernaut.
“I don’t think anyone really wants to destroy Facebook. It’s a valuable company and there would be so many bad outcomes,” said Murdoch.
A Meta spokesperson said: “The state AGs may call this a landmark case but their limited claims are unsubstantiated and their financial demands are vastly disproportionate.
“Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout. We stand by our record of creating strong protections for teens, and look forward to making our case in court.”
Or take the case of big tobacco. The US government sought $289bn from major tobacco companies – including Philip Morris – in one of its landmark cases, which was prosecuted under a US anti-racketeering statute. Philip Morris and its co-defendants lost the case.
But in the course of proceedings, the government’s original monetary demand was modified to less than 5% of the original amount – $14bn, to be paid over 10 years. Philip Morris continued doing business, although it and other tobacco companies were forced to put out statements about the harms of smoking, and change how they marketed their products in the US.
Thirty years later, although smoking continues its long-term decline in the developed world, Philip Morris’s revenues are at roughly $40bn a year – less than they were 20 years ago, but not by much. They have been steadily increasing for the past four years.
