Manz forecasts growth alongside industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:59 UTC
01:45:59 KST

Manz Taiwan Ltd (亞智科技), which specializes in panel-level packaging equipment manufacturing, yesterday said the semiconductor ecosystem has developed rapidly in Taiwan, boosting its business outlook.
The company supplies electrochemical deposition (ECD) equipment used in panel-level packaging, including chip-on-panel-on-substrate (CoPoS) and fan-out panel-level packaging (FOPLP) with square panel sizes ranging from 310x310mm and 510x510mm to 700x700mm.
That places Manz as the third company in the world — after Applied Materials Inc and Lam Research Corp — capable of supplying such equipment used in panel-level packaging production.
Photo: CNA
About half of the 50 ECD machines it has sold so far are for 700x700mm in panel size, but the 310x310mm equipment has been gaining popularity, the company said.
“As AI [artificial intelligence] chips become larger in terms of reticle size, production and cost efficiency become increasingly vital, pushing the shift to panel-level packaging,” Manz president Robert Lin (林峻生) said at a news conference in Taipei.
CoPoS is considered a successor to chip-on-wafer-on-substrate technology, which is used in packaging for Nvidia Corp’s AI chips produced by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), as a larger square panel offers better cost efficiency versus a 12-inch circular wafer.
A 310x310mm rectangular panel can boost production by 50 percent compared with a 12-inch circular one in advanced packaging, Lin said.
The CoPoS technology is mainly used to produce AI chips, while FOPLP is for the production of power management chips, radio frequency chips, microcontrollers or chips used in low orbit satellites, Manz said.
As localization is a growing trend for Taiwan’s advanced packaging industry, half of the company’s customers are from Taiwan, Lin said.
The company also exported equipment to the US, Japan, China and Malaysia, he said.
Manz, which previously focused on plastic circuit board and flat panel equipment manufacturing, entered the semiconductor industry 12 years ago by collaborating with chip packager and tester Siliconware Precision Industries Co (矽品精密).
The company aims to debut on the Taipei Exchange’s Emerging Stock Board in June next year and list its shares on the Taiwan Stock Exchange in 2028. Employees hold a 30 percent stake in the company after it signed an agreement with German parent company Manz AG and became an independent entity through management buyout last year.

For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.
EDITORIAL CARTOON

Taiwanese who do not support the ruling party should not dismiss the warnings as fearmongering or propaganda. Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:56 UTC
01:45:56 KST

Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) yesterday said higher natural gas prices caused by the Middle East conflict could increase its fuel costs by more than NT$120 billion (US$3.76 billion) this year.
The estimated cost increase comes as CPC Corp, Taiwan (台灣中油) has raised natural gas prices for power generators aggressively this year, with hikes of about 50 percent in April and May and another hike of 10 percent this month, Taipower vice president Tsai Chih-meng (蔡志孟) said during a news conference in Taipei.
Taipower’s data showed that the average purchasing price of natural gas in the first seven months of this year stood at NT$16.2910 per cubic meter, up from the average of NT$13.8013 per cubic meter last year.
Photo: Lin Jing-hua, Taipei Times
Every NT$1 increase in natural gas per cubic meter adds about NT$25 billion to Taipower’s annual fuel costs, company data showed.
If natural gas prices remain at this month’s level through the end of this year, Taipower’s fuel costs could rise by an additional NT$15 billion a month, pushing the full-year increase above NT$120 billion, Tsai said.
The state-run utility’s fuel costs in the first half of the year increased by more than NT$42 billion from pre-war levels, Taipower spokesperson Huang Mei-lien (黃美蓮) said.
Taipower posted a first-half loss of NT$25.7 billion, bringing accumulated losses to NT$376.4 billion, she said, adding that the utility needs the government’s support to improve its finances and stabilize electricity prices for households and industry.
Taipower plans to submit its fuel and operating cost data to a government-convened electricity price review committee next month, which would decide whether electricity rates should be adjusted in October, Huang said.
Separately, Taipower plans to spend NT$5 billion over the next two years to replace aging underground power cables in 18 districts across the six special municipalities, as growing urban electricity demand increases the risk of equipment failures, Taipower vice president Chen Ming-shu (陳銘樹) said.
Underground cable replacement brings major challenges, including limited underground space, cable damage from frequent public construction works, and construction constraints due to narrow roads, excavation bans and permit requirements, Taipower said.
While replacing aging cables, Taipower would build new conduits and backup lines in stages to reduce disruptions during construction and strengthen grid resilience, it said.
For long-term urban grid planning, Taipower is promoting shared utility conduits, with about 130 projects under way nationwide to ease future expansion and maintenance of underground infrastructure, the company said.

Japan yesterday underlined that security cooperation with the US and South Korea was “critical” for the region’s stability, after US President Donald Trump alarmed allies by scaling back military drills with Seoul while hailing his ties with Pyongyang.
Trump on Sunday abruptly announced that he had ordered the Pentagon to scale back “inappropriate and hostile” military drills with South Korea.
The following day he insisted he was making the situation “much safer” through his ties with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, whom he met three times in his first term, but has yet to encounter since his return to the White House.
Photo: EPA
While praising the leader of nuclear-armed North Korea, he rebuked key ally Seoul for failing to help Washington fight Iran — a war Trump says is aimed at stopping Tehran from getting an atomic bomb.
Pressed about whether Kim had responded to his messages, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office: “Yeah, he has.”
Trump said “it’s very positive” when asked what stage the conversations with Kim were at, but provided no further details.
He then doubled down on his praise for Kim, saying their ties reduced tensions.
“Kim Jong-un has always treated me with great respect,” Trump said. “I understand him. He understands me.”
The 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises with South Korea are designed to prepare for a possible war with North Korea, which decries the drills as dress rehearsals for an invasion.
Japanese Minister of Defense Shinjiro Koizumi strongly supported joint security cooperation with key defense backer Washington and neighbor Seoul.
“As Japan faces the most severe and complicated security environment in the post-war [World War II] era, the cooperation among Japan, the United States and South Korea is critical to the peace and stability of the region,” Koizumi told journalists during a visit to Australia.
His Australian counterpart, Richard Marles, said Canberra was “very concerned about North Korea’s nuclear program as well as its missile program, and we have consistently made that point.”
South Korean officials have said the exercises had begun as planned and that they hoped the personal chemistry between Trump and Kim would bring them back to talks.
The South Korean Presidential Office yesterday said the drills did not reflect “any intention to attack North Korea or escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula.”
However, its Ministry of Unification — responsible for relations with the North — said it could not confirm whether communications between Kim and Trump had taken place.
“While communication channels between the two sides exist, we cannot verify the specific content of the exchanges,” a spokesperson said.
Trump on Monday again called into question US support for South Korea and NATO allies that have refused to contribute to the Iran war.
“Wait a minute. We have 39,000 soldiers over there, guarding you from Kim Jong-un, your next-door neighbor, and you’re not going to help us on a very easy military operation in Iran. That’s strange,” Trump said in the Oval Office. “We can’t go around and protect all of these countries, especially when they’re not there to help us.”
North Korea has not responded publicly, although it has previously voiced anger at the regular joint maneuvers that take place in the South.

Detroit Tigers infielder Lee Hao- yu on Monday set the record for the most hits by a Taiwanese player in an MLB season after getting three hits in an 8-5 win over the Pittsburgh Pirates.
Lee entered the series opener tied with Yu Chang, who recorded 54 hits for the Cleveland Guardians in 2021.
Starting at second base and batting sixth, Lee surpassed Chang in his first plate appearance, grounding an RBI single to right field off Pirates starter Carmen Mlodzinski to give Detroit a 2-0 lead.
Photo: AFP
The 23-year-old reached the milestone in his 80th game and 205th at-bat, faster than Chang, who played 89 games and had 237 at-bats in 2021.
Lee singled to left with one out in the third before drawing a walk from reliever Isaac Mattson in the fifth.
He walked again with the bases loaded against Yohan Ramirez in the sixth to force in Detroit’s sixth run, then added an infield single off Gregory Soto in the eighth for his first three-hit game in the majors.
Lee finished 3-for-3 with two walks and two RBIs, reaching base in all five of his plate appearances. His batting average rose to .275, while his season hit total increased to 57.
He is within reach of Chang’s nine-run single-season MLB home run record for Taiwanese players. Lee has six so far this season.

Taiwan’s Asia Elite Pickleball League (AEPL) on Monday announced that its inaugural five-team season would begin on Saturday next week in Taichung.

Photo: CNA
Chang said the league was created in response to the popularity of pickleball in Taiwan and elsewhere in Asia in the past few years.
The AEPL aims to provide high-quality, competitive professional matches, he said.
At the event, Johnny Chang, CEO of the Taoyuan Taiwan Beer Leopards in the Taiwan Professional Basketball League, spoke about forming a pickleball team within the Leopards organization.
Johnny Chang said he had selected Willy Chung as captain of the Taoyuan Leopards pickleball team.

Johnny Chang added that Chung was given responsibility and free rein to select the team’s players.
On Leopards’ roster is 15-year-old Chiu Tsi-en, the youngest player in the AEPL.
Chiu said that she has been playing pickleball for almost a year after being introduced to the sport by a classmate.
She said she gradually fell in love with the game and plans to continue playing pickleball and tennis — which she has been playing for six years already.
Chiu said the two sports are similar in that both require strategic thinking, with the main differences being court size and whether the sports are played outdoors or indoors.

For next year’s season, the AEPL said that it aims to attract teams from places such as Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong and Macau.

EDITORIAL: The ‘beggars’ in the legislature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:52 UTC
01:45:52 KST

“The first step in liquidating a people is to erase its memory... Destroy its books, its culture, its history. Then have somebody write new books, manufacture a new culture, invent a new history. Before long the nation will begin to forget what it is and what it was. The world around it will forget even faster,” Milan Kundera wrote in The Book of Laughter and Forgetting, quoting Czech historian Milan Hubl.
The opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan on Friday passed the long-delayed third reading of this fiscal year’s general budget, with overall cuts of NT$48 billion (US$1.5 billion) across agencies, along with spending freezes. About NT$1 billion was slashed from the Ministry of Culture’s budget, with the NT$47.38 million publicity budget cut to zero. Funding for Public Television Service (PTS) was reduced by NT$21.85 million and NT$200 million was frozen until a new chairman is appointed, while the budget for TaiwanPlus, the PTS-affiliated English-language channel, was cut by NT$200 million.
It is the second consecutive year that the ministry’s publicity budget has been slashed entirely, while funding for PTS was again reduced and frozen. Last year, when Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) legislators proposed cutting PTS’ budget, and other arts and culture grants, KMT Legislator Chen Yu-jen (陳玉珍) called arts and cultural workers “beggars” who rely on government subsidies to survive, urging them to “throw away their bowl.” The KMT’s animosity toward the cultural industry is clear.
Minister of Culture Li Yuan (李遠) has criticized the opposition parties’ “horrendous plan,” saying that the KMT and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) are using the cuts to silence Taiwan’s voice, “destroying the nation by eliminating its culture.” KMT and TPP lawmakers dismissed Li’s remarks as “fearmongering.”
Culture is a nation’s soul. A nation survives on a sense of collective identity shared by people who imagine that they have a relationship with other members of the community across time. The concept of “imagination” does not make a community less real.
As Indian-American anthropologist Arjun Appadurai said, imagination is a collective, lived tool people use to construct everyday identity. A nation is constructed instead of being defined physically or materially by geographical borders. The social construction indicates a process of construction and manifestation of a collective through the spread of common ideas.
As Benedict Anderson put it, in an imagined community, mass media play an important role. Television, newspapers, books and works of art, using a common language, serve not just as channels for public communication, but also the foundation for spiritual and political life — they bring people together. People gain national consciousness and a deep sense of comradeship. In that process, scattered individuals can unite and take collective action to pursue what they consider best for their community.
That is what the opposition parties fear — Taiwanese realizing who they really are. It is why the KMT and the TPP are trying to erase the nation’s culture and memory. News is the first draft of history. All forms of art connect people by representing and exploring their existential state, fostering mutual understanding and empathy. If cultural development is stifled, people will begin to forget who they are and who they once were. A nation’s collective existence would vanish.
KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) earlier this month said that Taiwan has never been a country. That kind of self-denial is undoubtedly a brazen insult to the nation and those who fought for its freedom, democracy and survival with blood and tears. Who does she think she is to say those words on behalf of the nation?
People are still fighting for Taiwan’s dignity on the world stage. Taiwanese artists and curators participating in the Gwangju Biennale, a two-month art festival that South Korea is hosting from next month, stood up against the organizer for arbitrarily renaming the Taiwan pavilion and removing “Taiwan” from the poster. They issued a joint statement, titled “The censored Taiwan Pavilion,” to condemn the organizer’s political censorship.
At a turbulent time when Taiwan faces transnational oppression, Taiwanese must not consent to or engage in any denial of their own existence.
Those who should really “throw away their bowl” to stop begging are the traitors who live on taxpayers’ money, but collaborate with the enemy to betray their country.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

The new rules, which take effect on Sept. 15, expand the power of authorities to restrict travel on national, industrial and technological security grounds, question travelers about their reasons for leaving and inspect electronic data. Taiwanese who do not support the ruling party should not dismiss the warnings as fearmongering or propaganda. UN condemns Israeli strikes against Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:51 UTC
01:45:51 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
UN Secretary-General spokesman Stephane Dujarric on Tuesday condemned Israeli airstrikes against Syria, describing them as a “very worrying violation” of Syria’s territorial integrity and airspace.
Responding to a question about Israeli strikes against the Abu al-Duhur Military Airbase in Idlib province, Dujarric said the UN had seen the attacks and asked for them to stop.
“It's yet another very worrying violation of the territorial integrity and airspace of Syria. These airstrikes should stop, and we stand against them,” Dujarric told reporters at a UN briefing.
Turning to the occupied Palestinian territory, Dujarric said the UN was “deeply alarmed” by the deteriorating security and humanitarian situation in the occupied West Bank.
He said Israeli forces had instructed 10 Palestinian families in Tulkarm’s Jabal Al Nasr neighborhood to leave their homes temporarily during military activities near the adjacent Nur Shams refugee camp.
He added that Israeli military bulldozers damaged water and sewage networks while excavating a road and Palestinian land. Families returned after Israeli forces withdrew and municipal crews repaired the infrastructure.
In the Gaza Strip, Dujarric said humanitarian needs remained “immense,” while UN partners continued aid deliveries and other operations where possible. He cited a UN assessment that found only 3% of Gaza’s cropland remains accessible and undamaged.
He also expressed concern about continued Israeli airstrikes, shelling, gunfire and naval fire affecting civilians, primarily west of the so-called yellow line, where most of Gaza’s population is concentrated.

Indonesian neutrality and Beijing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:50 UTC
01:45:50 KST

On Wednesday last week an Indonesian frigate conducted exercises with the Chinese navy east of Taiwan, in waters Beijing has repeatedly used to demonstrate its capacity to encircle and blockade the nation.
What was Indonesia doing there? The answer comes readily from Jakarta. Indonesia was practising bebas aktif, or “free and active” foreign policy, working with competing powers while reserving the right to belong to none of them.
Indonesian personnel joined the US-led RIMPAC exercises in Hawaii this year, military contacts with Russia have continued, and the KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai met the Chinese frigate Honghe while sailing home from Russian exercises off Vladivostok. The engagements appear to offset one another and the freedom to engage is presented as a measure of Jakarta’s successful foreign policy.
Taipei would be mistaken to treat one exercise as a declaration of allegiance.
Taiwan’s objection concerns the waters rather than the partner, as Chinese military and coast guard activity east of Taiwan has increased in the past few years, and featured simulated missile strikes and blockades.
The Mainland Affairs Council called the most recent drill “political manipulation” intended to suggest that Beijing holds jurisdiction there, while the Ministry of Foreign Affairs asked Jakarta for clarification.
The Indonesian Navy said that it was a routine passing exercise, not warlike in nature, and that it reflected the country’s free and active foreign policy.
The explanation is credible and China’s Eastern Theater Command said the encounter was the first time its navy had exercised with a foreign navy in those waters. Beijing does not need Jakarta to endorse its sovereignty claims or say anything about unification. It gains something more modest and useful, a Chinese presence near Taiwan that no longer appears exclusively Chinese.
The two readings are not mutually exclusive. Indonesia can exercise its autonomy while China derives political value from the drills. Jakarta does not have to align with Beijing for its nonalignment to serve a Chinese purpose.
This is where the usual language of “sides” becomes misleading. It treats foreign policy as a line, with Washington at one end and Beijing at the other.
Indonesia instead occupies a field of commitments that bind different institutions, reward different groups and operate over different periods. A naval exercise with the US, a nickel complex financed by Chinese capital and a Taiwanese investment portfolio coexist because they do not perform the same function. They cannot be added together and declared balanced. Indonesia’s relationship with China is embedded in an industrial strategy built on nickel processing and battery production.
Two Chinese groups, Tsingshan and Jiangsu Delong, hold shares in refineries accounting for more than 70 percent of national refining capacity, and the Morowali Industrial Park in Central Sulawesi, a designated national strategic project, employs more than 80,000 people. Capital on that scale is entangled with ministries, state-owned companies, local authorities and private conglomerates. Sovereign choice is part of why the relationship with Beijing stays open. So is the constituency it has built inside the Indonesian state.
Taiwan’s presence enters the state through narrower channels: trade and investment, Indonesian students and workers, and semiconductor cooperation. The New Southbound Policy was designed precisely for that and on its own terms it has worked.
However, Taiwan matters to Indonesian businesses, universities and workers, while China matters to the industrial policy through which the Indonesian government imagines the country’s economic ascent. These interests do not carry equal institutional weight, which is why Jakarta can welcome Taiwanese investment while remaining detached from Taiwan’s security concerns and see no contradiction.
Is this Indonesian duplicity or evidence that the New Southbound Policy has failed? Neither. It is a limit built into the kind of relationship Taiwan has created. Economic density does not become strategic influence through accumulation alone. That limit is not permanent, but removing it requires a different argument from the one Taipei usually makes.
A blockade or military crisis would reach Indonesia quickly: semiconductor shortages in its factories and higher costs at its ports, as well as pressure on energy and financial markets that would not stop at the boundary drawn by the “one China” policy. Those consequences are Indonesian rather than borrowed from Washington, yet they surface in regional debate only after the arguments about democracy and coercion.
Taiwan cannot turn ASEAN states into security partners resembling US treaty allies. What remains available is narrower: making disruption in the Taiwan Strait legible as material risk inside the Indonesian institutions that already price risk, port authorities and industrial associations among them.
Indonesia has not moved into China’s camp, just as Jakarta insists. The exercises nevertheless assisted Beijing’s effort to make its military presence around Taiwan appear ordinary, as Taipei feared.
Both are true because strategic autonomy describes who retains the right to choose, not the wider order reproduced by that choice.
There was no Indonesian allegiance to lose, only an Indonesian calculation that Taiwan’s security has never entered. Years of economic and social engagement have built density without building consequence. Beijing asks nothing more of Jakarta than this: that an Indonesian ship enter the right waters under the name of neutrality.
Aniello Iannone is a lecturer in Indonesian and Southeast Asian politics in the Department of Political Science and Government at Diponegoro University in Indonesia. His research focuses on ASEAN regionalism, Indonesian politics and the international political economy of Southeast Asia.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. US Navy transits of Taiwan Strait drop under Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:46 UTC
01:45:46 KST

US warships have transited the Taiwan Strait significantly less frequently during US President Donald Trump’s second term than during his first term, or during former US president Joe Biden’s time in office, the Heritage Foundation said in a study published on the US news Web site Breaking Defense on Friday last week.
Allen Zhang, a researcher in the foundation’s Asian Studies Center, and Charity Ihrman, a member of its Young Leaders Program, said in the study that publicly available records project 14 transits for the entirely of Trump’s second term at the current rate.
The projected figure for transits during Trump’s second term would be a 50 percent decline from 28 transits under his first term and a 56 percent decline from 32 transits under Biden, the authors said.
Photo: AP
The article, titled “America is sailing through the Taiwan Strait less. Does it matter?” used data collated from official statements of US and foreign governments, news reports, US Navy statements and the Taiwan Security Monitor, they said.
US “transits project American military presence at a time when Chinese warships and aircraft have become routine fixtures around Taiwan,” they said.
“If America’s presence in one of the world’s most contested waterways is quietly fading, the strategic ramifications could be serious,” the authors wrote.
“China has declared the Strait to be its territorial waters, but virtually no other country, including the United States, recognizes that claim as lawful or legitimate,” Zhang and Ihrman wrote.
Moreover, China has been ratcheting up military pressure in the Taiwan Strait, conducting activities ranging from provocative military exercises, passages in unilaterally declared zones and undersea cable cutting, they said.
“On any given day, roughly five or six warships surround Taiwan at all times,” they said.
China’s “daily activity around the island, near weekly joint combat patrols and response exercises conducted during periods of heightened political tensions” have all set yearly highs, they said, citing the US Department of Defense’s 2025 China Military Report.
Some observers have argued that US military transits should be assessed qualitatively rather than quantitatively, and that the Trump administration might have been conducting “silent transits” not announced by official channels, the authors said.
“While true, naval transits play an outsized role in signaling non-recognition of unlawful Chinese maritime claims precisely because of their visibility and regular occurrence,” Zhang and Ihrman said.
While silent transits are preferable to no transits at all, publicly acknowledged naval transits signal to allies and the international community that the US opposes China’s illegal claims and “gray zone” operations in the strait, they said.
“A sudden drop in them can degrade perceptions of American priorities and credibility in both friendly and hostile capitals,” they said.
The Pentagon “should return to the standard tempo of publicly announced routine transits established across the last two administrations,” they added.

Japanese melons blocked at border over excessive pesticide residues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:45 UTC
01:45:45 KST

Two shipments of fresh melons imported from Japan were recently intercepted at the border after testing positive for excessive pesticide residues, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said yesterday.
The melons in the two shipments were found to contain 0.02 parts per million (ppm) and 0.04 ppm of tetraniliprole, respectively, above the 0.01 ppm limit for the pesticide, according to the FDA.
A total of 332 kilograms of melons were ordered returned or destroyed.
Photo: Chung Li-hua, Taipei Times
Liu Fang-ming (劉芳銘), director of the FDA’s Northern Taiwan Management Center, said the two shipments were imported by the same company, Chuan Yong Fruit Co, which has had three shipments fail inspection over the past six months.
Given that record, future melons imported by the New Taipei-based company will be subject to 100 percent batch- by-batch inspections, Liu said, noting that the border inspection sampling rate for Japanese melons in general will remain at 20-50 percent through Sept. 17.
The FDA also announced on Tuesday several other products that recently failed safety inspections, including frozen peeled shrimp from Vietnam, tamarind sauce from Thailand, and nemacystus, a type of algae, from Japan.
Regarding the nemacystus imported by Yanran International Co, the FDA said the product was found to contain 4.2 milligrams per kilogram of inorganic arsenic, exceeding the legal limit of 1 mg per kg for algae under Taiwan’s Sanitation Standards for Contaminants and Toxins in Foods.
Inorganic arsenic is a toxic heavy metal that can cause various health issues.
The 3 kg shipment was ordered to be returned or destroyed, said the FDA, which will also subject Yanran to stricter border inspections, with 20-50 percent of its shipments to be inspected.

Innolux confidently predicts huge growth in shipments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:43 UTC
01:45:43 KST

Innolux Corp (群創) yesterday said its fan-out panel-level packaging (FOPLP) business is expected to see double-digit percentage growth in shipments this year, along with a positive outlook for next year, company chairman Jim Hung (洪進揚) said during an earnings conference.
The company’s FOPLP monthly shipments have reached more than 40 million units, Hung said.
The shipments of its first chip-first FOPLP project have increased more than tenfold since its test run, he said.
Photo: CNA
To expand the FOPLP business, Innolux plans to invest in advanced packaging, including the “RDL-first” technology and the “Through-Glass-Via (TGV)” technology, with its partners due to technology complexity and heavy spending, Hung said.
The commercialization of the TGV technology is likely in 2028 or beyond, he said, declining to disclose the timeline of new investments and names of Innolux’s partners.
The company looks at FOPLP as a major revenue source, Hung said, adding that the combined FOPLP and glass core substrate market is forecast to reach US$8 billion in 2030, thanks to the artificial intelligence boom.
FOPLP uses large rectangular carriers to lower costs, while glass core substrates utilize TGV to offer superior electrical and thermal performance over organic substrates.
Innolux adopts chip-first technology at a less advanced 3.5-generation plant in Tainan to package chips used in ground receivers, or specialized front-end antenna modules, for a US-based low Earth orbit satellite company.
Despite intensifying competition from local rivals, Innolux remains confident in its technological edge, Hung said.
Unlike the commoditized flat-panel display industry, entering the semiconductor supply chain requires deep customer engagement and extensive, customized process steps, he added.
“It is not as simple as you think. It is not like buying milk at a convenience store. You cannot replace the existing [supplier] with a new one just because it delivers lower costs,” Hung said. “Trust matters more.”
Hung’s remarks came as the company updated its financial results, with non-display and commercial displays, which deliver high margins, contributing about 55 percent to its first-half revenue of NT$130.35 billion (US$4.08 billion).
On the company’s core display business, Innolux expects surges in memory prices to dampen customers demand for notebook computers over the next six to nine months and affect shipments of its computer panel business, Hung said.
The impact on TV and monitor panel businesses would be milder as the company focuses on niche and premium market segments, he said.
Net profit in the second quarter soared 177.91 percent to NT$4.53 billion from NT$1.63 billion a year earlier. The company reported a loss of NT$761 million in the first quarter. Earnings per share rose to NT$0.57, up from NT$0.2 in the first quarter and minus --NT$0.1 in the second quarter last year. Gross margin improved to 14.6 percent from 14.4 percent in the prior quarter and 8.4 percent a year ago.
Local rival AUO Corp (友達) last month said that it planned to tap into the advanced packaging industry, particularly RDL and TGV segments, after its board of directors approved an additional capital investment of NT$8.6 billion in advanced packaging and other technologies.
Innolux made inroads into advanced packaging in 2019 through licensing the FOPLP technology from the government-funded Industrial Technology Research Institute.

Investment going out from Taiwan greatly increases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:43 UTC
01:45:43 KST

Outbound investments approved by Taiwan’s government surged more than 200 percent from the year before during the January to July period largely due to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) spending heavily overseas, the Ministry of Economic Affairs reported on Monday.
The Department of Investment Review approved US$61.26 billion of outbound investment in 395 applications during the first seven months of this year, up 208.43 percent from a year earlier, the ministry said in a statement.
Significant growth came after TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, secured approval to raise capital investments by US$20 billion in its US subsidiary TSMC Arizona Corp, which runs the company’s wafer fab operations in Arizona, and to invest US$30 billion in the Cayman Islands-registered TSMC Global Ltd, which is in charge of the chipmaker’s financial investments worldwide, the ministry said.
Photo: Liao Chia-ning, Taipei Times
The growth also reflected a decision by DRAM chip supplier Nanya Technology Corp (南亞科技) to raise investments by US$1 billion in its Cayman Islands-incorporated subsidiary and another plan by power management solution provider Lite-On Technology Corp (光寶科技) to invest US$919 million into its US unit, the ministry added.
Meanwhile, foreign direct investment (FDI) into Taiwan over the same period rose 78.13 percent from a year earlier to US$13.92 billion, largely due to Singapore-registered Micron Semiconductor Asia Pte Ltd, a subsidiary of Micron Technology Ltd, obtaining the green light to invest US$7.45 billion in Taiwan, the ministry said.
In addition, Netherlands-based MIT Hai Long Wind Power BV secured approval to invest US$1.05 billion in Taiwan for green power development, it said.
The ministry said Singapore ranked as the largest foreign investor in Taiwan from January to last month, investing US$8.66 billion, or 62.23 percent of FDI, ahead of the Netherlands with US$1.22 billion, the British Virgin Islands and the Cayman Islands with US$1.19 billion combined, the US with US$781 million and the UK with US$630 million.
The ministry added that the local electronics component industry was the largest destination for these foreign investors, accounting for 56.27 percent of total approved FDI, before the financial and insurance industry, which made up 16.9 percent of total.
For China-bound investments, Taiwanese investors secured approval for US$572 million of applications during the seven-month period, down 25.87 percent from a year earlier, the ministry said.
The Chinese retail and wholesale, electronics component, financial and insurance businesses were the top three destinations for Taiwanese investors during that time, it said.
Over the same period, the government approved 12 applications filed by Chinese investors wishing to invest US$4.07 million in Taiwan, diving 95.97 percent from a year earlier, it added.

16:45:42 UTC
01:45:42 KST

CTBC Financial Holding Co (中信金控) expects earnings momentum to remain strong in coming quarters as robust banking and insurance businesses, overseas operations and capital-market activity underpin growth, executives said yesterday.
The company expects Taiwan’s strong economic growth and corporate profitability to sustain demand for banking, wealth management and insurance services, while overseas operations are becoming an increasingly important source of earnings, CTBC Financial president Rachael Kao (高麗雪) said at an earnings conference in Taipei.
CTBC Financial’s net profit rose 10 percent to a record NT$39.54 billion (US$1.24 billion) in the first half of this year, as its banking arm, CTBC Commercial Bank Co (中信銀行), posted strong growth across core businesses, with net interest income rising 24 percent from a year earlier and fee income increasing 26 percent. Wealth-management revenue surged 44 percent as buoyant capital markets lifted demand for investment products.
Photo: Lee Chin-hui, Taipei Times
CTBC Bank expects lending to remain a key growth driver in the second half of the year, after loans increased NT$500 billion in the first half, exceeding the increase recorded for all of last year.
A planned shift to an internal ratings-based approach for credit risk could give the bank additional room to expand, as CTBC Bank expects to adopt the approach as early as the fourth quarter, which could release as much as NT$100 billion in capital, based on a simulation using risk-weighted assets at the end of June, CTBC Financial acting chief financial officer Megan Hsu (徐旻傾) said.
The bank plans to deploy the released capital over five years, or about NT$20 billion annually, creating additional capacity for lending and other businesses, Hsu said.
CTBC Bank’s overseas pretax profit rose 4 percent to NT$13 billion in the first half, accounting for more than 30 percent of profit, while that in Southeast Asia and North America jumped 46 percent and 37 percent respectively, helped by Taiwanese companies expanding production facilities overseas, it said.
The bank expects overseas operations to continue contributing more than 30 percent of earnings as it expands in North America, Southeast Asia and Japan. Its Fukuoka office and Phoenix, Arizona, and Texas operations are scheduled to open next quarter, while a Los Angeles branch is planned for the first half of next year, CTBC Bank said.
CTBC Financial is seeking to strengthen its capital position and dividend capacity, Kao said.
The company’s statutory surplus reserve is expected to exceed paid-in capital by the end of this year, which could allow it to move beyond the legal limit on cash dividends from the reserve, she said.

Top-tier journals cover NTUH’s bacteria screening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:42 UTC
01:45:42 KST

A two-decade research effort by National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH) to develop a two-in-one screening program for Helicobacter pylori, bacteria that increase the risk of colorectal and stomach cancer, has been featured in leading international medical journals and could potentially be adopted by some eastern European and South American countries.
The study was published in the Journal of the American Medical Association last month, while guidelines developed in collaboration with experts from 20 countries were published in the New England Journal of Medicine.
NTUH Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology attending physician Lee Yi-chia (李宜家) yesterday said the hospital has long promoted the policy of screening for H pylori to prevent colorectal cancer, a policy it has helped implement in communities from Lienchiang County (Matsu) to rural townships in Taiwan proper.
Photo: CNA
H pylori also increases the risk of people being diagnosed with stomach cancer sixfold, but can be treated, Lee said.
While the number of people diagnosed with stomach cancer is lower than those diagnosed with colorectal cancer, the former is deadlier, she said.
While both types of cancer have mature methodologies for diagnoses, the method developed by the hospital allowed doctors to screen for colorectal and stomach cancers via bloody stool, she said.
The hospital’s screening method was financially sound and practical, she said, adding that a global guideline was developed in collaboration with 35 doctors from 20 countries and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).
The method has also been introduced in Bhutan, and might soon be introduced in eastern Europe, she said.
Some South American countries have expressed interest in introducing the method, but efforts were slow due to political instability in the region, she said, adding that other countries, including the US, are slowly introducing the method.
The US, Japan, South Korea, and China have a higher prevalence rate of H pylori, so they could consider adopting the method, she said.
Health Promotion Agency Deputy Director-general Lin Li-ju (林莉如) said the gastric cancer screening program was initially piloted in indigenous communities, with Lee’s team conducting H pylori testing.
The program was gradually expanded to the general population in 2024 and became the sixth cancer type covered by the government-funded cancer screening program this year, she said.
As of last month, 600,000 people had undergone screening, with a positivity rate of 22.4 percent, she added.

Japan to test hypersonic missiles in Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:42 UTC
01:45:42 KST

Japan will conduct tests of hypersonic missiles and other projectiles on Australian soil, the two countries’ defense ministers said yesterday as they deepened military cooperation, including with a codeveloped laser system.
Australian Minister for Defence Richard Marles said alongside his Japanese counterpart, Shinjiro Koizumi, in Canberra that the deal would see a “better and enhanced arrangement between Australia and Japan for Japan’s use of our missile ranges over the course of the next decade.”
“We have spoken previously about Australia being able to provide strategic depth to Japan across a range of areas, but one of them is the use of our ranges,” Marles said.
Photo: AFP
Koizumi welcomed the measure.
“If the Japan Self-Defense Forces are able to conduct test launches of standoff missiles, such as hypersonic missiles, in Australia, it would be a groundbreaking development,” he said. “We will therefore accelerate discussions toward realizing this objective.”
Australia and Japan have increased defense cooperation as they watch a rising China, mindful also of US demands that its regional allies spend more on their militaries.
The two countries agreed last year to one of Japan’s biggest defense export deals since World War II, in which Australia would pay A$10 billion (US$7.11 billion) over the next 10 years to acquire a fleet of stealth frigates.
Marles and Koizumi yesterday said they would cooperate on a new defense cooperation project called Boobook, named for an Australian owl that sees in the dark, featuring a codeveloped laser system to detect potential threats.
The project includes “enhanced laser capability that can be put on land combat platforms as well as littoral platforms,” Marles said.

Photo: AFP
“They are clear on our structures and their roles within the team, so we’re just making sure they are physically ready to go,” he added.

“We’re going to see how it is [with Ratima] over the next 48 hours. Obviously, we’re a little bit thin at No. 9 as it is, so getting Noah in will be good,” he said. “We expect Cam to be ready to go on the weekend. We’ve still got Kyle Preston if Cortez is no good.”

‘Tree Spirit Pagoda’ honors thousands felled in Alishan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:37 UTC
01:45:37 KST

Memorials honoring animal spirits are common in Taiwan during Ghost Month, but Alishan (阿里山) is home to the nation’s only “Tree Spirit Pagoda,” dedicated to the spirits of 100,000 trees felled during the Japanese colonial period, the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Chiayi Branch said.
Ghost Month, which falls in the seventh month of the lunar calendar, started on Thursday last week. In Taiwan, it is customary to hold Pudu (普渡) on the 15th day of the Ghost Month to honor the dead.
In 1934, the then-Japanese colonial government held a “Tree Spirit Festival” in Alishan to comfort the spirits of the 77 people who died during logging, including Japanese technicians and Taiwanese workers, as well as the spirits of 100,000 tree chopped down, the branch said.
Photo courtesy of the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Chiayi Branch
The Tree Spirit Festival was subsequently held twice a year, in March and September, with most participants being government officials from the forestry office and foremen of logging, timber-transport and railway work crews in the forest, it said.
Most were Japanese, with about 30 people taking part, it said.
The Chiayi County Culture and Tourism Bureau on Sunday said the festival continued to be held after World War II, but the Shinto rituals were replaced with Taoist rituals.
The ceremony also shifted from an expression of gratitude to a Pudu ritual that focused on sacrificial offerings, it said.
Participants were mostly civil servants and work-crew foremen, while on rare occasions, tourists and locals attended, the bureau said.
The number of participants fell with the decline in logging, and in 1969, the festival was officially suspended as logging operations had been discontinued, it said.
It is commonly believed that the Tree Spirit Pagoda was set up by Japanese on advice from Taiwanese or indigenous people to prevent the felled trees from taking revenge, the branch said.
However, research showed that such facilities do not exist in folk religious traditions elsewhere in Taiwan, it said.
The branch in 2014 commissioned Taipei National University of the Arts associate professor Huang Shih-chuan (黃士娟) to investigate the origin of the pagoda.
Huang’s research showed that the pagoda is related to Japan’s tradition of setting up “plant pagodas,” the branch said, adding that people in Japan would have monks set up plant pagodas at key spots for logging and transportation to make offerings.
It is a religious shrine where people pray for the safety of forestry workers, Huang said.
Plant pagodas are memorials for trees, established for reasons and circumstances similar to those behind the Tree Spirit Pagoda in Alishan, she said.
The Tree Spirit Pagoda comprises three sections, the National Cultural Heritage Database Web site says.
The first is a five-tiered set of concentric circular steps at ground level, with each step approximately 16.5cm high and 30cm wide, it says.
The second section is a stone-built cylindrical stele, consisting of a vertical cylindrical body, a platform at the base and three short semicircular pillars, it says.
The semicircular pillars stand along the outer edge of the cylinder, evenly dividing its circumference, it says, adding that the central gap features a curved bronze plaque inscribed vertically with the three Chinese characters meaning “Tree Spirit Pagoda.”
The third section of the tower had a bronze spire at the top, which the site says was stolen.

Taipei Dome to host WBSC games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:36 UTC
01:45:36 KST

The Taipei Dome is to host the opening and second rounds of the World Baseball Softball Confederation (WBSC) Premier12 in November next year, organizers announced on Monday as they unveiled a new 16-team format for the tournament.
At a news conference in Taipei announcing the hosting rights, organizers said Group A of the opening round would be played from Nov. 8 to 12, followed by the second round from Nov. 13 to 15. The four-team Super Round will be held in Japan.
The announcement provided more details after the Chinese Taipei Baseball Association (CTBA) said on Friday that Taiwan had secured hosting rights for part of the tournament.
Photo: CNA
Taiwan secured its place in the Premier12 by finishing second in the WBSC men’s baseball world rankings at the end of last year and would play in Group A at home.
WBSC executive director Michael Schmidt said the tournament is expanding from 12 to 16 teams for the first time, with four groups of four competing in round-robin opening-round play at four locations.
The top two teams from each opening-round group would advance, with the qualifiers from groups A and B forming one second-round group and those from groups C and D forming the other.
Each team would face only the two opponents they did not play in the opening round, with the top two teams from each second-round group advancing to the Super Round.
The other three teams in Group A and the hosts of Groups B, C and D will be announced later.
The field includes the top 12 teams in last year’s year-end rankings and four teams advancing from two qualifiers, Schmidt said.
The 12 automatic qualifiers are Japan, Taiwan, the US, South Korea, Venezuela, Mexico, Puerto Rico, Panama, the Netherlands, Cuba, Australia and the Dominican Republic.
Spain, Colombia, Italy and Germany are contesting the qualifier in Barcelona from Oct. 9 to 11, while China, Czechia, Great Britain and Nicaragua are playing in Zhongshan, China, from Nov. 26 to 28. The top two teams from each qualifier will advance to the Premier12.
CTBA president Jeffrey Koo Jr said securing hosting rights would not only showcase Taiwan to the world and improve Taiwan’s chances of winning.
“With the fans behind us, our chances of winning the championship are very good,” Koo said.
He talked about Taiwan’s triumph at the 2024 Premier12, where they punched out Japan 4-0 in the final at Tokyo Dome to claim their first title at a major senior-level international baseball tournament.
Next year’s Premier12 will be the tournament’s fourth edition. Taiwan has hosted games in every edition since the inaugural tournament in 2015.
The CTBA on Friday announced that Taiwan had secured hosting rights for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Baseball Final Qualifier, which is scheduled for March 2028 and features six teams competing for the final Olympic berth.
Organizers did not announce a specific competition format, date or venue for the qualifier on Monday.
The US, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela secured Olympic berths through this year’s World Baseball Classic. Next year’s Premier12 would award one berth each to the highest-finishing eligible teams from Asia and Europe/Oceania.
Taiwan can qualify directly by finishing ahead of the other eligible Asian teams at the Premier12. If they fail to do so, they would have another opportunity by winning the final qualifier.

Fishing community being eaten up by ocean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:35 UTC
01:45:35 KST

The beach shrinks every year in Ayetoro, in southern Nigeria, and what is left is peppered with the remains of homes swallowed by the ocean — some years ago, some just months prior.
“We are walking on people’s houses,” Thompson Akingboye, 35, said, moving along a narrow strip of sand only accessible by boat.
Nicknamed “The Happy Place,” Ayetoro — home to about 10,000 people — was founded in 1947 by a group of communist-inspired Christians seeking to create a society based on the communal sharing of assets.
Photo: AFP
However, its days seem numbered, as the community becomes one of Nigeria’s most visible victims of coastal erosion. Families whose homes are destroyed are constantly rebuilding further inland, only for the water to strike them again.
Coastal erosion in Ayetoro has steadily increased since the early 2000s. The story is the same in 19 other communities in Ilaje district. Aided by climate change, the Atlantic Ocean is encroaching and sweeping away everything in its path.
The town’s coastline receded by an average of 15m every year between 1987 and 2022 according to a study by spatial planning specialist Barnabas Ogirima James.
In 2024, the journal Scientific Reports estimated that the current rate of sea-level rise along west Africa’s Gulf of Guinea is approximately 3.9mm per year — about 10.5 percent higher than the global average.
“I took this photo 14 years ago. Today, if you stand in the exact spot where I was, you’ll see there are no buildings left,” said Oluwambe Ojagbohunmi, the traditional king of Ayetoro, outside his palace.
In old photographs, a telecom tower stands surrounded by houses. The tower is still there — now encircled by water and the remnants of swallowed-up buildings.
“My palace once had 100 rooms. Only about a dozen remain,” said the king, dressed in a white tunic.
His bedroom is now in part of the building closest to the ocean. At night, the sound of waves crashing against the walls disturbs his sleep.
“This is our land. Where can we go? It’s complicated,” he said.
In April, a storm saw the sea levels swell, trapping the palace occupants indoors for a week.
“I’ve become a refugee in my own community. Since losing my father’s house in 2019 — swallowed and destroyed by the ocean — the only thing I managed to save was my university degree certificate,” said Akingboye Thompson, a fisherman and personal assistant to the king.
Some families have moved more than three times, he added, standing in Ayetoro’s streets, which are littered with plastic waste brought in by waves.
The houses are built from wood and iron sheets, often connected by raised wooden walkways.
Part of the problem lies in what happens on land, said Oluwasegun Babatunde Esan, a landscape architecture researcher at the University of Lagos who collaborates with Harvard University.
In rapidly urbanizing Nigeria, floodplains, swamps and coastal areas that take in ocean surges or floodwater are often cleared out for human settlement — worsening erosion along the 850km coastline.
“There is growing demand for land, whether for housing or industrial activities,” Esan said — but it needs to be strictly regulated.
He also recommended developing more natural barriers by planting mangroves and coconut palms.
Ayetoro occasionally receives relief materials from government agencies and non-governmental organizations, although the community considers it insufficient.
The community’s sole health center has been lost to the waves.
“Sometimes the water reaches window level, yet we have to keep working. We help women give birth under these conditions. We have no choice,” said Omomiye Oluwaseun, a 26-year-old healthcare worker.
With brackish waters constantly inundating the community, “people suffer from high blood pressure and water-borne diseases like typhoid and diarrhea, because of the water they use,” Oluwaseun said. “The sea has already contaminated the water supply, yet they use it for cooking because it is the only water available to them.”
The ocean has also snatched away the stability that is supposed to come with each school year, said teacher Sunday Akinjoye, 45.
“Schools have been relocated several times, just like their homes. It takes a psychological toll on them. Their ability to concentrate on their studies drops drastically,” he said.
No matter what they do, the mighty Atlantic continues to gain ground.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) yesterday thanked the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (IPAC) and like-minded countries for expressing concern over the Ugandan government denying entry to Taiwanese.
Department of European Affairs Director-General Eric Huang (黃鈞耀) said the IPAC yesterday issued a statement expressing deep concern over the recent action of “Ugandan immigration authorities in forcing Taiwanese travelers to present People’s Republic of China (PRC) passports as a condition of entry.”
“This represents a clear act of coerced discrimination, wherein a sovereign third nation appears to have succumbed to pressure to enforce the political demands of the PRC,” he quoted the statement as saying.
Photo: CNA
The statement says that “arbitrarily rejecting valid Taiwanese passports and compelling travelers to claim documentation from a power that does not govern them violates fundamental principles of non-discrimination embedded in international civil aviation standards, including International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) guidelines.”
“The MOFA welcomes and thanks the IPAC and like-minded partners, for taking tangible actions to speak out for Taiwan and expressing their grave concerns over Taiwanese being denied entry at Uganda’s airport,” Huang said.
He urged the Ugandan government to “face the fact that the Republic of China (ROC), Taiwan has independent sovereignty, and that neither the ROC and nor the PRC is subordinate to the other.”
The ministry also urged Uganda not to impose inappropriate entry restrictions due to political factors, as they could have a negative effect on bilateral exchanges and mutual interests.
Separately, the ministry yesterday condemned and rejected Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s recent pro-China remarks, saying that they seriously threaten regional peace and stability.
Ibrahim in an interview on Sunday endorsed a “one China” policy and suggested that Taiwan is a separatist province of China.
Malaysia is a democracy, and Anwar has long portrayed himself as a champion of democracy and human rights, it said, adding that he should uphold universal values such as democracy, freedom, human rights and the rule of law, while respecting and safeguarding the will of the people.
Any political maneuvering that echoes calls to unilaterally change the “status quo” across the Taiwan Strait through threats or the use of force not only undermines the commitment of Taiwanese to safeguard a “democratic Taiwan,” but also severely damages political trust between Taiwan and Malaysia, it said.
Taiwan and Malaysia have long maintained close economic and trade ties, it said, adding that given the growing links between national sovereignty and economic security, Anwar’s one-sided support for China could undermine Taiwanese businesses’ confidence in investing in Malaysia.

Taiwanese pride in the successes of the nation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
16:45:32 UTC
01:45:32 KST

As Taiwan’s economy continues to grow, President William Lai (賴清德) on Monday announced that the government would distribute a NT$10,000 cash handout to all citizens next year. The announcement prompted me to reflect deeply: As Taiwanese, we should be proud of our nation.
Much of Taiwan’s latest economic growth has been driven by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. From chips and servers to other electronic components, Taiwanese companies occupy a crucial position in the global AI supply chain.
As the rest of the world is vying for AI computing power and advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity, Taiwan is not merely watching from the sidelines; rather, it is at the heart of the technological revolution.
The government’s announcement that some of the gains from the economic growth would be returned to the public is about more than simply handing out NT$10,000 in cash. It is a message to all Taiwanese that the benefits of the AI boom do not belong solely to technology companies. Instead, it should be shared by all citizens.
Compare the situation to what is happening in China, Not long ago, China was seen as one of the most promising economies in the world. Foreign investors rushed to enter the market and young people believed that if they worked hard, they would find decent jobs.
However, China today is facing a sluggish property market, weak consumer spending, excess production capacity and high rates of youth unemployment. Neijuan (內卷, “involution”) has become a common term among young Chinese to describe the feeling of diminishing returns.
Taiwan does not have a market as large as China’s, a population of 1.4 billion, or vast amounts of land and resources. Yet, through the efforts of generation after generation, Taiwan has established an indispensable position in the global tech industry.
More importantly, we live in a society in which people enjoy the right to openly criticize the government, vote freely and elect leaders. Economic growth is not a favor bestowed on citizens by the government — it is a result of the collective efforts of society.
I am proud to be Taiwanese. In this era when AI is rapidly altering the world, we have chosen not to “lie flat,” but instead use our efforts and expertise to establish ourselves at the very heart of the global tech industry. That is what Taiwan should be most proud of. The NT$10,000 cash handout next year might be spent quickly, but if we can turn this AI boom into opportunities for the next generation, and transform economic growth into higher wages, better education and a better quality of life, then what the payment truly represents would be much more than cash. It would be something we could proudly tell the next generation: This small nation has, time and again, relied on its own strength to establish a place in the world.
I am fortunate to be Taiwanese.
Lin Cheng-wu is a junior-high school teacher.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Photo: Bloomberg
“If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them,” Trump told Fox News journalist Trey Yingst, referring to ongoing talks between Oman and Iran on control of the strait, which lies between the two countries.
Oman, a US ally in the Gulf, has not publicly commented on Trump’s remarks.
Tehran and Muscat have been discussing for weeks future navigation arrangements through the route, and the Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs earlier on Monday said that the two sides were working on a joint declaration.
Iran’s coast flanks the northern side of Hormuz, while Oman sits on the south.
Their talks follow the collapse of a Pakistan-mediated US-Iran interim deal aimed at keeping Hormuz open to traffic.
Renewed fighting over the waterway quickly derailed the arrangement, spreading the conflict to Gulf allies and commercial shipping across the Middle East.
Trump also said that Iran should “put up the white flag of surrender,” according to Yingst’s account of the interview on X.
The US president has repeatedly insisted that the strait is under US control despite traffic remaining heavily throttled.
On Friday, he said he would declare the Strait of Hormuz part of US territory, prompting Iran to retort that the energy chokepoint “will remain Iranian.”
Before the war erupted on Feb. 28, the strait was considered an open, international waterway carrying roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies as well as other commodities.
Tehran has used its effective control over the strait as leverage against the US-led attempts to destroy its military and force it to abandon a controversial nuclear power program.
Trump insisted that he was in no hurry to reach a deal despite the unpopularity of the war and opposition Democrats seeking to take control of US Congress from the Republicans in the midterm elections.
He told Yingst that there is a direct back-channel between his administration and officials of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard.
“They’re good poker players, but they’re dying,” he was quoted as saying.
The rhetoric came as allies continued pressing for negotiations.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan discussed the conflict in a phone call with Trump, the Turkish state’s Anadolu Agency reported.
Erdogan stressed the importance of “fully utilizing diplomacy” to ease tensions between Iran and the US, and said Ankara would continue supporting efforts to secure peace.
The Strait of Hormuz remains the central flashpoint in the conflict. The narrow passage links Gulf producers to international markets and its closure triggered a surge in oil prices earlier in the war, prompting warnings from major importing nations about supply disruptions.
As Iran restricts traffic in Hormuz, its Houthi allies in Yemen have declared a parallel maritime blockade on Saudi ports in the Red Sea, the kingdom’s only alternative maritime route for oil exports.
Iran wants to control access to the strait and charge transit fees, powers it did not exercise before the war and which Washington strongly opposes.
The closure of Hormuz has driven up fuel prices for US consumers, creating another political challenge for Trump as November’s midterm elections approach.

A student yesterday livestreamed himself shooting another schoolmate dead before taking his own life at a high school in the Philippines, authorities said.
The school shooting, the country’s second in as many months, took place at Ateneo de Zamboanga University, a Catholic private institution in western Mindanao.
“What we know so far is that [the shooter] went to the classroom of our known victim. He shot the victim, and after doing that, he went up to the fifth floor and shot himself,” regional police spokeswoman Shella Chang said.
Photo: EPA
In a separate statement, Philippine Secretary of the Interior and Local Government Victor Remulla confirmed the ninth-grade suspect had livestreamed the incident on social media.
The alleged shooter’s Facebook account has since been disabled.
In the video, which was circulated by local media, the barrel of a gun can be seen moving down a hallway in the style of a first-person shooter video game before being pointed into a classroom and fired. Children in school uniforms are then seen screaming and rushing for an exit. It was not immediately clear how many were injured.
National police are now trying to “establish the motive behind the shooting, determine the ownership and source of the firearm used, and find out how it was brought inside the school campus,” the Philippine Department of the Interior and Local Government said in a statement.
Police have yet to release the ages of the shooter or victim.
Ateneo de Zamboanga president Father Guillrey Andal, confirming the two fatalities, said the school was “deeply saddened” by the shooting and was cooperating with the investigation.
“We are in process of working with the police for us to be able to identify them, so that we can communicate first with their loved ones,” he told reporters outside the school, acknowledging the incident had caused “deep concern and worry.”
“Prior to this, our security team had even been preparing a simulation exercise, precisely because we understand the value to everyone — our students, our personnel — of safety,” he said.
School shootings are rare in the Philippines, but three teenaged students were killed and 20 others wounded in an attack at a school in the central Philippines in June. Ateneo de Zamboanga last month became one of many schools across the country to conduct active shooter drills in the wake of that tragedy.
Legal gun ownership is tightly regulated in the Southeast Asian country, but a large black market exists for firearms.
