University of Granada: basic advice on how to deal with an earthquake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:26:01 UTC
21:26:01 KST

The Andalusian University Institute of Geophysics and Seismic Disaster Prevention is offering a set of basic recommendations on how to respond to these events.
Prevention, as in the case of natural disasters such as the wildfires that ravage the Iberian Peninsula every summer, is crucial when it comes to saving lives in areas of high seismic intensity such as the Granada basin, in the central sector of the Eastern Betics.
This is confirmed by the institute at the University of Granada dedicated to analysing this phenomenon, which has published a series of recommendations for both before and after an earthquake is experienced such as the one that has just struck the province of Granada.
Experts recommend having a plan in place in advance so as not to improvise when a hypothetical seismic event occurs. Homes should be stocked with first-aid kits, torches, radios and batteries for them, and you should know where to shut off basic utilities, since a damaged power supply could cause further damage to buildings. Any heavy object that is not properly anchored to the wall could pose a danger.
During the quake, you must remain calm: statistically it will be an event without sufficient magnitude to pose a threat to life. This is important because many accidents occur when people try to leave or enter buildings during earthquakes. You should wait for the shaking to stop before considering moving from where you are.
Indoors, the most important thing is to protect your head: seek shelter under tables or chairs if the shaking is strong, for example. You must stay away from objects, walls or windows that could injure you while the event is taking place.
If you are outside, move away from buildings and do not enter any: there may be further aftershocks that end up damaging them completely. If you are driving when the shaking occurs, stop where traffic conditions allow and stay inside the vehicle. If you are in an area near the coast, head for a distant, elevated place and pay attention to messages from the authorities: a tsunami warning could be issued.
When the phenomenon is over, if you consider it safer to leave the building, never use the lift and take the stairs instead. The condition of cracks in the structure will indicate the seriousness of what has happened. If they are more than 3 millimetres wide and follow a diagonal or stepped pattern, the structure is at risk; do not go inside, or leave it as soon as you can, calmly.
Once you have moved away from the immediate vicinity and are in an area where rubble or debris cannot fall on you, you must assess whether the building remains vertical or is leaning in relation to adjacent structures, whether the pavement in front of it shows damage, and the condition of nearby lamp posts.
Then examine the façade to check for possible cracks: the most dangerous are diagonal and between one and three millimetres wide. If they are less than one millimetre, the damage is generally minor and you may enter the building with caution.
You should not make calls that are not emergencies, so as not to overload telephone lines and leave someone who really needs them without service. If you hear someone trapped under the rubble, tell them to cover their mouth and nose to avoid inhaling dust and, as far as possible, to bang on a nearby object to indicate their position. If you see someone seriously injured but not trapped, you should not move them until the emergency services arrive.

Al Jazeera Untangles
Myanmar: The Architecture of Statelessness
How Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of citizenship, leading to mass expulsions and a genocide case at the ICJ.
The Rohingya of Myanmar have faced decades of discrimination and forced displacement, and a case alleging genocide now sits before the International Court of Justice.
This film describes how military regimes rewrote citizenship laws to exclude Rohingya from registers and used identity documents, checkpoints and travel permits to control movement. It also highlights how segregation, incitement and continuing waves of violence normalised their erasure from the community.
Focusing on the 2016-2017 “clearance operations”, the film documents village burnings, mass killings and the flight of hundreds of thousands of Rohingya to Bangladesh. Through survivor testimony and interviews with officials and legal experts, Myanmar: The Architecture of Statelessness examines whether these crimes meet the legal threshold for genocide, how Myanmar defends itself against the allegation and what is ultimately at stake when the court delivers its verdict.

Iran says Hormuz stays closed until US meets its demands
Iran has set out a series of conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, including the lifting of US sanctions and the release of frozen Iranian funds, a day after a deadline for Tehran and Washington to reach a final agreement expired without a deal.
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Tuesday that Tehran would not reopen the strategic waterway until Washington fulfilled commitments Iran says were included in a memorandum of understanding reached in June.
"The strait will not be opened unless America fulfils its commitments contained in the memorandums of understanding, including lifting the blockade, releasing frozen funds, lifting oil sanctions, ending threats and military operations on all fronts, and the other conditions America committed to," Ghalibaf said.
His remarks came a day after a 60-day deadline for Iran and the United States to reach a final agreement expired, leaving the two sides locked in a dispute over the waterway at the centre of the nearly six-month war.
Speaking during a virtual public session of parliament, Ghalibaf warned that Iran was "ready to inflict a greater defeat than the previous one on the enemy if it seeks to attack us".
He said Iran was acting under instructions from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, using both the "power of logic" and the "logic of power" to force what he called a "delusional America" to deliver what Tehran considers the rights of the Iranian people.
Ghalibaf also accused Iran's adversaries of shifting their focus towards economic pressure and attempts to exploit divisions inside the country after, he claimed, failing to defeat Tehran militarily or diplomatically.
"The enemy, in its new plan, seeks economic pressure and the destruction of the country's cohesion," he said.
He warned that any individual or institution that weakened national unity through its statements, conduct or decisions would be serving the enemy's objectives, whether intentionally or otherwise.
Ghalibaf said Iran had used the period created by the memorandum of understanding, including the easing of the blockade and the ceasefire, to strengthen its economic resilience and rebuild its defence capabilities.
He claimed Iranian authorities had information suggesting that their adversaries were looking for opportunities to foment unrest and combine it with military operations, including assassinations and separatist activity, alongside what he described as "cognitive warfare".
The parliament speaker also suggested Iran's adversaries could seek to exploit government measures intended to reduce petrol consumption.
While acknowledging that Iranians' economic grievances were legitimate and saying he respected political and social criticism, Ghalibaf argued that the country was at a moment that required unity.
Iran says Hormuz remains under its control
The deputy commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Major General Mostafa Izadi, separately underlined Tehran's position on the Strait of Hormuz, saying control of the waterway remained "entirely at the discretion of Iran's sons".
"The enemy does not know what to do," Izadi was quoted as saying by Iran's Fars news agency.
He described the strait as equivalent in strategic value to "nuclear power", pointing to its impact on global energy, agriculture and industry.
The comments reinforce Iran's insistence on retaining leverage over the waterway, which has emerged as the central obstacle to efforts to turn the ceasefire into a lasting settlement.
Araghchi says US failed to force Iranian surrender
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, meanwhile, said on Tuesday that US efforts to force Iran into "unconditional surrender" during the war had failed.
Araghchi said the US administration had entered the war seeking Iran's complete surrender, before subsequently pursuing regime change, the partition of the country and efforts to arm groups inside Iranian cities and western regions.
He said those efforts had also failed.
The United States, Araghchi claimed, "rushed" to seek negotiations shortly after the war began, despite initially demanding Tehran's unconditional surrender.
Iran initially rejected a ceasefire and continued fighting until the other side became convinced of the need to accept a truce and negotiate on Tehran's terms, he said.
Araghchi said the events would eventually be recorded "in detail in history", describing an exchange of multi-point proposals that culminated in an agreement based on an Iranian proposal for a ceasefire in April.
Months of negotiations followed, lasting longer than the war itself, before the two sides signed a memorandum of understanding on 18 June, he said.
Araghchi said foreign diplomats had told him that most of the memorandum's provisions favoured Iran, while only a small portion benefited the other side.
He claimed this was why the agreement began to be violated less than two weeks after it was signed, accusing Israel of being its most determined opponent and of seeking to prevent both its conclusion and implementation.
Monday marked the deadline for Iran and the United States to reach a final agreement under the Qatar- and Pakistan-mediated memorandum of understanding intended to bring the war to an end.
The agreement gave the two sides 60 days to negotiate a broader settlement covering issues including the future of Iran's nuclear programme and US sanctions on Tehran.
But the memorandum, which called for an immediate and permanent cessation of military operations on all fronts, quickly ran into difficulties as the two sides clashed over control of the Strait of Hormuz.

Russia summons Japanese envoy following Putin’s visit to disputed islands

Russia summons Japanese envoy following Putin’s visit to disputed islands
MOSCOW (AP) — Russia’s Foreign Ministry on Tuesday summoned the Japanese ambassador to protest Tokyo’s condemnation of President Vladimir Putin’s trip to the Kuril Islands, the Moscow-controlled Pacific archipelago that is claimed by both countries.
Last week, Putin visited Iturup, one of the four southernmost islands of the chain, which Japan calls the Northern Territories. The Soviet Union took them from Japan in the final days of World War II, and the dispute has kept the countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending their hostilities.
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Putin’s visit, his first to the islands, was “incompatible with the Japanese position on the Northern Territories” and was “absolutely unacceptable.” She said the visit was a further blow to already-strained ties between the two countries over Ukraine, and that Moscow should understand the consequences.
Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said Tokyo “strongly protests” Putin’s visit to Iturup, which Japan calls Etorofu, noting that “the Northern Territories, including Etorofu Island, are Japan’s inherent territory both historically and from the perspective of international law.”
On Tuesday, Russia’s Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin met with Japanese Ambassador Akira Muto to lodge a formal protest over the “anti-Russia” statements by Takaichi and Motegi.
“Russia’s sovereignty and jurisdiction over the southern Kuril Islands are absolutely unshakable,” Galuzin told Muto, according to the Foreign Ministry.
“These territories passed to our country as a result of World War II that was enshrined in the relevant agreements of the Allied Powers and the U.N. Charter,” the ministry said. “Any attempts by the Japanese side to directly or indirectly call this obvious reality into question are absolutely unacceptable and unlawful.”
Galuzin told the ambassador that in view of Tokyo’s adherence to Western sanctions against Russia and its support for Ukraine, “Moscow reserves the right to take appropriate countermeasures.”
The Japanese Embassy said in a statement that Muto, during his approximately 20-minute meeting with Galuzin, “appropriately explained the Japanese position on the Northern Territories and President Putin’s recent visit.”
It gave no other details, including how Muto responded to Galuzin’s comment on Russia’s territorial claim of the islands or if Japan is considering taking a retaliatory step, citing the sensitivity of the issue.
Decades of diplomatic efforts to negotiate a settlement haven’t produced any visible results. Moscow over the years has also bolstered its military presence on the Kurils in moves that appeared to underscore its firm stance in the dispute.
Speaking last week aboard a Russian warship taking part in the drills in the Pacific, Putin said Moscow previously “had developed constructive relations with a number of Japanese leaders, including the tragically deceased former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, who did much to bring Japan and Russia closer together, to align our positions.”
Japan imposed sanctions on Russia after it sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022 and “listed Russia as a source of primary threats,” a change in that constructive relationship, he added.
Russia remains ready “to cooperate with all its neighbors, including Japan and other states in the region,” Putin said.

SBU detains owner of network of companies that supplied Russia with materials for anti-drone nets
The SBU said this in a statement seen by Ukrinform.
The SBU uncovered the owners of a group of industrial companies based in the Kyiv region that supplied Russia's Investigative Committee with materials used to set up anti-drone protection, according to the statement.
The investigation found that the group consists of an extensive network of 39 Ukrainian companies engaged in the production of roofing and facade products.
According to investigators, the group's actual owners are a Ukrainian businessman and his son, who moved to Russia before the start of the full-scale invasion.
The younger suspect controls two more companies in Belgorod and Reutov, which effectively operate as branches of the suspects' Ukrainian business structure, the SBU said.
The investigation established that, under his management, both companies in Russia manufacture metal structures. One of the contracts carried out by these companies involves supplying anti-drone nets for the Russian Investigative Committee.
In addition, according to the SBU, the suspects have been actively financing Russia's armed aggression by paying taxes to the Russian budget and making direct investments in Russia's military-industrial complex.
The SBU said the suspects first transferred profits from their Ukrainian businesses to offshore companies controlled by them and registered to nominal owners. They then carried out foreign-currency transactions to the accounts of Russian companies under their control.
SBU officers documented the scheme and detained the senior suspect in Kyiv, while his son is hiding in Russia.
SBU investigators notified the detained man of suspicion under Part 1 of Article 111-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, concerning aiding an aggressor state.
The suspect is being held in custody without the right to bail. Authorities also plan to seize all of his accounts and property in Ukraine, including 30 apartments, 20 parking spaces and 29 vehicles of various makes.
The son's actions were also classified as aiding an aggressor state, and he was notified of suspicion in absentia.
As the suspect is currently in Russia, comprehensive measures are underway to bring him to justice.
In May 2026, law enforcement officers exposed a Kherson Regional Council deputy who, according to investigators, had organized agricultural business operations in the temporarily occupied part of the region in Russia's interests with the assistance of three businessmen.

Albares meets with British counterpart to strengthen bilateral relations
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
14:22:56 CEST
21:22:56 KST

The Minister for Foreign Affairs, the European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, welcomed his British counterpart, the new Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs, Edward Miliband, this Wednesday, at a time of renewed momentum in bilateral relations, the culmination of which has been the signing of the UK–European Union Treaty on Gibraltar, initialled on 14 July, and the removal of the fence.
“Our bilateral relations are very good, but the signing of the agreement on Gibraltar represents a historic opportunity to go further and deepen them. Furthermore, we have the Bilateral Strategic Framework signed in London in September 2025, and we wish to continue making progress on its implementation,” said Albares.
Climate emergency
During the meeting, the ministers signed a joint statement in which they recognised the need to prioritise the fight against the climate emergency in their foreign policy, in light of the record-breaking heatwaves and severe wildfires currently affecting Europe as a result of climate change.
They also agreed to jointly lead the green transition, convinced that decarbonisation, energy security and environmental protection are objectives that are inseparable from the prosperity and competitiveness of both countries’ economies.
The joint statement recognises that climate change is a global problem that must be addressed through effective multilateralism and respect for international law; it emphasises the need to adopt effective measures and to mobilise sustainable funding commensurate with the scale of the challenge we face.
Furthermore, Albares and Miliband have signed a cooperation agreement on gender equality to eradicate violence against women and girls, advance the Women, Peace and Security Agenda, and increase the presence of women in decision-making processes, particularly in the field of diplomacy.
Strategic relationship
Spain enjoys a privileged relationship with the United Kingdom, not only in economic terms – as the main market for Spanish exports outside the EU and the second most important destination for our direct investment abroad –; the United Kingdom is the fourth-largest investor in Spain.
“The ties that bind us are much deeper: one million Spaniards and Britons live in both countries, and 19 million British tourists visited Spain in 2025, making it the leading source market for tourists to our country. Spain and the UK are the two best-connected countries in the world by air, with around 400 daily flights in both directions,” Minister Albares pointed out.
Scientists, sportspeople, tourists, students, businesspeople and artists travel constantly between the two countries, bringing the number of British visitors to Spain in 2025 to 50 million. Furthermore, Spain is home to the largest British resident community in Europe, and one of the largest in the world.
International agenda
Albares and Miliband also discussed relations between the UK and the European Union, how to strengthen them and how to further enhance cooperation between the two regions – something essential for continuing to make progress on mutual support in the political, economic and security spheres.
In this regard, the Spanish minister noted that the United Kingdom’s return to the Erasmus programme is excellent news for young European university students.
Other topics discussed included European defence and the conclusions of the recent NATO summit in Ankara, as well as the need to remain united in supporting Ukraine, a sovereign and democratic State that has been the victim of an illegal act of aggression. Spain supports the UK’s participation in the military financial aid package for Ukraine and hopes that negotiations on this matter will conclude soon.
Finally, they also discussed the worrying situation in the Middle East, where it is clear that there is no alternative to diplomacy. “We must continue to demand respect for international law, including the Law of the Sea. The Strait of Hormuz must be reopened in accordance with international law and without any tolls or charges. And, for free transit to be viable, there must be a stable ceasefire and a return to the negotiating table by all parties,” insisted Albares.

The US military awarded Raytheon, an RTX unit, a $22.9 billion contract to sharply increase Tomahawk missile production as Washington seeks to replenish depleted stocks of high-tech weapons, according to Reuters.

The agreement formalizes a framework deal signed between the US military and Raytheon in February and is part of the Trump administration’s broader effort to expand the US defense industrial base.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions during the Iran conflict, raising concerns over inventories of air defense and precision-guided weapons.
Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said the contract would help ensure the US military maintains sufficient missile supplies.

US pushes broader weapons production
The Raytheon contract is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to secure multi-year agreements with major US defense contractors. The longer contracts are intended to give companies greater confidence to invest in new manufacturing facilities and equipment.

Discord suspends livestreams in Brazil amid backlash over girl's suicide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:22:25 UTC
21:22:25 KST

Discord suspends livestreams in Brazil amid backlash over girl's suicide
Rio de Janeiro — Discord, the popular platform for gamers to communicate online, said Monday that it had suspended livestreams in Brazil after criticism that it failed to protect children and adolescents. The move came in the wake of a suicide case.
Brazil's government, under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and the country's Supreme Court have tried to regulate the use of the internet by minors, with mixed results so far, at a moment when countries, including Australia, Canada and Indonesia, are undertaking similar efforts.
The decision came after Brazil's national agency of data protection ordered the suspension last week. The U.S.-based company added that it was in conversations "to seek a solution that allows us to reestablish those resources for our users in Brazil."
"We remain committed to working with public policymakers in Brazil to help create an online experience that is safer for all, on Discord and across the internet," said the platform.
In July, an underage girl in the state of Mato Grosso do Sul was allegedly coerced by other users into committing suicide during a livestream on the platform, putting the company under increased scrutiny.
Brazil's first lady Rosângela Lula da Silva, known as Janja, said on Aug. 6 that the platform should be taken offline, citing the case.
"I can't accept seeing a 13-year-old girl self-harming live on the internet, on Discord, hanging herself and dying," said Janja at a ceremony in the capital, Brasilia, during which Lula signed a law that increases the punishment for those who commit sexual violence against children and adolescents.
Five teenagers were arrested in connection with the death, according to an Aug. 4 statement by Brazil's justice ministry.
"Livestreams have been repeatedly used to facilitate violence, harassment and the incitement of self-harm and suicide," the country's data protection agency said in a statement Wednesday.
The agency cited robust evidence that the company had not sufficiently prevented risks of exposure to content that "represent serious violations of the rights of children and adolescents within its service, especially inducement, incitement, instigation, or assistance to violence, self-harm, and suicide," it said.
Discord has more than 90 million active daily users worldwide, according to its website.
In a statement to The Associated Press Wednesday, Discord said groups or individuals who promote or encourage violence have no place on the platform. It denied that the July case was shown live.
The platform said it was committed to user safety and has dedicated teams working "to disrupt violent groups, remove violative content and take action against bad actors on our platform."
It added that it had investigated a private server where individuals involved in criminal activity are believed to have encouraged self-harm, and shut it down before the recent death of the 13-year-old.
In recent years, Discord has been cited in investigations and reports worldwide involving extreme violence, including threats or planning related to school attacks, the distribution of abusive material, grooming and coercion of minors, and the encouragement of self-harm and suicide.
The number of complaints involving Discord between January and July increased by 54% compared to the same period last year, according to data from Safernet Brazil, a nonprofit that defends human rights on the internet.
The case of the 13-year-old girl "is not an isolated episode, but the tragic outcome of a pattern that we have documented and denounced for years," Thiago Tavares, the organization's president, said in a statement on Aug. 11.
Tavares added that Brazil's digital law imposed "clear duties of prevention, risk mitigation, age verification and cooperation with the authorities" and that non-compliance must generate accountability.
But Thiago Ayub, director of technology at Sage Networks, a company specializing in network engineering, criticized the agency's decision, which he attributed largely to Janja's comment.
"The most immediate consequence is the migration of users that inappropriately and even criminally use the platform to another one which isn't under the spotlight," Ayub said. "In this way, the protection of children and adolescents diminishes instead of increasing.
Authorities say Philippines school shooting was livestreamed
Discord is not unique among the big American tech companies in facing scrutiny over violence and incitement to violence on its platforms.
Authorities in the Philippines said Tuesday that a student livestreamed himself on social media as he shot a classmate dead and then turned the gun on himself at a private Catholic high school in the western Mindanao region.
Interior secretary Victor Remulla confirmed the ninth-grade suspect had livestreamed the incident on social media, and the alleged shooter's Facebook account was later disabled.
The video, circulated by local media, shows the barrel of a gun moving down a hallway, in the style of a first-person shooter video game, before being pointed into a classroom and fired, according to the French news agency AFP. Children in school uniforms are then seen screaming and rushing for an exit.
"What we know so far is that (the shooter) went to the classroom of our known victim. He shot the victim, and after doing that, he went up to the fifth floor and shot himself," AFP cited regional police spokeswoman Shella Chang as saying.
Wider efforts to protect minors online
Brazil rolled out a law seeking to boost protection of minors online earlier this year. The law requires that minors under 16 link their social media accounts to a legal guardian to ensure supervision.
Digital services must also implement an effective age verification mechanism that goes beyond self-declaration that the user is over 18 to protect them from accessing inappropriate or prohibited material.
In February, Discord postponed its controversial age verification policy after receiving backlash from users with concerns about their privacy. It later said in a statement that it was nonetheless rolling out age assurance measures to comply with Brazilian law.
The Trump administration has accused Brazil of targeting American social-media companies and cited the issue among the reasons for imposing tariffs on Brazilian imports. The White House has also been critical of governments in Europe and elsewhere for implementing restrictions on social media firms.
Earlier this summer, the U.K. became the latest country to announce plans to ban children under 16 from using social media. Prime Minister Keir Starmer said the U.K. would go even further than other nations, by also blocking children from accessing "harmful functions," including livestreaming and the ability to communicate with strangers, and by extending the restrictions to gaming sites.
He said the ban would protect children from content that is "designed to be addictive."
Australia banned under-16s from social media in December 2025 — the first country to impose such a measure. But around 70% of parents polled by Australia's internet regulator in March said their children remained on the platforms, having found ways to bypass age-gating systems.
In 2024, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered the shutdown of X until the network owned by Elon Musk complied with orders to remove accounts spreading disinformation.

Ex-Reform MP: No one's collecting signatures for Land's presidential bid
MP Meelis Kiili says there is no organized push to gather signatures to nominate TalTech rector Tiit Land for president, despite efforts to rally support among independents.
Kiili, who left the coalition Reform Party recently, told ERR Tuesday he has signed in support of nominating Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) rector Tiit Land, but is not collecting signatures from others.
"There is no such campaign to collect signatures," he said, adding that he is no campaign leader either.
According to Kiili, independent MPs have discussed the candidates and will decide individually whether to back Land or Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise for president.
"What the Center Party and Isamaa decide is up to them," he added.
The Center Party announced later Tuesday afternoon that it would be backing Land's bid.
Fellow independent MP Tõnis Mölder, meanwhile, said Kiili, Kalev Stoicescu and Leo Kunnas are gathering signatures for Land and have approached both Isamaa and Center about supporting the rector's nomination.
"That would pave the way for Land to secure at least the 21 signatures he needs to be officially nominated for president," Mölder explained.
Combined with party defectors, opposition parties Isamaa and Center have 19 MPs in the Riigikogu.
Mölder said Kiili, Stoicescu and Kunnas are not individually lobbying lawmakers, leaving the decision on whom to support up to each MP.
Still on the fence
While Kiili confirmed that he and Kunnas have already signed Land's nomination, Mölder expects Stoicescu to sign soon as well, if he has not done so already.
So far, Mölder added, no other MPs have signed in support of Land.
He said he plans to discuss the candidates with fellow MPs Enn Eesmaa and Kersti Sarapuu before deciding whether and whom to support.
The Riigikogu will convene to elect the next president of Estonia on September 2, with candidates to be formally nominated August 21–24.
Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise confirmed Monday that she will run for president, and as of Tuesday has the backing of 63 of the Riigikogu's 101 MPs.
With enough signatures, TalTech rector Tiit Land could emerge as her rival.

British shipyards could build warships for America
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
13:20:58 BST
21:20:58 KST

President Trump has ordered the Pentagon to open American warship construction to foreign shipbuilders under a model that would allow the first two ships of a class to be built abroad, provided the builder establishes or buys a shipyard in the United States and builds everything after that on American soil, according to a presidential memorandum issued on 13 August.
The memorandum also directs the Secretary of War to produce a plan to strip the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System and the Advanced Weapons Elevators out of the aircraft carrier CVN-81 and replace them with steam catapults and hydraulic elevators, reverting to the arrangement used on the previous generation of carriers.
Addressed to the Secretary of War, the Director of the Office of Management and Budget and the National Security Adviser, the document states that the Navy “has experienced a series of shipbuilding setbacks stemming from overly complex designs and iterative design change procedures, which have resulted in cost growth, delays, and cancellations.” It says a lack of capacity and competition among shipbuilders has produced large backlogs across six major programmes and a commercial sector that is not globally competitive.
The Finland Model
The mechanism for bringing in foreign builders is described in the memorandum as the Finland Model, taking as its template a memorandum of understanding signed with Finland in October 2025 covering medium icebreaker construction. It can be applied to up to three ship classes.
Under the conditions set out, a foreign supplier must simultaneously build a new American shipyard or take ownership or a majority equity position in an existing one, and build all ships after the first two in the United States. It must hire and train an American workforce, license the proprietary shipbuilding techniques and technologies used at the parent yard to the American yards, and source an American supply chain for construction and maintenance.
Building warships in foreign yards is generally prohibited under United States law. The memorandum delegates to the Secretary of War the authority to make the national security determination that a contract qualifies for a waiver and to notify Congress of each determination, with no contract permitted until 30 days after Congress receives it.
A new frigate competition
Within 90 days the Secretary of War is to submit a plan for what the memorandum calls “a new competitive acquisition approach for surface combatants with sufficient inherent capabilities to perform anti-submarine warfare, surface warfare, and convoy escort duties”, explicitly allowing proposals based on the international procurement model.
That description covers the ground occupied by the British Type 26 and Type 31, both of which are already exported. BAE Systems has sold the Type 26 design to Australia, Canada and Norway, the last in a £10 billion deal signed in 2025, while Babcock’s Arrowhead 140, the parent design for the Type 31, has been selected by Poland and Indonesia. Both are mature designs in production, which is what the memorandum says it wants.
The insistence on design stability runs through the document. It states that the Navy “shall not impose iterative design changes upon the original mature parent designs” within the programmes concerned, and that no changes may be made without the approval of the Secretary of War in consultation with the Navy Secretary, OMB and the National Security Adviser.
The target of that instruction is not named, but the Constellation-class frigate offers the obvious precedent. Derived from the Italian FREMM design and intended as a low-risk buy of a proven ship, it accumulated so many American modifications that commonality with the parent design fell away, and the programme ran years late amid heavy criticism from the Government Accountability Office.
Yards and repair capacity
Within 120 days the department is to submit a plan to increase nuclear submarine and carrier readiness, including the establishment of a fifth public Navy yard. The United States currently operates four, at Portsmouth in Maine, Norfolk, Puget Sound and Pearl Harbor.
The plan is to address drydock capacity for the planned growth of the attack submarine fleet over the next two decades, with locations proximate to the Pacific Fleet including the continental United States, Alaska, Hawaii and American territories, and site options covering up to three new drydocks sized for every current and projected class of submarine. Public-private partnerships are named as a possible financing route.
A separate plan, due within 90 days, covers a Component Repair Center to receive new parts and refurbish old ones for the submarine repair industrial base, holding at least one ship set of spare equipment for the Los Angeles, Virginia, Seawolf, Ohio and Columbia classes.
Naval Sea Systems Command is also to be reviewed within 120 days, with recommendations for personnel, organisational and structural reform. The stated objectives include introducing results-based accountability for NAVSEA leadership measured by speed of delivery, reducing bureaucracy, eliminating competing priorities within the command, and preventing it from imposing redesigns on mature parent designs.
The memorandum builds on an executive order signed in April 2025 titled Restoring America’s Maritime Dominance. It notes that implementation is subject to the availability of appropriations, and creates no enforceable right or benefit.

How TIME and Statista Determined America's Top Venture Capital Firms of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:20:05 UTC
21:20:05 KST

TIME has published the second annual "America’s Top Venture Capital Firms” ranking, in partnership with Statista, the leading global provider of market and consumer data and rankings, to recognize 350 firms at the forefront of the U.S. venture capital landscape.
Methodology
This year, we further developed the model, building on last year's foundation while incorporating direct feedback from the venture capital community. Based on conversations with VC firms and industry experts on how the market defines success, we refined the methodology by expanding it from three to four pillars and placing a stronger focus on deal-level investment data—capturing a firm's ability to identify and back winning companies early, and to sustain that conviction over time, while also recognizing the hands-on work investors do beyond simply writing checks.
Eligibility
To be considered, a firm must be headquartered in the United States and, as a core part of its business model, raise third-party capital and deploy it as direct venture capital funding to companies and startups across various venture stages and sectors. Firms whose investment activities are exclusively or predominantly focused on growth equity, private equity, fund-of-funds, venture debt, or similar non-VC-focused strategies are not eligible.
The four pillars
- Fundraising Strength (30%) captures a firm's ability to consistently attract and grow investor capital over time. It was measured by analyzing total capital raised across one-, five-, and ten-year horizons complemented by fundraising momentum indicators to assess both the scale and trajectory of each firm’s fundraising activity. New in this edition: the ten-year horizon, added in response to market feedback that a single strong vintage shouldn't overshadow a sustained track record.
- Investment Capacity & Activity (20%) reflects the operational firepower a firm brings to bear and the pace at which it deploys it. It was evaluated using each firm's assets under management and available capital, alongside deal volume across one-, five-, and ten-year windows, capturing both the scale of its investment operations and the intensity of its current deployment activity. New in this edition: deal volume, so this dimension reflects not only the capital a firm holds, but the rate at which it actually puts that capital to work.
- Performance & Conviction (40%) assesses each firm's ability to identify and back winning companies early, and to sustain that conviction over time. Firms were scored first on the scale of outcomes achieved by their portfolio, with particular credit given to companies that went public or reached significant private valuations, and second on the frequency and consistency of follow-on investments, rewarding firms that continued backing portfolio companies across successive funding rounds. To distinguish quality from volume, earlier-stage entry into successful companies carries greater weight than late-stage participation. Additional metrics include exit volume and efficiency across time horizons, as well as benchmarked fund return rankings. New in this edition: this dimension was rebuilt entirely on deal-level data, tracing outcomes and follow-on behavior investment by investment—reflecting market and firm feedback that outcome-based, granular data is a fairer measure of performance than aggregate, firm-level figures.
- VC Leadership (10%) captures the degree to which a firm acts as an active, hands-on partner rather than a passive capital provider. It was measured by the frequency with which a firm took a leading role in investment rounds and secured board representation in its portfolio companies. This pillar is new this year, added because firms and founders told us that capital and activity metrics alone don't capture the hands-on value a lead investor brings to the table.
Data collection
Statista gathered and scrutinized data for over 3,000 firms through desk research, online application forms, and collaborations with data and market intelligence companies.
Final scoring formula
Final Score = 30% × Fundraising Strength + 20% × Investment Capacity & Activity + 40% × Performance & Conviction + 10% × VC Leadership The 350 firms with the highest scores were awarded as “America’s Top Venture Capital Firms 2026” by TIME and Statista.

Amir Latif Arain
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
A Sydney library has withdrawn a book critical of US media coverage of Israel’s war on Gaza from its shelves for “review” following multiple complaints, including one from a survivor of the 2025 Bondi Beach attack, local media reported Tuesday.
How to Sell a Genocide: The Media's Complicity in the Destruction of Gaza, by American writer Adam Johnson, was removed from Waverley Library, The Sydney Morning Herald reported, citing Waverley Council.
The library serves Bondi and surrounding suburbs in Sydney’s east, home to one of Australia’s largest Jewish communities and close to the site of the December 2025 terrorist attack.
“The book has been removed from library shelves for review, and council will further consider processes to ensure closer oversight of book selection,” a council spokesperson said on Tuesday.
Waverley Council said it had received multiple complaints about the book, which remains listed in the library’s catalogue and is still available to reserve.
The council, however, declined to answer questions about how many complaints it had received, the criteria used to remove books from its collection, when the review would be completed or whether its findings would be made public.
Published in April by long-established British publisher Pluto Press, the book argues that Israel’s war on Gaza could not have continued without the “active, sustained complicity” of the US media.
It also says major news outlets “systematically sanitised Israel’s war crimes, hid the US’s central role, and dehumanized the Palestinian people”.
Johnson said the complaints appeared to be largely focused on the use of the word “genocide” in the title.
“But ‘genocide’ is not my word, or my finding. The fact of genocide in Gaza is the overwhelming consensus of the human rights world, and it is a wholly mainstream opinion among those tasked with studying and determining such matters," Johnson was quoted in The Guardian Australia.
"That it makes some people upset is unfortunate, but reality is often upsetting. This particular reality is especially upsetting … to the parents of the over 20,000 children killed by Israel in Gaza since October 2023. Do Sydney officials plan on removing pro-Israel books from their libraries because it potentially upsets these community members?” he further said.

Bahrain lets 64 political prisoners return home temporarily
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:19:05 UTC
21:19:05 KST

Breadcrumb
Bahrain lets longtime political prisoners return home temporarily
Sixty-four prisoners, including long-term political detainees who have spent around 14 years behind bars, have been allowed to return to their families from Bahrain's Jau Prison, marking the first substantial release of political prisoners since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
But the homecoming is temporary.
The prisoners have been granted leave until Friday, when their families will be required to return them to the authorities before they are transferred to the next stage of Bahrain's Open Prisons Programme in Hamala, Sayed Ahmed Al-Wadaei, Director of Advocacy at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (BIRD), told The New Arab.
Some of those allowed home were underage when they were arrested around 14 years ago, Al-Wadaei said, making the brief reunions particularly significant for families who have spent more than a decade waiting for their return.
"This is not an unconditional release or a royal pardon," Al-Wadaei told The New Arab. "The Open Prisons Programme is a phased system through which prisoners serving lengthy sentences are gradually moved out of conventional prison conditions and eventually into the community under alternative sentencing arrangements and electronic monitoring."
Al-Wadaei initially announced the releases in a series of posts on X, saying that 110 prisoners had been enrolled in the programme in Building 11 of Jau Prison.
Of those, 64 were allowed to return to their families on Monday. Another 41 will continue the programme at Jau Prison, while five prisoners who had signed up have been removed from the programme and will be placed in other buildings in the prison complex, according to Al-Wadaei.
He also shared images of some of the prisoners after they returned home, including Hashem Mohsen al-Darazi, who is serving a 37-year sentence following his arrest in 2015.
The 64 are expected to remain with their families until Friday before entering the next stage of the programme in Hamala. From there, prisoners serving lengthy sentences are gradually moved towards alternative sentencing arrangements and electronic monitoring rather than conventional imprisonment.
For some families, the programme has meant the temporary return of relatives imprisoned since the upheaval that followed Bahrain's 2011 uprising.
"The group includes long-term political prisoners, some of whom were underage when they were arrested around 14 years ago," Al-Wadaei said. "For families who have waited around 14 years to have their loved ones home, even temporarily, it is an enormously significant moment."
First major release since Iran war
The timing of the move is also significant because it comes amid a wider crackdown in Bahrain since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Al-Wadaei stressed that the 64 prisoners were not among those recently detained in connection with the conflict. Instead, the group includes prisoners who have been incarcerated for years.
"However, the timing is significant," he said. "This represents the first substantial release of political prisoners since the conflict began and is an important step."
Bahrain holds hundreds of political prisoners, with Amnesty International saying that some 322 people remain arbitrarily detained.
They include prominent human rights activists imprisoned over their role in the 2011 protests, among them Abdulhadi Al-Khawaja, who has spent more than a decade behind bars and whose health has deteriorated during his detention.
Since the beginning of the US-Israeli war on Iran, Bahraini authorities have stepped up arrests over alleged links to Iran, anti-war protests and social media activity related to the conflict.
In May, Bahrain's Interior Ministry said it had arrested 41 people, including dozens of Shia clerics, accusing them of links to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
Rights groups documented more than 300 arrests connected to the war between the beginning of the conflict and 5 May.
Those detained included people accused over social media posts about the conflict, including footage showing strikes on Bahrain, as well as people who participated in protests against the war.
Bahrain has also stripped at least 69 people of their citizenship over their alleged support for Iran during the conflict.
Al-Wadaei described the temporary return of the 64 prisoners as an important development, while stressing that they remain under sentence and state supervision.
"We hope this will be followed by further releases and ultimately the unconditional release of all those imprisoned for exercising their fundamental rights," he said.

Ukraine Reveals Patriot Missile Shortage to CNN as Launchers Sit Empty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:18:07 UTC
21:18:07 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Reveals Patriot Missile Shortage to CNN as Launchers Sit Empty
Ukraine faces a severe shortage of air defense interceptors, leaving advanced Patriot launcher units idling in rural fields.
Ukraine currently holds only 1% of US missile stockpiles, well short of the 5% requested by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to secure air coverage through the winter, according to CNN on August 17.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A system spotted near Kyiv has 16 tubes showing signs of past use, but its unit chief engineer, Dmytro, noted the launcher had not fired in six weeks.
This deficit follows heavy consumption of interceptor missiles in the Persian Gulf during March and April, where coalition forces used an average of 225 interceptors daily over a four-day period against low-cost Iranian drone attacks.
Meanwhile, manufacturer Lockheed Martin produced 620 interceptors in 2025 (roughly 1.7 per day), creating a usage-to-production gap of 132 to 1.
In response, the Pentagon signed a seven-year agreement in January to increase output to 2,000 units annually by 2030. The shortage of interceptor missiles leaves crews unable to stop incoming strikes aimed at civilian areas and infrastructure, as reported by CNN.
Dmytro recalled experiencing his first complete depletion of interceptor ammunition in December 2025. "It’s really a terrible sight when you have the equipment, but you can’t intercept a single missile," Dmytro said.
"Ballistic missiles fly over your head, and you can do nothing about them, while civilians are behind you." Dmytro described the experience: "It’s hard to describe—strong and bad feelings. It’s like you’re learning to walk, but you can’t walk. You know how to breathe, but you can’t breathe."
Operating the system involves complex tracking equipment, remote command centers, and tactical decision-making under intense pressure. A crew member named Heorhiy explained that deciding which target to engage relies heavily on experience.
"It’s complicated, because you see targets flying and threatening the civilian population, critical infrastructure, as well as the families of my comrades and my own family," Heorhiy stated, describing the moment of firing an interceptor as "something magical."
Ukrainian leadership forewarned that heavy usage of defense assets in Middle Eastern operations would impact supplies needed to counter ballistic missiles during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"We predicted that we would have problems. We were very shocked by how many missiles they launched at once... the same missiles that we could have used against Russian ballistic missiles," Dmytro noted.
To secure future supplies, President Zelenskyy proposed allowing US defense manufacturers Raytheon and Lockheed Martin to build interceptors directly in Ukraine under license, offering them full ownership and operational control.
"It will be your company," Zelenskyy recalled telling the defense companies. "It will be our minds, our hands, our engineers. And I will do everything possible to build a big company for them. Because I don’t need to sell interceptors to anyone else who I need for my country."
Addressing global inventory levels, Zelenskyy noted: "I know the production, facilities, military, and stockpiles of almost all countries in Europe, including the United States. Not everything, but a lot."
Following a NATO summit in Ankara in June, former US President Trump floated licensing options for local manufacturing, leading to executive visits to Kyiv.
However, subsequent statements cast doubt on licensing approvals. "I want to get this," Zelenskyy said. "I think his word is the word of the President of the United States. And I hope that I will get it."
A White House official clarified that no final decisions or guarantees regarding local manufacturing have been granted, pointing to strict security requirements for US technology.
Regarding whether localized production could begin quickly if restrictions were removed, Dmytro expressed skepticism: "No. Definitely no, because it is a very complex procedure, and it requires a lot of knowledge, a lot of technical information."
On August 9, 2026, The Atlantic reported that Ukraine’s efforts to manufacture Patriot air defense systems domestically faced resistance from US defense contractors Raytheon and Lockheed Martin.
While the companies officially cited concerns over intellectual property theft and technology security, a Republican congressional official disclosed that their primary fear was commercial—specifically, that Ukrainian manufacturers would streamline the system to produce it faster, better, and at a significantly lower cost.
This industrial friction unfolded as Ukraine faced severe interceptor shortages during intensified Russian missile strikes, leaving President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to pursue immediate missile deliveries alongside long-term domestic licensing agreements.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Putin Squeezes $4.6 Billion From Businesses Through “Voluntary Contributions” to Plug Budget Deficit
Large Russian businesses have been forced to transfer hundreds of billions of rubles to the federal budget following Vladimir Putin’s demand for so-called “voluntary contributions” as the country struggles with a record budget deficit.
AAccording to Vedomosti on August 18, as of mid-August, so-called gratuitous payments to the federal budget had reached 383.69 billion rubles (about $4.6 billion). Before Putin’s March meeting with representatives of major Russian businesses, contributions from non-governmental organizations stood at just 15.6 billion rubles (around $187 million).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Following Putin’s appeal, the volume of transfers increased tenfold within a month, reaching 159.7 billion rubles (almost $2 billion). Payments rose by another 45.5% in May and 27% in June, before increasing by a further 30% during July and the first half of August.
Alexander Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs, confirmed that business owners had transferred funds to the state, saying the money came not only from corporate structures but also from family foundations.
The Russian government, meanwhile, expects to receive around 300 billion rubles (nearly $4 billion) in such payments by the end of the year.
The contributions come as Russia’s public finances face mounting pressure. Between January and July, the federal budget deficit reached 6.455 trillion rubles (approximately $77.5 billion), 1.4 times higher than during the same period last year and nearly twice the amount initially planned for the entire year.
According to The Moscow Times, Russia’s mounting fiscal pressures have coincided with the growing cost of its war against Ukraine. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, the Russian federal budget has spent nearly 50 trillion rubles (about $600 billion) on the war.
To cover military expenditures, Russian authorities have already used three-quarters of the liquid assets held in the National Wealth Fund and confiscated private assets worth 4 trillion rubles (arout $48 billion). The government has also raised corporate profit taxes, personal income taxes, value-added tax, and levies on small businesses.
Amid these mounting fiscal pressures, Russian authorities have also reduced public access to information about the country’s remaining financial reserves. The Moscow Times reported on August 13 that the government had stopped publishing official figures on cash reserves held in its single treasury account, a key financial cushion for unallocated budget funds.
Russia’s Federal Treasury removed daily operational data covering ruble deposits placed with commercial banks, money market transactions, and the total amount of cash available across different levels of the budget system.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The landlocked Caspian Sea is bordered by five countries: Russia, Iran, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and Azerbaijan. Because Western navies, including the US Navy, do not operate in these waters, they cannot interdict shipments moving between the two allies.
In late March, Israel targeted the Iranian port complex of Bandar Anzali on the Caspian coast. Israeli officials said the facility was used to transport weapons from Russia. Shipments through the port restarted shortly after the operation.
The reliance on this supply route highlights a growing strategic alliance between Moscow and Tehran. Iranian forces have used drones and missiles against US military bases in the Middle East, leading to the deaths of at least 18 American service members since the start of active hostilities.
During the early stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Tehran provided primary support to Moscow. Iran supplied ready-to-use Shahed strike drones alongside production technology. Russian engineers later upgraded the design and established mass production inside Russia.

US and Iranian officials agreed to a 60-day ceasefire in mid-June, which was extended for another two months in August. Reports from The Wall Street Journal state that Tehran is using this pause in fighting to rebuild its military inventory. Iranian officials aim to inflict sufficient damage on US and Israeli forces to deter future large-scale strikes on Iranian territory.
On July 25, 2026, Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) launched long-range drone strikes against multiple Russian military and logistical targets, hitting air defense systems in Rostov-on-Don and naval assets in the Caspian Sea.

In the Caspian Sea, Ukrainian drones targeted the Filanovsky offshore oil platform alongside two sanctioned cargo ships, the Port Olya 2 and the Begey, which had been transporting Iranian military equipment and ammunition to Russia.

The Admiral Kasatonov, a modern Russian frigate capable of long-range strikes and anti-submarine warfare, was spotted last week near Fehmarn, a German island and popular tourist destination in the Baltic.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Kushner's visit to Netanyahu deepens Gaza's frustration on deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18

21:17:32 KST

Breadcrumb
Kushner's visit to Netanyahu deepens Gaza's frustration over deadlocked talks
The lengthy meeting between US envoy Jared Kushner and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday has deepened frustration in Gaza, where Palestinians see negotiations over the ceasefire's next phase as trapped in a cycle of disputes over Hamas's weapons, Israeli withdrawal and promises of reconstruction.
The meeting lasted about eight hours and included Israeli officials and representatives of the so-called "Board of Peace", Israeli media outlets reported.
Netanyahu's office claimed in a press statement that the talks ended with an agreement to establish two working groups, one focusing on the disarmament of Gaza and another on sanitation, water and public health.
While Netanyahu's office described the discussions as "constructive and in-depth", many Palestinians saw little to suggest that the meeting would resolve the issues preventing the transition to the next phase of the supposed ceasefire.
Kushner met a Hamas delegation in Cairo before traveling to Israel. He said Hamas leaders "said all the right things" but emphasised Washington would judge them by their actions, not words.
He said disarmament progress could start in 30 days, with the US aiming for weapon removal and tunnel destruction in 60-90 days. Washington will not allow Gaza to rebuild until disarmament is done, but Israel retains the right to self-defence against perceived threats.
For Gaza residents, such timelines are disconnected from the daily reality of displacement, destroyed homes and shortages of basic necessities.
Reconstruction remains hostage
The central concern for many Palestinians is no longer how Hamas's weapons will be handled, but whether the political process can deliver a permanent end to Israel's violence, remove an Israeli occupation, and begin meaningful reconstruction.
"Kushner's meeting with Netanyahu offered little hope to families still struggling to survive," Radi Abu Afash, a father of six from Gaza City, told The New Arab.
"People in Gaza want to see results on the ground, not another series of statements and promises," he said, adding that his priority was for his children to live safely and have access to food, water and healthcare.
Abu Afash said that Palestinians were following the negotiations with concern because Israeli demands appeared to be dominating the process, while the needs of Gaza's population were pushed aside.
Salah Abu Hasira, who lives in a tent on Gaza City's beach after losing all his brothers and three of his sons, told TNA that the political discussions had become increasingly disconnected from the reality facing Palestinians.
His family, he said, had already paid an enormous price during the war. Any political initiative would mean little unless it brought a tangible improvement to people's lives.
"What Palestinians need now is an end to their suffering, dignified shelter, rebuilt homes and a future for children who have lost their parents and relatives," he added.
He said that the absence of Palestinian voices from high-level discussions reinforced the feeling that decisions about Gaza's future were being made without its residents.
For Samira Ayoub, also from Gaza City, the political debate comes amid the burden of caring for around 15 grandchildren after losing four of her children during the war.
Ayoub told TNA that the loss of her children had transformed her life, leaving her responsible for her grandchildren while living through extremely difficult conditions.
"Gaza's families can no longer endure more waiting," she said. "People who have lost their children, homes and livelihoods need concrete steps to restore security and stability."
"Palestinians wanted more than an agreement on paper: they wanted children to return to school, families to secure food and water, and survivors to rebuild their lives," she added.
A wider crisis
Frustration has grown with each new round of meetings that produces fresh working groups and deadlines without visible changes in Gaza.
Taysir Abdullah, a Gaza-based political analyst, told TNA that the expectations that Hamas would surrender its weapons completely and immediately were unrealistic.
He argued that Hamas could manoeuvre, delay, and adjust its positions but unlikely to take a step that could undermine its political and organisational existence. As an ideological movement deriving strength from its resistance identity, publicly surrendering its weapons could be seen as an admission of defeat.
Abdullah said Hamas might accept a gradual disarmament if conditions protect its political and symbolic standing, such as avoiding footage of weapons handovers, extending the process, and using a non-Israeli or non-American mediator.
He believes Hamas is relying partly on time, Turkish and Qatari political support and possible changes in Israel's political landscape, particularly ahead of elections.
Mustafa Ibrahim, another political analyst, takes a more pessimistic view. He describes the current proposals as "cosmetic concessions" that could restore aspects of daily life in Gaza without addressing the underlying political crisis.
Allowing limited sanitation, water and infrastructure projects, Ibrahim says, could reflect Israel's concern over the humanitarian and health consequences of Gaza's devastation rather than a genuine move towards ending the blockade or occupation.
"The danger is that these concessions become a substitute for a political solution," he added, warning against treating Gaza merely as a humanitarian, health and security problem requiring containment.
Political analyst Esmat Mansour, meanwhile, believes Hamas's acceptance of a disarmament process, regardless of how it is ultimately implemented, represents a significant strategic shift.
He argues that Hamas's adherence to the agreement could serve its interests as the confrontation moves from the military arena to the political and diplomatic one.
With Palestinians lacking sufficient leverage to impose their demands by force, Mansour believes the movement must rely on Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, the United States and international pressure to push Israel towards implementing the agreement.
Israel blocks next phase
Amid the uncertainty, Palestinian factions met in Cairo on Monday, including Hamas, Islamic Jihad, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine and the Democratic Reform Movement.
Hamas said its political bureau chief, Khalil al-Hayya, briefed the factions on meetings with Egyptian officials, mediators and guarantors in El Alamein, as well as subsequent discussions on the roadmap for the second phase of the ceasefire agreement.
The factions noted Israel was obstructing the transition to the second phase, accusing the government of reneging on understandings reached during the first phase and continuing violations.
They also discussed efforts to halt what they described as escalating aggression and prevent Gaza from becoming a casualty of Israel's political and electoral struggles, while accelerating relief, recovery and reconstruction.
Israeli media, citing political sources, reported that Netanyahu insisted during his meeting with Kushner on maintaining the Israeli army's freedom of action in Gaza. The meeting reportedly included the Shin Bet chief and the head of Military Intelligence, who presented what Israel described as evidence of Hamas violations.
Trump, meanwhile, said it would be better if Israel did not attack Gaza again, remarks welcomed by Hamas, which urged the US president to pressure the Israeli government to honour the understandings reached for the second phase.
For Palestinians, however, the contradiction remains stark: Washington is pressing for progress while Israel continues to insist on security conditions and freedom of military action.

Russia Classifies Beer, Wines and Vapes as “Strategic Goods” Under New Law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:17:26 UTC
21:17:26 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Classifies Beer, Wines and Vapes as “Strategic Goods” Under New Law
The Russian government has added light alcoholic beverages—including still and sparkling wines, beer, and ciders—along with electronic cigarettes, vape liquids, and nicotine salts to its list of strategically important goods, as reported by The Moscow Times on August 18.
Under the newly effective updates to Article 226.1 of the Russian Criminal Code, individuals caught bringing these items across the Russian border or the Eurasian Economic Union without proper customs clearance face up to five years in prison if the shipment exceeds 100,000 rubles ($1,100).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Previously, undeclared transport of these specific products was treated as an administrative violation resulting in monetary fines or compulsory labor.
Prior to 2022, criminal charges for illegal alcohol and tobacco transport applied only to shipments worth over 250,000 rubles ($2,750), with prison sentences restricted to cases involving organized crime groups or officials abusing their positions.
Although hard spirits and traditional tobacco were added to the strategic goods list in 2022, other alcoholic drinks and electronic smoking devices were omitted, creating a legal gap that operated for over three years.
Under the new regulations, bringing just two bottles of premium vintage wine or high-end champagne without declaring them can trigger criminal penalties.
Illegal transport of high-value wine in personal luggage has remained common practice, with Federal Customs Service data showing attempted illegal alcohol imports reaching 413.5 million rubles ($4.5 million) last year, up from 266.7 million rubles ($2.9 million) the year prior.
Primary origin points include Georgia, Thailand, Estonia, and Turkey. In one recent incident on August 9, customs officers at Domodedovo Airport discovered 15 bottles of 2021 Sassicaia wine valued at 2 million rubles ($22,000)—roughly 133,000 rubles ($1,460) per bottle—in a flight attendant’s luggage from Vietnam.
The individual faced administrative fines equal to twice the goods' value alongside total confiscation. Legal personal imports into Russia remain strictly limited to five liters of alcohol above 0.5% ABV, with any amount over three liters requiring formal declaration and a duty of 10 euros ($10.80) per excess liter.
Direct exports of European wines priced above 300 euros ($325) are prohibited under international sanction measures, while standard import routes face elevated Russian protective tariffs, recently raised from 20% to 25% with a minimum charge of 2 euros ($2.15) per liter.
Former government economist Oleg Vyugin noted that due to complex transport routes and rising tariffs, "European wines in restaurants cost like an airplane wing," adding that "if you want to drink good wine, you have to spend everything you earned over the last two months, or be an oligarch."
Previously, it was reported that spirits company Bacardi launched full-scale commercial bottling of its Martini brand in Russia, significantly expanding its footprint while boosting revenues.
Its subsidiary, Bacardi Rus LLC, saw its annual revenue increase by 71.45%, rising from approximately $380.5 million in 2021 to $572.6 million in 2025.
Production was handled in Dagestan by Alvisa, which planned to produce approximately 10 million liters of vermouth annually for the Russian market to bypass elevated import duties.

Iran wins medal, honorable mentions at Intl. Geography Olympiad
TEHRAN – Iranian students succeeded to win a bronze medal and three honorable mentions at the 22nd International Geography Olympiad (iGeo) held from August 11 to 17 in Istanbul, Turkey.
The International Geography Olympiad is the world’s premier academic competition for secondary school students. It is held under the auspices of the International Geographical Union (IGU) and organized by the IGU Olympiad Commission. This year’s competition brought together more than 180 participants from over 50 countries.
Helia Khodabandelou grabbed the bronze medal, while Setayesh Haqnazari, Artina Heidari, and Sana Karbalaei received international diploma of honors.
The iGeo consists of three main parts: Written Response Test (40 percent) which involves analytical questions covering physical, human, and regional geography; Multimedia Test (20 percent), including map interpretation, graphs, photos, and data analysis; and Fieldwork Exercise (40 percent), including real-world data collection and analysis (at Istanbul sites this year).
The four students attended the Open International Geography Olympiad (OpenGeo) 2026, winning four medals, including a silver medal and three bronze medals for the first time. Heidari won the silver medal; Haqnazari, Karbalaei Vali, and Khodabandelou received the bronze medals, IRIB reported.
The achievement showcased the Iranian students’ comprehensive expertise in geography. The OpenGeo aims to promote interest in geography among secondary school students worldwide; develop geographical thinking, analytical, and practical skills among school students and future geographers; and support international connections between young geographers.
Recent achievements
Iranian students clinched medals and an honorable mention at the 9th International Economics Olympiad (IEO 2026) held from July 12-20 in Shenzhen China, and the 38th edition of International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) held from August 9 to 16 in Tashkent, Uzbekistan.
This year, 270 students from 54 countries attended the IEO competition. MobinKarimiDizicheh secured silver medal. He received an honorable mention and also won Best in Finance, Borna news agency reported.
Mohammad-Hossein Rahiminejad, Alireza Atashi, and Ehsan Zolfaghari won the bronze medals.
IEO is an annual competition for high school students around the world in the areas of Economics and Finance. The Olympiad is supported by Eric Maskin, winner of the Nobel Prize for Economics in 2007.
Meanwhile, a total of 386 students from more than 97 countries participated in this year’s IOI competition.
Hamed Ghaffari-Aghdas and Arash Ostadsharif-Memar grabbed the silver medals, while Mohammad Shayan won the bronze medal. Moreover, Bahamin Shafaqi received an honorable mention.
The IOI is one of the several international science Olympiads held annually around the world. Exceptional high school students from various countries compete in the prestigious algorithmic competition to sharpen their informatics skills – such as problem analysis, design of algorithms and data structures, programming, and testing.
Iranian students won a gold medal, two silver medals, and a bronze medal at the third edition of the International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (IOAI 2026), held from August 2-8 in Astana, Kazakhstan.
IOAI is the International Science Olympiad in AI for high school students. It aims to inspire young people globally in science, focusing on AI. The competition provides a platform for top AI students selected through national competitions to compete, exchange ideas, and build connections, fostering a dialogue on AI’s opportunities and ethical challenges among students and the community.
Shayan Rezaeizadeh grabbed the gold medal, Mohammad-Reza Darvishi, and Mohammad-Amin Nazmfar won the silver medals, while Mani Monjipor received the bronze medal, IRNA reported.
This year’s competition brought together over 120 teams, more than 500 students from 103 countries and territories around the world to compete in AI and machine learning (ML) challenges.

Radin Bayani, Mohammad-Reza Vaezi, and Amir-Hossein Nosrati grabbed gold medals, while Amir-Hossein Hemmati won the silver medal, IRIB reported.

Iranian, Indonesian universities ink MOU to boost scientific ties
