Copper tests new record amid AI and energy demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:09:56 UTC
18:09:56 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu, Emirhan Yilmaz, and Emir Yildirim
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
Copper reached a new record, rising as high as $6.73 per pound on Monday due to strong artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investments, growing renewable energy demand and cost pressures further exacerbated by Middle East tensions.
Copper prices have continued to trend upward since last year, and the base metal has gained more than 18% this year amid accelerating global investments in data centers, energy infrastructure and power transmission systems. Expectations of stronger industrial production activity also drove up copper prices.
Supply constraints also contributed to the rise in copper as disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and resulting issues in the sulfur supply chain affected copper production, fueling supply concerns. The combination of strong demand and supply-side issues drove copper to historic highs.
Slowing US inflation and rising concerns over the country’s economic growth eased hawkish expectations for the Fed’s future monetary policy decisions, providing upward support for commodity prices.
Copper later stabilized at $6.56 per pound.
Zafer Ergezen, a futures and commodities expert, told Anadolu that copper is one of the commodities with the highest demand, primarily due to AI investments, while other sectors like electric vehicles (EVs) and the global energy sector are major drivers.
“Reports consistently show a supply shortage in this area, so even if supply increases, the demand would grow at a much stronger rate,” he said.
Ergezen stated that US tariffs and the US-Israel-Iran conflict have been instrumental in the rise in copper prices, as mounting logistics and energy costs due to Middle East tensions increased prices across the entire mining sector.
“The most significant increase in demand for copper comes from the AI sector, and we’ve seen this particularly rapidly in China,” he said.
“We’re seeing massive investments, one-time deals worth $100 billion being signed in the AI sector, and these will continue in the coming period, which means copper demand will continue to rise and remain strong, meaning copper prices will continue climbing,” he added.
Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Capital, said the intense supply competition between the US and China pushed copper above $6.70 per pound, while major copper producers struggled to meet their production targets.

Jobs to go at Ferguson Marine shipyard in Port Glasgow
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:07:45 BST
18:07:45 KST

Ferguson Marine has opened a voluntary redundancy programme expected to see up to 70 employees leave the Port Glasgow yard, as work on the ferry Glen Rosa winds down and before contracts for four new vessels are finalised, the company stated.
The yard is moving into the final outfitting and commissioning phases of Glen Rosa ahead of delivery in the fourth quarter of 2026, and says the workload is naturally reducing as a result. Formal consultation has begun.
Graeme Thomson, chief executive of Ferguson Marine, said: “Our immediate focus remains the safe, high-quality handover of Glen Rosa in Q4 2026. However, as the vessel nears completion, we face an inevitable gap in workload while we work with the Scottish Government to make the relevant preparations to enable us to proceed with contract negotiations.
“Shipbuilding capability relies on continuity and while changes of this nature are difficult, taking proactive action now ensures we protect the long-term viability of the yard and remain lean, modern, and ready to cut steel on the new fleet as quickly as possible.”
He said: “We take our responsibility to our workforce and community incredibly seriously. By offering a voluntary redundancy path, we want to support team members who have given so much to shipbuilding on the Clyde as they consider their next steps. At the same time, we are doing everything in our power to ensure the yard is structured to offer secure, long-term careers once the new build programme gets underway.”
The Scottish Government announced in March 2026 that it intended to make a strategic direct award to Ferguson Marine covering four vessels: two ferries for Caledonian Maritime Assets under the Small Vessel Replacement Programme, along with a marine protection vessel and a marine research vessel. Due diligence on that award is still under way.
Ferguson Marine says the changes announced are designed to address the size of the business and align skills across the yard so it is ready to begin work as soon as the contracts are settled, and that the consultation will not affect the remaining work or the delivery schedule for Glen Rosa. A phased transition plan is in place across active projects.
GMB Scotland, the largest union at the yard, called the job losses a betrayal of a blameless workforce and blamed ministers for failing to deliver new contracts while sending work overseas.
Louise Gilmour, GMB Scotland secretary, said 70 jobs are at risk while the Scottish Government refuses to sign off contracts promised before the Holyrood election in May.
She said: “Shipbuilders needs ships to build so where are those promised to Ferguson Marine? If they ever come, who will build them? Fergusons was once Scotland’s ferry factory with a worldwide reputation for excellence and should be again.
“Instead, skilled and experienced shipbuilders are being encouraged to leave as those in charge send contracts everywhere but here. The lack of support, ambition and industrial strategy is abject.”
Ms Gilmour, who noted that a third of CalMac’s current fleet was built at the yard, tied the losses to a long-standing failure to open a pipeline of work after Glen Rosa and Glen Sannox.
She said: “Its reputation has been battered for ten years because of two calamitous contracts decided and driven by those in charge of our ferry network. Their hubris and incompetence have failed a blameless workforce that deserves the chance to turn the page.”
Glen Rosa is the second of two dual-fuel ferries ordered for the Clyde and Hebrides network in 2015, a contract that ran years late and far over budget, and which led to the yard being taken into public ownership in December 2019 after Ferguson Marine Engineering went into administration. Her sister ship Glen Sannox was handed over in early 2025, around seven years behind the original schedule.
The pattern the redundancies illustrate is the one that has dogged smaller British yards for decades. A yard that finishes one order without another already cut in steel loses the people who built the first, and the welders, pipefitters and outfitters who leave rarely come back. Ferguson Marine is arguing that shrinking now protects its ability to staff up when the new programme starts.
The yard also carries out fabrication work for BAE Systems on the Type 26 frigate programme, producing structural units that are shipped up the river to Govan for assembly, and is partway through a transformation project intended to modernise the site.
Ferguson Marine has operated at Port Glasgow since 1903 and is the last commercial shipbuilder on the lower Clyde.

Campaigners call for Amsterdam to pull plug on giant data centre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:07:39 UTC
18:07:39 KST

Campaigners call for Amsterdam to pull plug on giant data centre
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
More than 500 people have joined a campaign to stop a huge data centre being built in Amsterdam-Zuid, arguing that it will bring “zero benefits to the area”.
The Dutch government has introduced restrictions on the size of data centres in recent years following criticism from provincial and municipal governments about the strain on the electricity network. Data centres accounted for 4.6% of all electricity use in the Netherlands in 2024.
But the plans to build a 24,000 m2 facility on Amsterdam’s Science Park were submitted by US firm Equinix before the ban, which only applies to new developments, took effect in 2022.
Local residents have also become increasingly vocal in opposing the construction of data centres, while campaign groups Geef Tegengas and Extinction Rebellion both staged demonstrations this summer against a Microsoft project in Amsterdam Sloterdijk.
“There are already enough data centres to keep everything running. This is becoming overkill,” Dylan Bakker of Stop Datacenter Zuidoost told NOS.
Amsterdam city council, which wants to build 8,000 homes in Zuidoost to help relieve the national housing shortage, has attached extra conditions to the site, such as requiring the residual heat from the plant to be used for domestic heating.
Water and electricity
There are also concerns about the strain on water supplies, which have been exacerbated by the summer drought. Equinix said in its planning application that it would need 274 million litres of water a year for the first stage of the project, rising to more than a billion litres when the data centre is complete in 2036.
But the municipality says it would face legal action and penalties if it tore up the permit to build the data center at this stage.
Equinix has said it will only build one of four planned 60-metre data towers initially, until electricity grid operator Tennet can supply enough power.
Tennet warned earlier this year that the network was nearing capacity, leading to a six-month moratorium on new connections in Utrecht.
The complete campus in Zuidoost will consume 779 kWh of electricity a year, almost as much as all the households Amsterdam combined, which currently use 869 kWh.
Michiel Eielts, director of Equinix Benelux, argued that the data centres were an essential part of modern infrastructure. “Every house needs the internet. We need data centres for the growth of our companies, our public services and our security,” he said.

DUSHANBE, August 18. /TASS/. Servicemen from a sniper rifle company of the 201st Russian Guards Military Base, stationed in Tajikistan, practiced neutralizing a simulated enemy at the Lyaur mountain training range during a live-fire exercise, the press service of the Central Military District reported.
It said that according to the exercise scenario, unmanned aerial vehicle crews detected a concentration of "enemy" forces in one of the mountain gorges during aerial reconnaissance and transmitted the data to the command post. Snipers, having received the order to neutralize the targets, moved on foot to the designated area and then established primary and backup positions for observation and firing, using improvised and specialized camouflage equipment.
"After detecting the ‘targets’ and determining firing positions, the service members engaged the targets at ranges from 300 to 1,000 meters in sniper pairs. Fire was conducted using SVD, SVD-M, SVD-K, and SV-98 sniper rifles," the statement said.
The Central Military District’s press service emphasized that the exercise was conducted taking into account experience gained in the Russian special military operations in Ukraine, as well as the specific features of mountainous terrain. "The service members practiced engaging targets from various cover positions, including from simulated urban structures, adjusting their fire based on elevation angles," according to the statement.
The 201st Russian military base stationed in Tajikistan is Russia’s largest military facility outside its borders. Located in two cities, Dushanbe and Bokhtar, it includes motorized rifle, tank, artillery, reconnaissance, air defense, NBC defense troops and communications units.

Ministers tread carefully as Trump scales back US drills in South Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:06:03 UTC
18:06:03 KST

Australia and Japan tread carefully as Trump scales back US drills in South Korea
In short:
Japan's defence minister has stressed that cooperation between Australia, Japan and the US is growing ever-more important.
Australia and Japan's defence ministers sat down in Canberra today to discuss the rapidly expanding defence ties between the countries.
It comes as President Donald Trump has scaled back military drills with South Korea.
Australia and Japan's defence ministers have side-stepped questions about Donald Trump's pronouncement that he will scale back military exercises with South Korea — as well as the US president's overtures to North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un — while signalling they still see Pyongyang as a serious security threat.
Shinjiro Koizumi and Richard Marles sat down in Canberra today to discuss the rapidly expanding defence ties between the two countries.
Both countries are increasingly anxious about China's rapidly swelling military might, as well as the Trump administration's chaotic and unpredictable behaviour.
The US president promised on Monday that he would scale back US participation in the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises because Seoul had not helped the US war effort in Iran, and this morning suggested that North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un had responded "positively" to the move.
The joint exercises that started yesterday are scheduled to run until later in August, with about 18,000 South Korean military personnel taking part -as well as a small contingent of 13 ADF personnel who are serving as part of United Nations Command.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said this morning the annual exercises are defensive and not intended to attack North Korea or raise tensions on the peninsula.
Last week, Mr Lee proposed talks to officially end the war with Pyongyang, although North Korea has routinely tested ballistic missiles and strengthened its military ties with Russia.
'Critical' cooperation
Analysts and US senators on both sides of the aisle have warned Mr Trump's move risks alienating South Korea and undercutting US credibility in Asia, while Korean media have quoted a Japanese foreign affairs official warning "we must not weaken our posture to respond to threats."
But Mr Koizumi was much more careful when asked about the announcement, simply saying that countries like North Korea and Russia were posing an increasingly severe threat to Japan's security, and that US allies needed to deepen cooperation in response.
"The missile enhancement and coercive and unilateral challenge to the status quo by other countries and North Korea … is getting stronger," he told journalists in Canberra.
"Our cooperation with Australia, Japan and the US is ever more important."
Mr Marles also would not be drawn on the US president's announcement, saying "obviously what the United States does is a matter for it."
But he stressed that Australia was still "very concerned" about North Korea's nuclear and missile programs, saying that South Korea was a "critically important" defence partner for Australia.
"In the challenging world we face — and there are many challenges but North Korea is the author of quite [a lot] of them — we greatly appreciate our relationship with South Korea and we very much appreciate our relationship with Japan,"
The chief executive of the Australian Institute of International Affairs and a Japan expert, Bryce Wakefield, told the ABC that both countries would be monitoring the US administration's moves very closely.
"Tokyo's response to this development won't be panic, but it reinforces Japan's concern that longstanding alliance arrangements can become bargaining chips in Trump's personal diplomacy," he said.
"We saw this in the US president's first-term approaches to North Korea, and we're now seeing it at a time when North Korea is still testing missiles."
Dr Wakefield said that Canberra would be "uneasy for much the same reason" as Japan.
"Australia puts a lot of stock in exercises and interoperability," he said.
"It will worry less about this particular drill than the signal that the US is now changing regional commitments abruptly, according to Trump's transactional approach."
One Japanese government source said the two ministers "referred" to the president's plans in their meeting but said the overwhelming focus was on the way the two countries — often labelled as "quasi-allies" — could continue to quickly build up defence ties.
Japan to test hypersonic missiles in Australia
Australia announced last year that a Japanese company had won a multi-billion-dollar contract for Australia's next generation of warships, and signed a contract for the first three frigates in Melbourne earlier this year.
The two ministers confirmed they were pressing ahead with plans to expand Japan's access to Australia's missile ranges to allow it to conduct sophisticated tests — including with hypersonic missiles.
Japan has moved to rapidly increase defence spending to respond to China's massive military build-up, including by investing in advanced equipment such as long-range missiles and hypersonic weapons.
"We have agreed to progress a better and enhanced arrangement between Australia and Japan for Japan's use of our missile ranges over the next decade across a range of missile capabilities," Mr Marles said.
Mr Koizumi said it would be only the second time Japan would have a missile test range arrangement, behind the United States.
"If the Japan Self Defence Forces are able to conduct test launches of stand-off missiles, such as hypersonic missiles in Australia, it would be a groundbreaking development," he said.
Both ministers also said the two countries were making good progress on a new high-energy laser that they were developing together called the Boobook project — named after an Australian owl.
Mr Marles said tests had been successful and it would offer "greater protection and situational awareness by using laser to optically detect incoming threats."
Mr Koizumi also met with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Canberra, but told journalists they did not discuss Mr Albanese's comments about the melons gifted to him by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi — despite the political furore it provoked in Australia last week.
"Before I visited Australia, the Australian side already told the Japanese side … that [the prime minister] did not mean it that way," he said.

Syria issues death sentence to detained Assad cousin Wassim al-Assad
A Syrian court on Tuesday issued a death sentence to detainee Wassim al-Assad, a cousin of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad who was himself sentenced to death in absentia a week ago.
Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan said Wassim al-Assad was convicted of multiple murders and "murder accompanied by torture and brutality... classified as crimes against humanity and war crimes", adding that "he is therefore sentenced to death".
Last week, the same Syrian court sentenced ousted president Bashar al-Assad, former security chief Atef Najib and seven other former officials to death on Tuesday over the violent suppression of protests in Daraa at the start of the 2011 uprising.

Najib, who is in Syrian custody, was sentenced in person, while Assad and the remaining defendants were sentenced in absentia.

Amnesty, however, criticised the trials, saying that they "should take place before ordinary civilian courts, with the participation of victims and without resorting to the death penalty", adding that they should also be part of a victim-centred process ensuring truth, justice and reparations.
In the same statement, the group also called on the government more generally to "abolish in absentia trials, end the use of the death penalty, criminalize core crimes covered by international law in domestic legislation, and undertake comprehensive judicial reform to ensure that all judicial proceedings fully respect fair-trial guarantees, international law, and international standards".

Nasdaq confirms 23-hour trading from December with new overnight session
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:05:17 UTC
18:05:17 KST

Nasdaq will begin trading US stocks for nearly 23 hours a day from 6 December, adding a new overnight session from 9pm to 4am ET, as the exchange races to compete with round-the-clock crypto and tokenised markets and with investors abroad clamouring for access.
The Nasdaq announced it will begin trading US stocks for nearly 23 hours a day from Sunday 6 December onwards.
The move, still subject to SEC approval, means Nasdaq's trading day will stretch from Sunday evening to Friday evening with barely a pause.
For European investors, the new window of 9pm to 4am ET will be 3am to 10am CET, meaning Europeans could be trading Nasdaq-listed stocks for almost an entire session before London opens.
Nasdaq already runs extended sessions from 4am to 9:30am, called pre-market session, and 4pm to 8pm ET, named after-hours session, around its core 9:30am to 4pm hours, but access to that early and late trading has largely been exclusive to institutional investors with direct market connections.
Nasdaq president Tal Cohen has framed the expansion as a way to "broaden investor access and expand wealth-building opportunities" for everyone else.
The pitch is also backed by numbers as foreign holdings of US equities reached $17 trillion (€14.6tn) by mid-2024, up 97% since 2019, a surge Nasdaq wants to capture directly rather than cede to platforms already open around the clock.
A market that increasingly never sleeps
Traditional exchanges have been under mounting pressure to broaden access and increase available hours.
Geopolitical shocks under the Trump administration have repeatedly landed when Wall Street was shut, most notably when US and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear sites were announced on a Saturday morning in February, forcing traders onto crypto exchanges and decentralised platforms to price oil, gold and silver in real time.
Those venues, along with newer tools such as tokenised real-world assets, which are digital tokens representing ownership of stocks, bonds or commodities, and perpetual futures contracts that let investors bet on an asset's price with no expiry date, have shown that demand for round-the-clock trading does not wait for exchanges to open.
Nasdaq is also not moving alone.
Rival NYSE has already won SEC approval for a 22-hour day running from 1:30am to 11:30pm ET, while Cboe, the largest exchange for options contracts in the US, has outlined similar ambitions.
Nasdaq first signalled its own intent to go nearly continuous back in March with this week's announcement filling in the details.
The new evening session serves as the first concrete building block, opening the market for nearly 23 hours in a five-day trading week, as the exchange ultimately wants to offer 24/7 trading.

Valtori clarifies data protection practices in its agreements with Microsoft
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:04:07 EEST
18:04:07 KST

Valtori clarifies data protection practices in its agreements with Microsoft
The Finnish Government ICT Centre Valtori has introduced a new, more detailed appendix to its data protection addendum with Microsoft. The appendix clarifies Microsoft's role as a data processor and further specifies its data protection obligations.
The new appendix complements the existing data protection addenda between Microsoft and Valtori. It is the outcome of contract negotiations carried out as part of the Ministry of Finance's Cirrus project, which conducted a comprehensive assessment of contractual and technical data protection measures.
The project was responsible for cooperating with suppliers and defining contractual terms. It ensured that the agreements meet the central government's stringent data protection and information security requirements and respond to its preparedness needs. This included ensuring an adequate level of protection for personal data stored by Finnish public sector organisations in Microsoft's cloud services.
Valtori’s supplementary appendix to its agreement with Microsoft introduces more detailed provisions on the processing of personal data in Microsoft services and sets out Microsoft's obligations when processing data on behalf of Valtori and its clients. Public sector organisations in Finland can continue to use Microsoft services in compliance with EU and Finnish legislation while benefiting from secure cloud-based solutions.
The new appendix provides greater clarity on Microsoft's role and strengthens data protection for Valtori's clients. At the same time, it reduces risks associated with data processing in public administration and reinforces contractual safeguards. The new appendix establishes more transparent rules for the use of cloud services and supports the central government's transition to secure cloud-based solutions.

 Kirsi Janhunen, Senior Specialist, Ministry of Finance, tel. +358 295 530 077, kirsi.janhunen(at)gov.fi
 Katri Harjuveteläinen, Data Protection Officer, Government ICT Centre Valtori, tel. +358 29 346 0286, katri.harjuvetelainen(at)valtori.fi

Taiwan audit office warns past cash handouts lack effectiveness assessments

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s National Audit Office warned in its 2025 General Final Accounts of the Central Government, released July 24, that the government’s previous cash handouts lacked adequate planning before implementation and effectiveness assessments afterward.
Citing a survey published by Academia Sinica in July, the office suggested the previous two cash handouts had limited effects on boosting consumption, per ETtoday. It added that research from the US and Japan found that roughly one-third of cash handouts are spent on consumption, instead of saving or repaying debt.
The office noted that the government estimated in September 2025 that its NT$10,000 (US$314) cash handout would increase GDP by 0.145%. However, the estimate was based on the effects of previous stimulus vouchers rather than research on cash handouts.
To address the issue, the office requested in 2024 that the Ministry of Finance include effectiveness assessments in its plans for cash handouts. The office said the ministry responded that follow-up studies would be conducted if sufficient time and resources were available.
The office recommended adjusting Taiwan’s industrial structure to address economic challenges. It stressed that Taiwan still needs to raise NT$869.6 billion for fiscal 2025 and ongoing special budgets, per UDN.
President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) announcement of a planned NT$10,000 cash handout in 2027 has drawn criticism from those who had opposed the opposition’s NT$10,000 cash handout proposal in 2025 alongside the DPP. Hsuan Chuang University Professor Shih Chao-hwei (釋昭慧) urged the government to allocate the funds to Taiwan’s struggling industries or more vulnerable members of society, per Liberty Times.
NPP Chair Wang Wan-yu (王婉諭) warned that cash handouts do not leave lasting benefits, such as infrastructure, for Taiwan, per Z.Media. She said the NT$230 billion spent on the 2025 cash handout could have funded enough social housing for 84,000 households, offsetting some of the 100,000-unit reduction from Lai’s campaign pledge.
In related news, DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) said that because the cash handout is tied to the budget, the legislature could decide whether the public could receive the money before the Lunar New Year, per Mirror Media. Chuang stressed the government had allocated funding for key projects before proposing the cash handout.
TPP Legislative Caucus Convener Chen Ching-lung (陳清龍) said Lai’s proposal would not affect how his party reviews the government’s 2027 budget, per UDN. TPP Chair Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) previously argued that returning surplus tax revenue to the public through cash handouts was a rational policy.
KMT Legislator Lai Shyh-pao (賴士葆), meanwhile, called on the government not to give the opposition a reason to reject the government’s budget, per SETN. He asserted that the ruling DPP’s decision not to countersign the Special Act on Taiwan Future Accounts and other legislation passed by the legislature amounted to the executive branch overriding the legislature.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) became the first premier in Taiwan’s history not to countersign a law passed by the legislature, citing the paralysis of the Constitutional Court at the time. Under Taiwan’s Constitution, if the legislature passes the same legislation after the Cabinet requests reconsideration, the premier is required to enforce the legislation or resign.
In Taiwan’s constitutional system, countersigning is intended to give the premier a mechanism to restrain the president, per Taiwan FactCheck Center. However, because the president has the power to appoint the premier at will, the mechanism has rarely, if ever, been used.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) shared three youth policy proposals at a party press conference on Tuesday.
Shen said he planned to establish an urban youth fund for those aged between 18 and 22, CNA reported. As long as one parent lives in Taipei and the applicant has been registered in the city for a certain period, the city government would contribute NT$1,500 (US$46.99) per month into a dedicated account.
The fund would be managed as a long-term savings scheme, and young people would be encouraged to add their own savings to grow the principal, per CNA. Combined with the Cabinet’s child development allowance savings program, this fund could help students accumulate nearly NT$500,000 by the time they graduate from university, Shen said.
For disadvantaged youth, the monthly contribution would be increased to NT$3,000. If participants are convicted of offenses such as drug use or fraud during the program, only their own contributions would be returned, Shen said.
The legislator proposed a youth AI platform that connected different AI models and managed usage quotas. Under this program, Taipei-registered university and master’s students aged 18 to 25 would receive NT$300 per month, according to CNA.
For AI-intensive courses, teachers or schools could apply to raise their monthly stipend to NT$500–1,000 to support learning and hands-on practice, Shen said. For projects, competitions, or cases requiring heavy data or video generation, an additional one-time subsidy of NT$2,000 to NT$10,000 would be available.
In the future, the program would also support Taiwanese AI startups, CNA reported.
Shen also devised a follow-up support program for Taipei youth who join the education ministry’s Youth Overseas Dream Fund. The scheme would offer professional consultation, training, venues, and startup funding to bring overseas talent back to the city.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung's MRT Red Line could gain two additional stations under an updated feasibility study, including a connection to Taiwan Railway's Fengyuan Station, according to a city government press release.
The proposed changes are part of the city's planned Fengke Axis, a proposed transportation corridor intended to extend the MRT into Fengyuan District and surrounding commercial areas. The expansion would also improve connections to Central Taiwan Science Park in Houli.
Under the revised plan, the Red Line (Chongde-Fengyuan Line) would have 11 stations spanning 15.4 kilometers. The line would serve as a major north-south transportation corridor and would primarily use elevated viaducts.
Taichung Rapid Transit Bureau Director Su Rui-wen (蘇瑞文) said the project would extend the city's transportation network northward while providing a long-term transportation solution to help reduce the gap between urban and rural communities. The line would connect five administrative districts: North, Beitun, Tanzi, Shengang, and Fengyuan.
The bureau said its feasibility study found that the area around TRA Fengyuan Station is densely populated with extensive commercial activity. Thus, connecting this area to the MRT system could improve convenience for commuters while increasing the overall efficiency of the city's public transportation network, per the press release.
Su said the city government would also integrate transfers, pedestrian access, and other services around the stations based on transit-oriented development principles. He said the new stations would connect with existing public transportation while promoting more balanced regional development.
The feasibility study for the Red Line began in April, with an interim report expected to be completed by December, with submission to the central government next year. The bureau said it will continue evaluating land use, construction impact, and financial feasibility as it continues to refine the proposal.

A Lithuanian executive who previously headed one of Belarus’ largest wood-processing companies was detained and jailed in June, LRT RADIO has learnt from its sources.
Vytautas Slankauskas worked as head of internal audit at HS Belacon, an Austrian-owned company operating in Belarus. He previously served as the company’s chief executive for three years.
Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry confirmed to LRT RADIO that the Lithuanian Embassy in Belarus had been informed of his detention. The ministry declined to provide further details, citing privacy concerns.
Slankauskas was recruited by Austrian investors from Timber Group because of his experience overseeing the construction of large industrial plants in Lithuania and Belarus. He previously worked for Western Wood Group and at the Mebelain factory in Belarus, which was built by a Lithuanian company.
According to information obtained by LRT RADIO, Slankauskas was accused of supplying defective components to Russia and Belarus. Further details of the allegations were not immediately available.
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has closely overseen the country’s industrial sector, including its wood-processing industry, while the government has taken control of numerous businesses.
Political analyst Vytis Jurkonis said Slankauskas was not the first Lithuanian businessperson working in Belarus to be imprisoned and warned that anyone traveling or working there should carefully assess the risks.
“This is not the first case, and I am afraid it will not be the last,” Jurkonis said. “It does not matter what kind of capital the company has or what kind of business it is. No one can protect you here because Belarus is not a state governed by the rule of law.”
He cited the 2021 forced landing of a Ryanair passenger flight in Minsk and cases involving long-haul truck drivers as examples of the risks faced by Lithuanians in Belarus.
Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry reiterated its recommendation that Lithuanian citizens not travel to Belarus and urged those currently in the country to leave immediately.

====================================================================================================

The Powerful Chinese Model Experts Warned About—and Waited for—Is Here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

It’s now even easier to find—and exploit—vulnerabilities in computer systems using AI.
Last Friday, the Chinese AI company Z.ai announced a powerful open-weight model that it says is capable of automating cutting-edge coding and cybersecurity tasks almost as well as the best publicly available models from Anthropic and OpenAI.
The new model, GLM 5.3, could be a gift for companies looking to secure their systems against attacks, providing a cheaper way to scan for hidden bugs and other weaknesses. Open-weight—or free-to-download—models can be run on one’s own hardware and are often significantly less costly than closed models like Claude and GPT. Alongside the new model, Z.ai released OpenVuln, a service for scanning code repositories for vulnerabilities using GLM 5.3.
For now, the new model is in a limited release with trusted partners, but it shows how quickly open-weight models are gaining superhuman hacking skills. And that might pose problems if the model is harnessed by criminals and other bad actors.
That prospect is especially sobering following a string of startling incidents involving rogue AI agents with advanced cyber-skills. In recent weeks, OpenAI, Anthropic, and independent security researchers have revealed examples of agents escaping from testing environments and autonomously hacking into outside systems, including the research platform Hugging Face, to complete tasks.
On Monday, OpenAI president Greg Brockman warned in a blog post that the Hugging Face incident would go down as “a watershed moment for cybersecurity because it gave a peek into how the capabilities of a typical threat actor will evolve in upcoming months.”
Brockman argued that AI models are becoming so good at scouring codebases for unknown flaws and analyzing systems for misconfigurations that it’s crucial for organizations to use AI to scan their systems and identify issues before they can be exploited.
OpenAI would, of course, like companies to use its AI to do that. So far, it’s moving carefully in providing access to its most capable AI. Like Anthropic, OpenAI has made its most advanced models available to a limited number of partners prior to full release. The US government is also wrestling with the issue and now reviews frontier models as part of their releases.
Some believe that open-source AI will be crucial to shoring systems up from attack; Nvidia recently announced an alliance to promote the use of open AI for cybersecurity. A previous version of Z.ai’s GLM was used by Hugging Face to shore up its systems after an unreleased OpenAI model went rogue and broke them last month.
In a post on X, Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, a web design and hosting company, said his engineers had tested GLM 5.3 as a tool for scanning sites for bugs. “Given its lower costs, I expect this to be a boon for defensive security work,” Rauch wrote in his post. “It’s the new open frontier.”
Z.ai said in a post announcing GLM 5.3 that it had improved the model by “post-training,” which involves giving a model examples of solved problems and letting it learn through experimentation. The company cited coding and cybersecurity benchmark scores that show GLM 5.3 nearing or even exceeding the scores of Anthropic and OpenAI’s models in some cases, like one popular cybersecurity benchmark called CyberGym.
Z.ai also acknowledged the risk of releasing powerful open models in its post. “These capabilities can help defenders identify weaknesses earlier, validate risks, and accelerate remediation,” the company wrote. “They also create clear dual-use risks. We are therefore taking a staged approach to release. Selected security partners will first evaluate GLM-5.3 in controlled settings.” Z.ai says that full access to the model will be available in two weeks.
“This model looks exceptional, with a somewhat astounding increase in scores,” Nathan Lambert, a prominent AI expert, wrote in a post about GLM 5.3. “This is another step towards the inevitable proliferation of very strong cyber capabilities across the economy.”
Z.ai’s latest release also highlights China’s edge in open-weight models. Although the US has sought to restrict the country’s access to the most advanced chips for training AI models, recent months have seen the release of several extremely powerful open-weight models, including Qwen 3.8 Max from Alibaba and Kimi 3 from Moonshot AI. Z.ai has previously said that it used Chinese-made chips from Huawei to train some of its models. Meta, which appeared to have abandoned open-source AI, now seems poised to lead the US challenge with a powerful model called Muse Spark.
The US government is developing a framework designed to mitigate the impact of AI’s advancing cyber capabilities. A big remaining question is what it should do with open models—especially as they introduce more potential risk.

Russia’s War Recruitment Helped Empty Prisons—Now Its Penal Infrastructure Is Shrinking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
08:55:54 UTC
17:55:54 KST

- Category
- World
Russia’s War Recruitment Helped Empty Prisons—Now Its Penal Infrastructure Is Shrinking
The number of inmates in Russia's Altai Krai has nearly halved over the past four years, with the region's human rights ombudsman citing military contracts for the war against Ukraine among the reasons.
The figures came from Anton Vasiliev, the Altai Krai human rights ombudsman, who presented them to the regional broadcaster Vesti Altai in comments that The Insider carried on August 17.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Over the past decade, the number of people held in the region's penal colonies fell from 15,000-17,000 to roughly 5,000-6,000, Vasiliev noted, with the population nearly halving in the last four years alone.
He pointed to three main drivers. The first is the option for inmates to sign a contract with Russia's Defense Ministry and deploy to the war against Ukraine, which brings release from criminal liability.
The second is a broad decline in registered crime, and the third is lighter sentencing for some offenses, with courts increasingly imposing suspended terms or fines for economic crimes rather than prison. Vasiliev added that the region's pre-trial detention centers are working under strain, though not overcrowded.
Vasiliev framed the decline as a nationwide trend, noting that in some regions it has already led to the closure of penal facilities, among them Krasnoyarsk Krai and the Sverdlovsk and Vladimir regions. Plans to shut down several colonies in Krasnoyarsk Krai were flagged in 2024 by the region's ombudsman, Mark Denisov.
The link between military recruitment and Russia's shrinking prison population has been acknowledged at the federal level. In May 2026, the head of the Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN), Arkady Gostev, confirmed a steep national decline in the number of detainees.
The total fell from about 465,000 at the end of 2021 to 282,000, and Gostev listed "the work to select contract servicemen" among the causes, alongside wider use of alternative punishments. Officials have released no breakdown showing how much of the decline recruitment alone accounts for.
Earlier reports indicated that the Kremlin's search for manpower to sustain the war has extended well beyond its own penal system.
Thousands of foreign nationals, many from African countries, have been lured to the front through false promises of well-paid civilian jobs, training abroad, or Russian citizenship, only to be handed Russian-language contracts and sent to the deadliest sectors of the front.

Russian Hypersonic Missile-Capable Frigate Spotted Near Germany Island After Going Dark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
08:55:47 UTC
17:55:47 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Hypersonic Missile-Capable Frigate Spotted Near Germany Island After Going Dark
Russia deployed the frigate Admiral Kasatonov off the German island of Fehmarn in the Baltic Sea last week, the second Russian warship spotted in the strategic waterway in recent weeks, according to The Telegraph on August 17.
The frigate was observed off Fehmarn, a popular tourist destination, following Kremlin threats to attack British and EU vessels, The Telegraph reported.
Shipping data reviewed by the newspaper indicated the vessel sailed with its location transponder switched off, and it was unclear whether it remained near the island by Monday afternoon.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking last week during an inspection of a Russian warship, the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, warned that Moscow would retaliate against British and EU vessels that attempted to seize Russia-linked ships.
"It's nothing but piracy and robbery," Putin declared, adding that his country would be "forced to respond in kind" wherever it judged necessary.
Fehmarn lies close to the Danish straits, the main passage linking the Baltic Sea to the North Sea and the Atlantic, and a chokepoint through which Russian ships transit toward open water.
The frigate's presence there, within reach of German, Danish, and allied surveillance, appeared to mark the latest escalation between Russia and NATO.
The deployment followed a run of Western operations against Russia's shadow fleet, the network of aging, obscurely flagged tankers Moscow uses to move sanctioned oil.
In June, Royal Marine Commandos boarded the Smyrtos off southern England during a six-hour operation, and French forces had earlier seized the Tagor in the Atlantic with support from a British military helicopter.
UK officials had by then sanctioned nearly 600 shadow-fleet vessels, describing the roughly 700-ship network as a vital lifeline that funds Russian missiles and drones.
Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, echoed the threats, asserting that Moscow had the right to strike merchant ships of enemy states suspected of carrying cargo for its adversaries.
Commissioned in 2020, the Admiral Kasatonov is a Project 22350, or Admiral Gorshkov-class, frigate and among the most modern surface combatants in the Russian navy, built for long-range strikes and anti-submarine warfare.
The 135-meter, 4,500-tonne ship carries a Ka-27 helicopter and mounts a 130mm gun, Redut surface-to-air missiles, and close-in Palash systems. Its sixteen universal vertical launch cells can accommodate Kalibr cruise missiles, Oniks anti-ship missiles, and Zircon missiles, which Russia describes as hypersonic.
The frigate is capable of carrying such weapons, but the composition of its munitions during the current voyage was not disclosed.
The frigate's appearance has sharpened concern over Russian intentions toward NATO's eastern flank.
US intelligence recently warned European governments that Moscow may be preparing hybrid operations against Poland and the Baltic states, including sabotage of critical infrastructure and possible false-flag incidents.

The oldest Iberian orca, &quot;Granny,&quot; may have been injured by humans - what injuries the animal sustained
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
11:55:36 EEST
17:55:36 KST

The oldest Iberian orca, "Granny," may have been injured by humans - what injuries the animal sustained
Kyiv • UNN
A 60-year-old orca named Tonia was found in the Strait of Gibraltar with injuries resembling shotgun pellet wounds. Spanish authorities have launched an investigation; the animal's condition is not critical.
Spain has launched an investigation after one of the oldest killer whales in the Iberian population was found in the Strait of Gibraltar with injuries resembling shotgun pellet wounds. UNN reports this, citing Spain’s Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge (MITECO) and Western media.
Details
The whale is an approximately 60-year-old female named Tonia, also known as La Abuela - "Grandmother."
The killer whale was spotted on August 10 in the Strait of Gibraltar together with two other individuals - Pingu and Scarlet. Researchers recorded a number of round injuries on her dorsal fin and back that had not been present during previous observations of the animal several weeks earlier.
Representatives of the conservation organizations WeWhale and Iberian Orca Guardians said that about ten marks resembling shotgun pellet impacts had been found on the killer whale’s body. It is possible that some pellets are still lodged in the injured animal’s body, as not all of them passed through or struck at a tangent.
At the same time, the Spanish authorities have not yet confirmed that the animal was actually shot. MITECO only states that the killer whale’s injuries resemble shotgun pellet wounds.
The ministry received information about the killer whale’s condition on the evening of August 11, and the very next day the Directorate-General for Biodiversity, Forests and Desertification launched a preliminary investigation. The authorities must establish the circumstances in which the injuries appeared and identify possible perpetrators.
Researchers do not rule out the possibility that the incident occurred off the coast of Portugal. Before returning to the Strait of Gibraltar area, Tonia traveled from Galicia along the Portuguese coast. She had previously been seen near Faro without any characteristic injuries.
In connection with this, the Spanish side has already contacted the competent Portuguese authorities. The exact location and time of the possible shooting have not yet been established.
Despite the injuries, the killer whale’s condition is not currently considered critical. Specialists continue to monitor her. The animal is able to swim and hunt, but if pellets remain embedded in her tissues, there is still a risk of inflammation or infection.
Context
Tonia is considered the oldest known female in the Iberian killer whale population, which inhabits the area around the Strait of Gibraltar and the Gulf of Cádiz. Her age is estimated at approximately 60 years.
The Iberian killer whale population is very small. According to various estimates, it numbers only a few dozen animals. The International Union for Conservation of Nature classifies this subpopulation as Critically Endangered.
Since 2020, individual Iberian killer whales have regularly interacted with yachts and other vessels off the coasts of Spain and Portugal. The animals most often make contact with boat rudders, which in some cases has led to serious damage and even the sinking of vessels.
At the same time, scientists have no evidence that killer whales deliberately attack people. Possible explanations for this behavior include play, investigative interest, or a behavioral habit spreading within the group.
Spanish law prohibits the intentional killing, pursuit, capture, or harming of these animals. If the investigation confirms that Tonia was deliberately shot and the perpetrator is identified, they could face liability for violating environmental protection legislation.

Firefighters pushing to 'definitively encircle' east Belgium wildfire, authorities say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
08:55:02 UTC
17:55:02 KST

Europe has been swept by weeks of devastating wildfires fuelled by dry conditions and a historically hot summer, with France, Greece, Portugal and Spain also battling major fires.
Firefighters launched a potentially decisive push to encircle Belgium's largest wildfire in a century on Tuesday, despite wind and rain hampering air support operations over the High Fens nature reserve.
The blaze charring the vast expanse of boggy peatlands, pine trees and hiking trails grew over the weekend to half the size of Manhattan with hundreds of firefighters working night and day to wrestle it under control.
"We are trying to definitively encircle the fire today," regional government spokesperson Nicolas Yernaux told the AFP news agency.
In areas where firefighters could operate, he confirmed the fire was "under control and contained."
But a hard-to-access front towards the German border remains a concern, with some residents in the border town of Monschau already under evacuation orders due to the smoke hazard.
Firefighters worked through the night to make a crucial link-up between the eastern and northern fronts, under very difficult access conditions.
"We're talking about one or two kilometres and we're on the verge of achieving it," Yernaux told AFP, despite "sustained winds" blowing towards the German border.
Water-bombing aircraft from several countries have been deployed, with two Norwegian helicopters the latest to fly in on Monday night, but they have been repeatedly grounded by low cloud and rain. There are also aircraft from Germany, Sweden and the Netherlands.
Yernaux said it was unclear given weather conditions when they would be able to take off again.
"There may be windows of opportunity this morning, but it may not be before tonight."
A huge area has been blanketed by a thick plume of yellowish smoke, with fumes detected as far as eastern France, where authorities issued an air-pollution alert.
The smoke triggered evacuations in one Belgian village and two hamlets of a second, with residents of the hamlet of Sourbrodt given the green light to return home on Monday night.
The finish line
Europe has been swept by weeks of devastating wildfires fuelled by dry conditions and a historically hot summer, with France, Greece, Portugal and Spain also battling major fires.
The High Fens blaze broke out in an area that was ravaged by massive fires in 1911, during a similar period of heatwaves.
It is the country's largest wildfire since.
During a visit on site with King Philippe on Monday, Belgium's interior minister Bernard Quintin told media it could take "several weeks" of soaking and dousing the area to prevent the fire from reigniting, even once brought under control.
On-site operations have been made much harder by the fens' terrain, a patchwork of heath, peat bogs and raised wooden boardwalks where heavy vehicles risk sinking into the ground, and firefighters struggle to tackle the fire at close range.
They have been counting heavily on aerial assistance to bring the situation under control.
Local farmers have also poured in to help, working shifts to oversee a ballet of tractors pulling in tankers of water from a nearby lake.
"We'll take it in turns as long as it needs, the team is all set," a farmer from nearby Waremme, told AFP. "We'll keep going until the finish line."
Like much of Europe, Belgium has experienced a new spell of intense heat and drought in recent days.
Temperatures reached as high as 37C in some parts of the country last week, creating conditions conducive to wildfire outbreaks.

NEW DELHI: The Bihar government has told the Supreme Court that a constable deployed during student protests in Siwan fired four rounds from an AK-47 only after he was "trapped and surrounded by protesters."A video showing a policeman firing an AK-47 during the protests went viral, triggering widespread outrage and backlash.The Samrat Choudhary government said the firing was directed into the air and did not injure any protesters.
The government's response was filed before the apex court in connection with petitions alleging excessive police force during protests linked to the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led student movement.According to the affidavit, the AK-47 incident took place on July 25 near JP Chowk in Siwan. Assistant Sub-Inspector Nilesh Kumar Singh allegedly fired two rounds from his 9mm pistol near Hathi Chowk to disperse the crowd.The Bihar government maintained that police exercised restraint during the protests and did not use disproportionate force.The state government said Kumar's firing occurred only after he was surrounded by the crowd. It also pointed out that the AK-47 was not intended for routine crowd-control or regular law-and-order duties.Kumar has since been suspended over what the government called "undesired conduct", and departmental proceedings have been initiated against him.
The state govt further told the court that the AK-47 carried by Kumar was a "platoon-level weapon" meant for special operations and not for routine law-and-order deployment.The use of an assault rifle during a protest is among the issues raised before the Supreme Court, with petitioners alleging excessive use of force by police.While the Bihar government has defended the circumstances of the July 25 firing, the petitions have raised wider concerns over police action against protesters.The Samrat Choudhary government's affidavit forms part of the ongoing proceedings before the Supreme Court. The court is examining allegations about the police response, including the circumstances of the firing, injuries reported during the protests and whether the force used was proportionate.

‘Where are you hiding Moshe Yair?’ Hezbollah chief lampooned after quoting fictitious Israeli writer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
08:53:26 UTC
17:53:26 KST

Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem has become the target of ridicule in Lebanon and across Arab social media after quoting a purported Israeli commentator during a major speech — only for checks to find that neither the writer nor the article he cited appears to exist.
Qassem delivered the speech Friday evening to mark 20 years since the Second Lebanon War. About 22 minutes into his remarks, while criticizing the Lebanese government and its direct negotiations with Israel, he introduced what he described as the writings of a Jewish thinker named “Moshe Yair,” whom he said worked for the Yedioth Ahronoth media group, which also includes ynet and its English-language arm ynet Global.
Qassem presented the purported article as evidence supporting Hezbollah’s argument that Israel was exploiting what the Iran-backed terrorist group portrays as the naivete of Lebanon’s political leadership.
“The text I am reading to you was written after the framework agreement,” Qassem said. “I am embarrassed by some of the expressions, but I will read the text as it is. I have nothing to do with its content or these expressions.”
He then read aloud an excerpt from what he claimed Yair had written in Yedioth Ahronoth, the daily newspaper and ynet’s parent publication.
“Fortunately for us, they [the Lebanese government] sent a delegation that loves Israel and America more than its own country,” the purported passage said. It went on to attack Lebanese officials as foolish and accuse them of helping Israel “occupy their country, whether they realize it or not.”
There was one problem: No such commentator appears to exist, much less work for Yedioth Ahronoth.
The episode quickly became fodder for Lebanese and Arab media, particularly outlets and commentators opposed to Hezbollah.
Adding to the questions, Hezbollah-affiliated Al-Manar omitted the passage about the supposed Israeli commentator when it published a transcript of Qassem’s speech on its website. The remarks, however, remained audible in the accompanying video. It was unclear whether the omission reflected awareness that the attribution was false.
Lebanese media goes looking for ‘Moshe Yair’
Lebanese broadcaster Al-Jadeed reported that it had attempted to establish the identity of “Moshe Yair” but could find no such writer at Yedioth Ahronoth.
The broadcaster noted that Qassem had relied on the quotation to bolster his political argument, despite the apparent absence of both its supposed author and an original article.
The fictitious persona also appears to predate Qassem’s speech.
For some time, pro-Hezbollah and pro-Iranian social media accounts and websites have circulated articles attributed to a supposed Yedioth Ahronoth writer named Moshe Yair. Their content typically aligns with narratives promoted by Hezbollah.
Al-Jadeed raised the possibility that the identity was invented to circulate political messages under the guise of an Israeli source, giving them greater credibility among Arab audiences.
An online search also found that the passage Qassem read had circulated months earlier without a credible original source.
On June 10, the Lebanese website Al-Haqa'iq published the text and attributed it to “Jewish thinker Moshe Meir” — rather than Moshe Yair — supposedly of Yedioth Ahronoth.
‘The article does not exist’
MTV Lebanon, an outspoken opponent of Hezbollah, seized on the episode Sunday.
“The article does not exist, and neither does the Jewish thinker by that name,” the broadcaster wrote.
It described the supposed author as an invention by media outlets aligned with the Iran-led axis, accusing them of relying on fabricated material and artificial intelligence-generated images and videos to manufacture “imaginary victories” or damage their opponents
“The senior figure in Iran’s most important arm in the region becomes an object of ridicule as he quotes an article that was never written,” MTV said.
The episode also prompted mockery on social media, with some users questioning whether Qassem had simply fallen for unreliable pro-Hezbollah sources or had been involved in promoting the fabrication himself.
Lebanese journalist Sawsan Mhanna mocked the Hezbollah leader on X.
“If I weren’t afraid of being accused of normalization, I would personally contact Yedioth Ahronoth and ask them: Where are you hiding Moshe Yair?” she wrote.
“If Naim doesn’t have a smartphone to search for him, he should assign the task to the brothers in Hezbollah. Maybe they can find Yair before he quotes him in his next speech.”

World chess champions Veselin Topalov and Garry Kasparov meet in match in USA

News
World chess champions Veselin Topalov and Garry Kasparov meet in match in USA
The chess masters will take part in an exhibition match in the U.S. city of St. Louis
Tuesday 18 August 2026 11:10
Tuesday, 18 August 2026, 11:10
PHOTO Chessbase
Font size
Two world chess champions will open a new chapter in their legendary rivalry. Bulgaria’s Veselin Topalov and Baku-born Garry Kasparov will take part in an exhibition match in the U.S. city of St. Louis. The match will begin on September 11, and over three days the two will play twelve games of Chess960, also known as “Fischer Random Chess,” named after its creator, Bobby Fischer.
In this variation of classical chess, the pieces on the first rank are arranged randomly in order to eliminate the advantage of memorized opening lines and require creative thinking from the very first move. The grandmasters will play four games per day - two rapid games (25 minutes + 10 seconds per move) and two blitz games (5 minutes + 2 seconds per move).
The last game Garry Kasparov played, in 2005, was at the Linares tournament, against the Bulgarian chess player. Veselin Topalov defeated his opponent on that occasion. The two also met in an exhibition match in St. Louis in 2018, with the Bulgarian winning again.

Moldova will now carry Ukraine’s grain to Romania at half price, and President Maia Sandu is defending that choice against Moldovan farmers who stand to lose from it. What Kyiv was still negotiating a week earlier is now a signed tariff cut, and the growers left to absorb it have threatened mass protests.
Sandu ties Ukraine’s harvest to Moldova’s security
Speaking on Radio Moldova, Sandu argued that helping a wartime neighbor keep its export income is worth the strain at home, NewsMaker reported.
“If Ukraine cannot sell its products and has no money to defend itself, then we will have bigger problems than we do today,” she said. “We cannot turn our backs on Ukrainians who are bombed every night and every day wake up, grow grain, and resist. Through their resistance, they protect our peace too.”
She set Moldova’s role against that of larger backers: “Other states help them much more—with financial aid, with military aid. Here we can help them, with these transit routes.”
Farmers set a 21 August deadline
Moldova has halved rail transit tariffs on Ukrainian goods from 10 August to 31 December 2026, a move that could earn Moldovan Railways several million euros and route around 10% of Ukraine’s expected six million tons of 2026 cargo through its territory, Curs de Guvernare reported.
The cut has unsettled local growers. The association Forța Fermierilor (Farmers’ Force) says they face real risks and wants a seat in overseeing the transit. After meeting Prime Minister Vasile Tofan on 17 August, it warned of “massive” protests unless the government shows progress by 21 August.
Trending Now
Russian strikes push grain onto the rails
Ukraine wants the overland route because Russia’s strikes have made the sea route unreliable. Odesa’s ports handle about 90% of Ukraine’s grain, and an overnight strike on Odesa on 17 August damaged another foreign civilian ship.
In July alone, Russian attacks damaged 28 vessels at Greater Odesa’s ports and killed 21 sailors, monitor Andrii Klymenko reported. The rail line to Romania’s Constanța port is the safer alternative. Even in 2023, when Moldova moved to shield its market from Ukrainian grain, it kept transit open.

Ghana has publicly demanded that Russia halt the recruitment of its citizens to fight in the war against Ukraine, following 17 August talks between the two countries' foreign ministers in Moscow, The Moscow Times reported. Ghana's top diplomat said Moscow agreed to work on the matter, while Russia confirmed that Ghanaians had signed military contracts but defended the practice.
Ghana brings its dead and missing to the table
Ghanaian Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa accused Russia of the "illegal recruitment" of Ghanaians for the war on Ukraine. After the Moscow talks, he said his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, agreed to work toward resolving the issue, according to Interfax Russia. Ablakwa reported that 62 of his compatriots had died in Ukraine, with a further 15 listed as missing, Bloomberg reported.
Russia confirms the contracts, then justifies them
Lavrov confirmed that Ghanaian citizens had signed contracts with Russia's Defense Ministry. He claimed the Ghanaians had signed out of solidarity with a country that had helped Africa fight racism and for financial reasons. He stated that Moscow had received similar appeals from other countries, and that a dedicated Defense Ministry structure reviews such cases and would examine the additional requests raised by the Ghanaian side.
Fighters from 51 countries now held in Ukraine after fighting for Russia, ombudsman says
A pattern stretching across two continents
The recruitment of African nationals to reinforce Russian forces has alarmed governments across the region. Kenya and South Africa had already pressed Moscow with similar demands. In February, Kenyan intelligence said Russia had deceptively lured more than 1,000 Kenyans into the war, many of them promised jobs as truck drivers or security guards.
In December 2025, South Africa detained five people suspected of recruiting mercenaries for the Russian army. Last fall, Duduzile Zuma-Sambudla, daughter of former South African President Jacob Zuma, was reportedly involved, convincing 20 young men they were traveling to Russia for bodyguard training to later work in her father's party. Botswana in July reported the deceptive recruitment of its citizens, saying the number of victims was "growing at an alarming rate," and Panama later leveled similar accusations. Russia's Foreign Ministry claimed the signed contracts were voluntary.
Over 1,000 Kenyans lured into Russia’s war in Ukraine, 50+ Ghanaians killed there — three governments confirmed it, none confronted Moscow
Ghana's confrontation echoes earlier ones
Ukrainian officials say the death toll among African recruits has climbed into the hundreds, turning what Moscow frames as voluntary service into what several governments describe as trafficking.
In March, three governments had already confirmed their citizens were being lured to the war, including more than 1,000 Kenyans and over 50 Ghanaians killed. Kenya said the same month that Russia had agreed to stop using its recruits, though families of the missing were still waiting.
A European Parliament resolution has separately accused Russia of stripping African recruits of their documents and sending them to the Ukrainian front.

Sports Direct owner Mike Ashley tightens hold on Hugo Boss

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18

The retail billionaire Mike Ashley has signalled that his summer shopping spree may be far from over, after he increased his stake in Hugo Boss to nearly half.
  Ashley’s Frasers Group, which last week bought the Harvey Nichols department stores for a reported £40m, increased its shareholding in the German fashion house to 48%, just short of taking full control.
  In June, Frasers made a nearly €2bn (£1.73bn) takeover offer for the luxury group, but its board rejected the bid as “inadequate” and urged shareholders not to accept it.
The new, higher stake is a result of 17.6% of shareholders accepting Ashley’s offer, which amounted to €38 a share. That bid reflected only a 4% premium to Hugo Boss’s shares when it was tabled.
 Axel Rudolph, an analyst at the investing platform IG, said it was “another major step towards gaining control” of Hugo Boss. Ashley’s new shareholding put Frasers “firmly in the driving seat as it looks to increase its influence”, he added.
Frasers, which has stocked Hugo Boss products in its stores for some years, has taken an increasingly activist role since it first took a stake in the German group in June 2020. It has pushed for change at the company, which has faced struggling sales in women’s clothing and sluggish demand in its important Chinese market.
The Hugo Boss chair, Stephan Sturm, said on Tuesday: “We appreciate Frasers Group’s continued long-term commitment to Hugo Boss and look forward to maintaining a constructive relationship with them as our single largest shareholder.”
Ashley has been building his interests in luxury fashion in recent years with the Flannels chain and a large stake in the British handbag maker Mulberry.
The businessman also recently became the fifth-biggest shareholder of Burberry, taking a 4.2% stake last month that was worth about £160m. The 170-year-old trenchcoat maker has struggled amid a global slowdown in demand for luxury goods, and last year said it would cut 1,700 jobs after posting a £66m loss.
Ashley bought Harvey Nichols out of administration last week after the upmarket chain, which has 13 stores and 1,200 employees, said it could run out of money if it did not find new funding.
If he did eventually take control of Hugo Boss, it would add another brand to the group that already owns the Frasers department stores, formerly House of Fraser, as well as Sports Direct and the bicycle retailer Evans Cycles.
The entrepreneur, who is known for his controversial business tactics, retains a 73% stake in Frasers, which he built from a single sports store in Maidenhead, Berkshire, opened in 1982 with £10,000 from his parents. He stepped down from the board in 2022.
His wealth grew by £317m to £3.44bn last year, according to the Sunday Times rich list.
The retail analyst Nick Bubb wrote on Tuesday that the Hugo Boss bid was “surprisingly successful, getting up to nearly 48% ownership of the business, despite the apparently token nature of its €38 offer”.
Ashley also launched a bid for the Australian footwear business Accent Group this summer.

Israel, Honduras revive defence ties amid Latin America shift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
08:48:36 UTC
17:48:36 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel, Honduras deepen defence ties amid Latin America rightward shift
Israel and Honduras have signed a new memorandum of understanding aimed at deepening defence cooperation, marking the latest sign of a broader shift in Latin American relations with Israel despite its nearly three-year genocidal war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, nearly one-third of them children.
The agreement between the two countries places military and security cooperation at the centre of a relationship that had appeared to cool under Honduras' previous left-wing government.
In a statement, Israel's Defence Ministry said Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and his Honduran counterpart, Enrique Rodríguez Burchard, signed the agreement to "deepen defence cooperation" between the two countries.
The signing was attended by Israeli Defence Ministry Director-General Amir Baram, the senior deputy head of the Policy and Political-Military Bureau, Israel's defence attaché to Honduras and other senior officials from both countries.
"The MOU signed today constitutes a significant milestone in strengthening defense relations between the two countries and establishes a framework for long-term cooperation based on shared interests and values," the Israeli ministry said.
The Honduran delegation was also given a window into the military experience Israel has accumulated during years of warfare across the region.
"The Honduran delegation received a briefing on the security and operational challenges Israel has faced in recent years, including key lessons from the multifront war and from contending with evolving and emerging threats in the region," the ministry said.
According to the statement, Honduran officials were also briefed on the Israeli Defence Ministry's current activities and "key aspects of Israel's defense and defense-industrial establishment".
Marta Tawil Kuri, a research professor at the Center for International Studies at El Colegio de México, told The New Arab that the agreement signals a strengthening of Honduras-Israel relations and a return to a familiar model.
"It signals a return to the pattern under [former president] Juan Orlando Hernandez: military cooperation as the central axis of the bilateral relationship," Kuri said. "The MOU signed by [Honduran President Nasry] Asfura with Katz reproduces that same logic: security/defense as the priority instrument of the relationship, rather than the Palestinian question as such."
From Gaza criticism to defence cooperation
The agreement marks a shift in tone from Honduras' position during the early stages of Israel's assault on Gaza.
Under former president Xiomara Castro, Honduras recalled its ambassador to Israel for consultations in 2023, after condemning the war and alleged violations of international law in the Gaza Strip.
But Honduras never severed diplomatic relations with Israel.
The country appointed a new ambassador earlier this month, who was received by Israeli President Isaac Herzog, and is now seeking deeper defence and security cooperation.
"Castro's pro-Palestinian gestures were limited, since Honduras never broke relations, kept diplomatic staff at the Jerusalem embassy, and took no formal position on South Africa's case against Israel at the International Court of Justice," Kuri said.
"In other words, the 2023 'tension' was more symbolic than structural. Asfura's turn does not break with an estranged relationship. It openly resumes a relationship that, according to the authors themselves, was never fully severed, only made less visible."
The Israeli Defence Ministry described Honduras as an "important partner" in Central America, highlighting in particular its record of supporting Israel in international forums.
Honduras was among just nine countries that voted against a 2017 UN General Assembly resolution rejecting the US decision to recognise Jerusalem as Israel's capital.
In 2021, Honduras became one of the first countries to move its embassy to Jerusalem, joining the US, Guatemala and Kosovo.
That history, Kuri said, points to a relationship in which defence and security ties have gone hand in hand with diplomatic support for Israel.
"Under Netanyahu, Israel systematically capitalized on the rise of right-wing governments in Central America (multiple Netanyahu visits to the region since 2007) to sell weapons and security technology — the Honduran case of 2016-2018 was paradigmatic — in exchange for Honduran diplomatic support in international forums, such as Honduras's 2017 vote against the UN resolution condemning the US embassy move to Jerusalem," she said.
The same calculation has acquired greater significance as Israel faces mounting international pressure over its conduct in Gaza, Kuri added.
"With Israel's current international isolation over Gaza, that same calculation repeats itself: every Latin American ally willing to deepen military cooperation (selling it equipment, buying its equipment) is also a vote and a voice of political backing at a moment of intense global diplomatic pressure."
Latin America's rightward shift
Honduras' decision to deepen its alliance with Israel under the new agreement comes amid a broader political shift across parts of Latin America, where right-wing governments have sought closer relations with Israel.
Kuri argued that leaders such as Asfura were also linking relations with Israel to "the need to show Washington an unambiguous alignment".
In Colombia, the nationalist government of President Abelardo de la Espriella recently reversed the decision by his left-wing predecessor, Gustavo Petro, to sever diplomatic relations with Israel in protest at the Gaza war.
Venezuela and Israel, meanwhile, have agreed to establish a mechanism to resume consular services after 17 years.
In Central America, Kuri described Honduras' trajectory as the "most volatile of the three" when compared with El Salvador and Guatemala, largely because Honduras "has seen genuine party alternation (right-left-right)".
"Guatemala maintained near-continuous alignment with Israel from Pérez Molina through Giammattei (2012-2024), and El Salvador moved from pro-Palestinian FMLN governments (Funes, Sánchez Cerén) to Bukele, markedly pro-Israel despite his Palestinian origin," she told The New Arab.
"The August 2026 agreement confirms that Honduras is realigning with the regional pro-Israel bloc."
That realignment comes even as Palestinians continue to be killed in Gaza despite the ceasefire agreed between Israel and Hamas in October 2025.
Israeli fire has killed more than 1,250 Palestinians in Gaza since the ceasefire, most of them civilians, according to Palestinian authorities.

Hong Kong customs arrests 10 over HK$56 million cannabis haul bound for Europe, Africa

Hong Kong customs has arrested 10 people and seized suspected cannabis buds worth an estimated HK$56 million (US$7 million) in a month-long operation targeting a syndicate accused of smuggling the drug from Southeast Asia to Europe and Africa via the city.
“We targeted transit baggage from Southeast Asia for inspection. The average visitor arriving in or transiting through Hong Kong should carry different types of clothing and personal items for a long-haul journey,” Senior Inspector Chan Kai-hin said.
“However, X-ray scans showed that the luggage contained no personal items, and instead revealed suspicious uniform parcels tightly packed inside the suitcases.”
He added that another indication was the condition of the suitcases.
Those used to transport the suspected cannabis were new, unlike the luggage typically used by tourists, which might show signs of wear and tear, including scratches, stickers and labels from previous trips, the department said.
Chow Kai-kwong, a senior customs investigator, said an investigation was launched immediately based on the passenger information displayed on the baggage. Ten people were subsequently identified and arrested at the airport.

Flat vacancy rates rise slightly in Zurich and Winterthur
The number of vacant flats has risen slightly in canton Zurich. Nevertheless, housing remains extremely scarce in the two Swiss cities.
The cantonal vacancy rate has risen from 0.48% to 0.52%, the canton announced on Tuesday. As was the case last year, the rate remains below 1% in all regions of Zurich.
More
Zurich: Welcome to the world capital of housing shortages!
In the city of Zurich, exactly 252 flats were vacant on June 1. That is 17 more than the previous year, which corresponds to a very low figure of 0.11%. In Winterthur, the authorities counted 116 unoccupied flats, 12 more than the year before. The vacancy rate there stands at 0.2%.
A key reason for the ongoing housing shortage and low vacancy rates is the low level of construction activity in recent years.
