Poland has not yet made a decision on Patriot missiles for Ukraine, but the US is pressing - government official
Kyiv • UNN
Polish Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk said that a decision on transferring Patriot missiles to Ukraine has not yet been made. He noted that the US, in particular General Hrynkevych, is actively urging the Polish government to do so.
Poland has not yet made a decision on providing Ukraine with additional Patriot missiles, but the Americans are pressuring the Polish government over these interceptors, Poland's Deputy Minister of National Defence Cezary Tomczyk said on air on Polskie Radio 24, UNN reports.
Details
Tomczyk was asked whether Poland would provide Ukraine with Patriot missiles. "No decisions have been made on this matter," Tomczyk said. He recalled that Poland has so far supported Ukraine with several such missiles "out of the hundreds we have." He assured that Poland is safe. "Polish stocks are full, secure, and being replenished," he added.
He noted that any decision to transfer missiles must be made at the highest level. "First, the Minister of National Defence submits recommendations, and then the Council of Ministers makes the decision," he explained the procedure.
"Ukraine's main need today is protection against ballistic missiles. Cities such as Kyiv and Lviv are attacked by Russia every day. Obviously, Ukraine is asking its Western partners to provide or enable the purchase of missiles for Patriot systems," the Polish deputy defence minister said.
He stressed that Poland receives most of the calls from the United States.
"It is precisely the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Grynkiewicz, as well as the US administration, who very often convey these appeals to the Polish government to provide missiles for Patriot systems whenever possible," he acknowledged.

UK pay growth slows as Iran war prompts cost of living squeeze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:18:19 UTC
16:18:19 KST

Wage growth in the UK slowed in June and vacancies hit a five-year low as workers came under pressure from a renewed cost of living squeeze amid the economic impact from the Iran war.
Figures from the Office for National Statistics show average growth in total earnings, including bonuses, fell to 4.1% in the three months to June, down from 4.4% in the three months to May.
The pay slowdown could deter the Bank of England from raising interest rates this year, some economists suggested.
Liz McKeown, the ONS director of economic statistics, said the data showed “some softening” in the jobs market despite a broadly unchanged picture overall, in a potential sign of stabilisation after a sharper slowdown earlier this year.
“Regular wage growth has remained broadly stable in recent months. However, private sector pay growth has continued to ease, while public sector pay growth remains elevated due to the timing of the latest NHS pay awards,” she added.
Pay growth excluding bonuses strengthened slightly from 3.4% to 3.5%. City economists had forecast the rate would remain unchanged. The number of workers on company payrolls fell by 13,000 in July, matching the decline in June after larger falls in previous months.
However, earnings growth, excluding bonuses, in the private sector slowed to 2.8%, the weakest growth rate since October 2020. Pay growth in the public sector strengthened to 6.1%, reflecting the payment of NHS staff pay rises earlier in 2026 compared to 2025, which distorts the figure.
Vacancies fell to a five-year low as small businesses warned they were facing a rise in employment costs. There were 707,000 in May to July, a drop of 6,000 compared with the previous three months and the lowest level since spring 2021.
“Ongoing weakness in private sector hiring and wage growth suggests the bar is still relatively high for a rate hike in 2026, barring a severe and prolonged spike in energy prices,” said James Smith, a developed markets economist at the Dutch bank ING.
Modupe Adegbembo, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said there was little in the data to make the Bank of England more worried about labour-market-driven inflation pressure.
“Whilst the adjustment still looks orderly rather than disorderly, we think the BoE will remain cautious around the state of the labour market,” Adegbembo added.
Money market pricing shows City economists expect one increase in UK interest rates by the end of the year, which would lift the Bank rate from 3.75% to 4%.
The headline rate of unemployment remained unchanged at 4.9%. City economists had forecast a drop to 4.8%.
The snapshot comes as households face a fresh hit to living standards as the fallout from the Middle East conflict rattles the world economy. Official figures due on Wednesday are expected to show that a rise in energy bills drove UK inflation close to 3% in July.
Annual growth in earnings after taking account of inflation was 1.3% in the three months to June. However, workers could face a squeeze as rising inflation approaches the slowing rate of earnings growth.
The figures highlight the challenge for Andy Burnham’s government to ease the financial pressure on households before a difficult autumn budget.
The prime minister used his first week in office to announce a series of “breathing space” measures to ease the cost of living, and he has promised to combat unemployment as young people bear the brunt from recent higher rates of joblessness.
Ministers are awaiting a review into youth jobs from Alan Milburn, the former Labour cabinet minister, after the number of 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet) surpassed a million earlier this year for the first time in more than a decade.
Before a final report this autumn, Milburn told the Guardian this week that he would call on the government to “turbocharge” the provision of internships for young people with special educational needs.
Earlier this month he told this newspaper he would recommend new requirements for English primary schools to take steps to identify children at risk of leaving education at 16 without finding a job.
Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said: “It’s encouraging to see signs of progress in the latest figures, with employment on the up and a continued fall in unemployment rate.”
He said the government had put in place measures to overhaul the benefits system and to support people to find work, including a youth jobs grant to encourage businesses to hire young people.
“We will continue to reform welfare and employment support so that more people can live independently and restore opportunity across the country,” he added.
Economists said the figures showed signs of a slowing jobs market that could strengthen the case for the Bank of England to hold back from raising interest rates.
Threadneedle Street has signalled that a weaker backdrop in the labour market could help limit the capacity for stubbornly high inflation becoming entrenched in the economy.
Jake Finney, a senior economist at PwC UK, said: “On the face of it, the latest labour market report looks relatively benign. Unemployment, employment and inactivity remain broadly stable, while vacancies edged down but are essentially levelling off. The jobs market remains soft, but it isn’t collapsing.”

Japan protests South Korean survey ship near Takeshima
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:18:04 UTC
16:18:04 KST

- Japan's Coast Guard confirmed South Korea's survey ship Tamhae 3 conducted an unauthorized marine survey in Japan's EEZ near Takeshima on August 7.
- South Korean vessels conducted similar unauthorized surveys near Takeshima at least three times in June 2026 and once in May 2026, each drawing a Japanese protest.
Japan’s Coast Guard confirmed a South Korean survey ship, the Tamhae 3, was conducting an unauthorized marine survey inside Japan’s exclusive economic zone west of the Takeshima islets on August 7, prompting formal protests from Tokyo, Japan’s Foreign Ministry and Coast Guard said.
A Japan Coast Guard patrol vessel spotted the Tamhae 3 at around 1:33 p.m. on August 7, roughly 17 nautical miles (31 kilometers) west of Takeshima, extending what appeared to be a wire-like device into the water from its stern. South Korea had not submitted a prior request for Japan’s consent to conduct the survey, according to Japan’s Foreign Ministry.
The Coast Guard’s patrol boat radioed the Tamhae 3 to demand it halt the activity, saying marine research without Japan’s consent was not permitted. The survey ship crossed the geographic midline to the west at around 6:34 p.m. that evening, and the Coast Guard confirmed no further unusual activity afterward.
Japan’s Foreign Ministry lodged formal protests through two channels the same day. Masaaki Kanai, director-general of the ministry’s Asian and Oceanian Affairs Bureau, protested to Sang-yeol Lee, deputy chief of mission at the South Korean Embassy in Tokyo. Separately, Kazuo Nakajo, deputy chief of mission at the Japanese Embassy in Seoul, raised the issue with Min-kyung Lee, director-general of the Asia-Pacific bureau at South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
South Korea rejected Japan’s protest. Its Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the survey was legitimate under international and domestic law and reaffirmed its position that the islets, known as Dokdo in South Korea, are its sovereign territory. “Japan filed an issue with an activity that is legitimate under international and domestic laws,” the ministry said, adding that Japan’s objections had been rejected through diplomatic channels.
The August 7 sighting was not an isolated case. South Korean research vessels conducted similar unauthorized survey activity in the same waters three times in June 2026 alone, each prompting a separate protest from Japan’s Foreign Ministry, and a further instance was recorded in May 2026. Japan’s Foreign Ministry and Coast Guard have logged a recurring pattern of these incidents dating back years, including episodes in 2022 involving the South Korean research vessel Hae Yang 2000, which was also observed trailing wire-like equipment north of Takeshima. In one 2022 case, the Coast Guard asked the vessel’s crew what they were doing, but the ship declined to answer, citing South Korea’s claim of sovereignty over the islets.
Takeshima, a small island group in the Sea of Japan controlled by South Korea and referred to there as Dokdo, has been administered by Seoul since the early 1950s. Japan disputes that control and claims sovereignty over the islets, making them one of the longest-running points of friction between the two U.S. treaty allies. Japan’s exclusive economic zone claim around Takeshima overlaps with waters South Korea also claims, and the two countries’ boundary in the area remains contested rather than formally delimited, which is why Japan characterizes vessel movements there in terms of a “geographic midline” rather than an agreed maritime border.

Russian agent who registered 27 Starlink terminals for Russian forces arrested – photo, video

Source: Kharkiv Oblast Prosecutor's Office; Security Service of Ukraine (SSU)
Quote from Kharkiv Oblast Prosecutor's Office: "In the frontline city of Izium in Kharkiv Oblast, a 33-year-old man registered 27 satellite communications terminals. One of them later ended up in the possession of Russian forces in the temporarily occupied part of Zaporizhzhia Oblast. Under the procedural supervision of Kharkiv Oblast Prosecutor's Office, he has already been served with a notice of suspicion of treason committed under martial law."
Details: The suspect is an unemployed internally displaced person from the temporarily occupied city of Khrustalnyi in Luhansk Oblast. After moving to Izium, he looked for work on social media, where, according to investigators, he was contacted by a representative of Russia.
They continued communicating via Telegram. The Russian handler offered to pay the man to register Starlink terminals. He agreed.
To activate one of them, the suspect enlisted a front person and then sent the Russian representative photographic evidence that the task had been completed. He received UAH 1,500 (about US$30) on his bank card in return.
Investigators later established that one of the terminals registered by the man was used by Russian forces in the temporarily occupied part of Zaporizhzhia Oblast. It was used to provide communications and control attack drones.
The man registered a total of 27 terminals. Law enforcement officers are currently investigating a possible Russian connection and establishing all the circumstances surrounding their use.
Ukrainska Pravda has learned that the man was detained on 6 August.
The court remanded the suspect in custody without the right to bail.

More

Russia warns Britain of 'consequences' for supplying drones to Ukraine
LONDON, Aug 18 - Russia warned Britain on Tuesday it would face consequences for supplying drones to Ukraine which are used to attack targets on Russian territory.

Four indicators to determine the increase in the minimum wage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:16:10 UTC
16:16:10 KST

Tuesday 18 August 2026 09:25
Tuesday, 18 August 2026, 09:25
PHOTO Pixabay
Font size
The government and social partners have agreed on a mechanism for determining the country’s minimum wage, the government press service announced.
Changes in four indicators, each given equal weight, will determine the extent to which the minimum wage can increase. These are the price index for the small consumer basket, gross median and gross average wages, and gross value added per employed person over the past 10 years.
The lower limit of the wage will be the minimum wage for the previous year, while the upper limit will be determined by the weighted average of the four indicators for the same period.
Employers and trade unions will have until May 15 to negotiate the level of the minimum wage, and until May 31 to prepare a report, based on which the Council of Ministers will determine its final amount for the following year.

The U.S. Congress is struggling to deal with AI-generated errors - Politico
Kyiv • UNN
More and more U.S. congressional staffers are relying on generative AI to prepare bills. However, this is leading to errors.
U.S. congressional lawyers are struggling to cope with a flood of legislative proposals created using artificial intelligence tools, many of which are riddled with errors and contain careless wording. UNN reports, citing Politico.
Details
The workload of the House Office of Legislative Counsel is increasing as more congressional offices and outside groups rely on generative AI to draft bills. This is evidenced by interviews with eight current and former officials who work or worked in the office.
They noted that artificial intelligence’s ability to quickly generate huge volumes of text is forcing the Office of Legislative Counsel’s lawyers to spend significantly more time reviewing and reworking proposals. In many cases, the drafts contain errors that could have consequences far beyond Washington - delaying the passage of legislation and creating the risk of lawsuits because of incorrectly cited legislative acts or inaccurate legal definitions.
Artificial intelligence is useful in many areas. But it is not capable of drafting bills that you would want to enact into law
However, four congressional staffers involved in drafting bills told Politico that the use of AI is becoming increasingly widespread in the House of Representatives, with staffers and civil society organizations relying on it in their daily work, including when analyzing and drafting legislation.
These staffers are preparing for artificial intelligence to increase their already heavy workload. This was indicated by OLC Director Warren Burke during a March hearing - even in the absence of any errors. He declined to comment for this article.

South Korean president pushes to reclaim wartime military command by 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:14:58 UTC
16:14:58 KST

South Korean President Lee Jae-myung has reaffirmed his commitment to regaining wartime operational control (OPCON) of South Korean forces from the United States before his term ends in 2030, according to a local media report.
Speaking on Tuesday at a Cabinet meeting, Lee said the transfer should be completed during his presidency in line with the government’s original plan, Yonhap News Agency reported.
He also ordered officials to accelerate plans to acquire nuclear-powered submarines and said South Korea’s efforts to strengthen its own military capabilities should complement rather than weaken its alliance with the US.
South Korea transferred wartime operational control to the US-led United Nations Command during the 1950-53 Korean War.
It later came under the South Korea-US Combined Forces Command in 1978. Seoul regained peacetime operational control in 1994, while wartime OPCON remains under US command.
Lee’s comments came after US President Donald Trump said he had ordered the Pentagon to substantially reduce joint military exercises with South Korea amid apparent efforts to encourage dialogue with North Korea.
The allies began their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises on Monday.
Lee said OPCON transfer was essential as warfare evolves towards hybrid forms and the global security environment rapidly changes.
He also called for the planned integration of South Korea’s three military academies into a single institution to proceed “without wavering.”
“When the alliance is firm, the foundation for security will become stronger,” Lee said, adding that South Korea’s importance as an ally would grow as it strengthens its own capabilities.

Ukraine's parliament returns with defence and foreign ministry crises unresolved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:13:19 UTC
16:13:19 KST

Ukraine's parliament reconvenes on Tuesday with the defence and foreign ministries still without permanent heads, a month after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy abruptly dismissed Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister.
Ukraine's parliament returns to work on Tuesday after its summer break, reconvening with two of the government's most sensitive wartime portfolios still without heads.
When the Verkhovna Rada voted in Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi’s new cabinet on 16 July, it approved every post except two: defence minister and foreign affairs minister.
For a month now, the defence ministry has been without permanent head, amid Russia's intensifying ballistic missile attacks, an unusual situation for a country defending itself from the full-scale invasion for over four years.
Under Ukraine's constitution only the president can submit nominees for the two posts, since both fall within his direct authority as supreme commander-in-chief and head of the country's foreign policy.
Zelenskyy has so far yet to do so for either ministry.
Andrii Sybiha, who had already been permanent head of foreign ministry before the cabinet reshuffle, was kept on as acting foreign minister under a similar Cabinet order.
In the meantime, the defence ministry has been run by Yevhenii Khmara, the former acting head of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU), whom Zelenskyy tasked with the job on 16 July.
The ousted defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov suggested Khmara is not starting from scratch: in an interview on 6 August, he said he had personally handed his successor a detailed "war plan" and walked him through it.
"This was the first thing I did, I showed it to him personally," Fedorov said, adding that he had "explained the logic - how that logic of the war plan then deconstructs into procurement, into development," breaking an overall strategy into hundreds of individual projects, from weapons production to financing.
Street protests continued
Street protests over Fedorov's removal have continued regardless.
On 16 August Dmytro Koziatynskyi, a war veteran and one of the protest organisers said the aim was "to remind the president of the importance of dialogue between the authorities and society, as well as of the fact that the president himself must bear responsibility for the consequences of all questionable personnel decisions."
A petition read out at the latest demonstration and later handed to a representative of the Presidential Office pointed to one concession already won - Zelenskyy’s decision to replace Oleksandr Syrskyi with Mykhailo Drapatyi as commander-in-chief - while pressing him to explain other contested picks, including Rustem Umerov's move to head the Foreign Intelligence Service.
Notably, the petition focused less on the minister and more on preserving the reform agenda Fedorov had championed, including anti-corruption measures in military procurement, a more accountable chain of command and Ukraine's push into drone and data-driven warfare.
Zelenskyy has said he offered Fedorov "a prominent position in the government" centred on the tech sector, but Fedorov rejected every alternative, saying he will only return as defence minister.

foldable aluminum beach wagon integrates electric propulsion for soft-sand mobility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:08:50 UTC
16:08:50 KST

LITEFAR B1 Wagon reimagines the journey from car to shore
LITEFAR B1 is a foldable electric beach wagon designed to transport chairs, coolers, towels, and other equipment from vehicles to the shoreline across pavement, wooden paths, grass, and soft sand. The design integrates the frame, wheels, power system, and controls into a single structure, combining an aluminum-alloy frame with internally routed wiring, dual hub motors, and wide balloon tires. The B1 is organized around a series of vertical columns that define the frame, folding mechanism, and electrical system. Motor and control wiring is routed inside the structure, keeping the exterior free of exposed cables and separate technical components.
Hub Motors and Balloon Tires Adapt B1 to Changing Terrain
The aluminum-alloy frame provides the structure for the fabric cargo compartment while incorporating the handle, battery, lighting, and control system. Its upright geometry also allows the wagon to fold into a more compact configuration for transport. Soft sand can cause conventional utility wagons to sink and experience increased drag. The B1 addresses these conditions with wide, low-pressure balloon tires combined with two 600W brushless hub motors integrated into the rear wheel assemblies. The wheel-mounted drivetrain eliminates exposed chains, belts, and external transmission components, keeping the propulsion system contained within the wheels. The aligned wheel configuration also reduces drag when turning across loose terrain.
A pressure-sensitive smart handle adjusts motor assistance as the wagon is pulled or pushed. Remote and app-based controls provide additional options for adjusting speed and movement, while releasing the handle activates electronic braking. The electronics, controls, and wiring are contained within the frame, allowing the various systems to operate without introducing additional external components. LITEFAR B1 (see more here) is equipped with a removable 24,000 mAh battery that powers the wagon and can also function as a portable power source for phones, cameras, and other devices. A telescopic light is integrated into the frame, while interchangeable wheels allow the wagon to operate across grass, gravel, and compact trails in addition to sand. The combination of these elements extends the wagon’s use across different environments while maintaining the same overall structural configuration.
the smart handle provides intuitive motor assistance as the user guides the wagon along the shoreline
A Modular System Extends LITEFAR B1 Wagon’s Serviceability
The B1 has been developed as a production product rather than a speculative mobility concept. LITEFAR has completed small-batch manufacturing and conducted testing across soft sand, wooden ramps, grass, gravel, and inclined surfaces. Testing has focused on loaded movement, motor assistance, folding reliability, braking response, and transitions between different ground conditions. The modular construction allows key components, including the battery, wheels, and control accessories, to be installed, replaced, or serviced independently, reducing the need to replace the complete product when individual modules require attention.
The B1 brings propulsion, power, storage, lighting, and control systems together within a foldable aluminum structure. Its design addresses the different surfaces encountered between a vehicle and the shoreline, using integrated electric assistance to reduce the physical effort involved in transporting equipment. The LITEFAR B1 is currently available on Indiegogo, with initial deliveries scheduled for October–November 2026.

modularized open steel grid reshapes family living on tight site in taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:08:47 UTC
16:08:47 KST

MOM House Replaces Concrete House with Expandable Steel Grid
Located at the end of a narrow dead-end alley in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, MOM House by Supra-Simplicities + KCCS replaces an aging two-story reinforced concrete dwelling with a lightweight steelresidence for a retired mother and flexible accommodation for her two adult children. The site is enclosed on three sides by neighboring houses and a school, with a single point of access and limited daylight and natural ventilation. Its adjacency to the school’s sports field, however, provides an open outlook that becomes a key spatial and environmental element of the design. To minimize the family’s displacement during construction, the project uses a prefabricated steel construction system that allows for rapid assembly and reoccupation. Named MOM House, or Modularized Open Model, the residence is conceived as an expandable structural framework based on a repetitive grid of steel modules. The open system is designed to accommodate changing domestic requirements through incremental expansion and spatial reconfiguration, while also simplifying fabrication and on-site assembly.
The prototype consists of eight steel grid modules arranged along a linear axis, with one intentionally irregular structural bay interrupting the repetitive sequence. This deviation serves several functions within the structural system. It accommodates rainwater drainage by directing runoff toward the garden below, while also establishing a joint that can support future extension. Environmental infrastructure is therefore incorporated directly into the structural framework rather than treated as a separate technical layer. The modular system also establishes the house’s spatial organization. The ground floor is arranged around the daily routines of the retired mother, with the main living spaces connected directly to an internal garden shared with her two dogs. Guest rooms for the adult children occupy the upper levels and are supplemented by skylights. Between these spaces, a family lounge and communal terrace open toward the adjacent sports field, creating a vertical sequence of shared and private areas.
Modular Aluminum Facade Responds to Light and Environment
The sports field provides a visual opening within an otherwise enclosed urban setting. The upper-level terrace and family lounge are positioned to take advantage of this outlook, while skylights introduce additional daylight into the upper rooms. The arrangement uses the site’s limited openness to establish connections between the interior, garden, and surrounding landscape. The vertical organization also allows the compact footprint to accommodate different patterns of use. The mother’s everyday living spaces remain connected to the ground-level garden, while the upper floors provide more flexible accommodation for visiting family members. This arrangement allows the house to respond to both current and future household needs within the modular framework.
The collaborative design team between Supra-Simplicities KCCS extends the steel grid into the building envelope, which is clad in prefabricated matte-finished aluminum panels. The modular facade follows the logic of the structural system, supporting efficient fabrication and allowing individual panels to be replaced in the future. Its subtly reflective surface responds to changes in daylight, vegetation, and the surrounding buildings. The lightweight steel structure and prefabricated envelope establish a construction system suited to the constrained site. By combining repetitive structural modules, prefabricated components, and provisions for future expansion, MOM House treats adaptability as part of the building’s initial design rather than as a later modification. Across the project, the structural grid organizes construction, program, environmental systems, and the potential for future growth. The resulting residence replaces the previous concrete dwelling with a lightweight framework designed around the family’s present routines while retaining the capacity to accommodate changing domestic requirements over time.

Belarus’ PM visits Orsha Meat Canning Plant

2026-08-18
07:07:00 UTC

ORSHA, 18 August (BelTA) – Belarusian Prime Minister Aleksandr Turchin visited Orsha Meat Canning Plant on 18 August, BelTA has learned.
The plant has been placed under the trust management of Agrokombinat Dzerzhinsky. Key topics of discussion included capacity utilization, development of the raw material base, and prospects for increasing production volumes, including canned meat and baby food.
The enterprise is one of the country’s largest producers of canned meat and meat-and-vegetable products for baby food, as well as general consumer products. It operates an automated line for baby food production, using meat from young animals raised without growth stimulants or antibiotics. The plant produces 12 types of meat purees for infants and has switched to glass packaging for baby food. The range of canned meat and meat-and-vegetable products includes 16 items, and animal feed - four. In July alone, the plant sold 1,109,000 cans of canned meat, in addition to baby food.
 
 
  
 
 
 
 
According to Pavel Rynzak, manager of Orsha Meat Canning Plant, the products are actively supplied to the domestic market and Russia. “Adult canned food production volumes have grown by about 15% over the past six months. We are launching a new, more automated and advanced canned meat production facility, which will allow us to further increase volumes and meet all consumer demand. In the future, we plan to build another facility on the site to produce pet food in pouches - so we will be producing both dry and wet pet food,” he said.
 
 
 
 
  
  
  
  
 Konstantin Chekhovsky, head of sales at Orsha Meat Canning Plant, noted the growing export potential of the enterprise. “Over the past few months, the processing facility has seen a significant increase in capacity utilization, and the plant now has a large volume of raw materials, which is primarily directed toward canned meat production. Today, our focus is shifting toward export supplies, but we have not forgotten the domestic market. With the increased raw material flow, we have significantly expanded our external market potential. For example, in the first seven months of 2026, we exported 500,000 more cans of canned meat compared to the same period last year. In previous years, we also saw steady growth. Cost reductions have helped us achieve high competitiveness for the finished product,” he said.

In addition, Vitebsk Oblast First Vice Governor Sergei Levkovich briefed the prime minister on the prospects for agricultural development and processing enterprises in the agro-industrial complex of Vitebsk Oblast. The oblast’s processing sector comprises four meat processing plants and eight dairy plants. The raw material zone includes 153 agricultural organizations with a total dairy herd of 149,000 cows. There are 331 dairy farms and 107 dairy complexes and farms equipped with milking parlors. The dairy complexes house 68,000 head, accounting for 50.8% of the oblast’s total milk output. In 2025, the average milk yield was 4,641 kg, while on the complexes it reached 5,937 kg, 28% above the regional average.
 
  
  
  
  
 A number of large-scale projects are planned for beef production. Agrokombinat Dzerzhinsky plans to build six cattle fattening complexes with a capacity of 4,000 head each (two each in Vitebsk District, Orsha District, and Tolochin District). This will provide an additional 12,000 tonnes of meat per year. In addition, the modernization of four existing complexes with a total capacity of 14,000 head will yield an additional 7,000 tonnes. A complex for breeding beef cattle with a capacity of 3,200 head is expected to come online in September 2026. In pig farming, the oblast is showing steady growth: in 2025, production reached 58,700 tonnes of pork, with plans to exceed 70,000 tonnes by 2028. The implementation of all planned projects will significantly strengthen the region’s food security and boost its export potential.
 
Next stop on prime minister’s itinerary - PAK Plant. An investment project titled Organization of ring rolling production with reconstruction of a production building block is being implemented at the site of BelAZ’s branch - Industry of Rings in Orsha. The project aims to set up a modern import-substituting facility for producing ring blanks for flanges, bearings, planetary gear ring gears, adapters, shells, and wheel rims for mining dump trucks. The project is valued at Br330.4 million and is scheduled for completion in the first quarter of 2027.
The main stages of mechanical equipment installation and process piping assembly have already been completed on most sections of the line. Work is underway to install equipment for the heat treatment section for ring blanks. Until now, ring blanks were purchased from foreign suppliers. Once the project is completed, ring blanks will be produced at the company’s own ring rolling facility, ensuring full import substitution of these products both for BelAZ and for other enterprises in Belarus and Russia.

At a Gaza zoo, war takes its toll on the animals
- The Gaza zoo animals suffer malnutrition and stress due to food shortages and ongoing conflict, with owner Mahmoud Gomaa moving animals multiple times to keep them alive.
- Many animals died or disappeared during the war, showing the direct impact of conflict and hardship on wildlife in Gaza.

AI generated
GAZA/CAIRO - As children walked into the zoo near Gaza’s Nuseirat refugee camp, they found a lion barely looking back at them through the bars of its cage and chimpanzees sitting listlessly in their enclosure.
Many of the animals were malnourished, weakened by shortages of food, medicine and vaccines.
But they were still alive, largely thanks to the efforts of zoo owner Mahmoud Gomaa.
He originally ran the attraction in the southern city of Rafah, but said he had to flee when Israeli troops attacked and occupied part of the area in 2024.
As the conflict raged, he moved the surviving animals from town to town before finding a place in Nuseirat in central Gaza earlier in 2026.
There, he reopened the zoo, hoping to give traumatised youngsters something to enjoy after nearly three years of destruction.
“In the beginning of the war, people were looking for a way to survive... and I was looking for a way to save the animals more than saving myself,” Gomaa told Reuters.
There were a number of zoos in Gaza before the conflict between Israel and Hamas erupted, displaying exotic and wild animals including lions and eagles, municipal records show.
Anyone trying to keep one open now faces enormous challenges, vets and animal experts said, not least in getting food in a territory struggling to feed its human population.
“Owners are currently feeding them frozen meat,” veterinarian Nidal Fadel said. “This is a catastrophe and a wrong nutritional plan because in nature they eat fresh prey.”
The animals themselves are bearing the brunt of the war – sometimes directly.
When Gomaa fled Rafah, he said he had to leave behind three lions, several crocodiles and some African ostriches.
A few months later, Gomaa returned and only found the bones of the crocodiles and the ostriches.
Those three lions, which he had locked in their cages, had disappeared.
There is also the trauma caused by the sound and sight of the conflict raging around them.
“Lions can detect sounds and disturbances that humans may not notice,” said Amir Khalil, a veterinarian who has led several trips to Gaza by the animal welfare organisation Four Paws and rescued other zoos’ animals.
“Bombing and constant conflict create enormous stress and fear for them,” he added.
In Nuseirat, the surviving lion barely looked up at the visitors.
But the children had better luck with some of the other animals, letting parrots ride on their shoulders and petting smaller monkeys.
It was a rare chance to relax in an enclave still facing regular airstrikes, despite a fragile ceasefire.
Israel’s military, which says its attacks are aimed at militant targets, did not immediately respond to questions about the conflict’s impact on civilian facilities like zoos and their animals.
“Today, there is no avenue for children to play,” said visitor Karam Al-Mazin, 42.
“There is nothing except rubble, stones and tents, so children today are bored and are in a difficult situation.” REUTERS

Detainees death revives Syria's memories of torture in prisons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:05:27 UTC
16:05:27 KST

Breadcrumb
Detainee's death revives Syria's memories of torture and abuse in prisons
The death of a young man with a serious medical condition who was arrested and allegedly beaten by Syrian security forces has stirred up dark memories of torture and other abuse in detention centers under the Assad dynasty’s decades-long totalitarian rule.
Syrians have taken to social media and the streets in recent days to demand answers about the death of Mohammad Ghamira, who was buried Monday in his hometown of al-Haffah in coastal Latakia province.
When insurgents unseated former President Bashar Assad in December 2024 after a nearly 14-year civil war, they opened the country's notorious prisons. During Assad's rule, rights groups say, thousands of prisoners were killed in mass executions or died from injuries and disease. Detainees were subjected to torture, beatings and rape.
Officials with the government of interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa have promised accountability in Ghamira's case, but rights groups say it is not an isolated incident and that abuses persist in detention centers.
Ghamira, a 29-year-old father of two, was a former volunteer with the White Helmets civil defense organization, which operated in opposition-held areas before Assad's fall.
He died in a hospital in Latakia on Sunday after being released from jail. He had been detained days earlier following an "allegation of theft involving a sum of money," Latakia’s internal security command said in a statement, without giving more details.
Syria’s Minister of Emergency and Disaster Management Raed al-Saleh, who was previously head of the White Helmets, said on X that Ghamira had died of "complications from cerebral and gastrointestinal hemorrhaging" that "resulted from a beating he sustained after being detained at the al-Haffah police station."
Al-Saleh and Ghamira's relatives said he had hemophilia, a condition affecting the blood's ability to clot.
Ghamira's uncle, Issam Ghamira, said in a video interview with state news agency SANA that the family had told the police chief in al-Haffah that his nephew had hemophilia and warned against hitting him. Despite that, he said, his nephew was hit while in custody.
Syria's interior ministry announced an investigation into Ghamira’s death and said seven interior ministry personnel were detained for questioning.
Syria's Interior Ministry spokesperson Noureddine al-Baba, speaking to journalists, acknowledged "shortcomings and deficiencies" in some of the country's police departments but said others were doing "exceptional" work.
"God willing, this painful incident will serve as a catalyst for positive change in the operations of the ministry of interior," he said.
Part of a wider problem 
In a report released in March, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic said it had documented "torture and ill-treatment" in 18 official detention facilities and 12 "makeshift facilities" in different areas of Syria between January and October 2025, in the months following Assad's ouster as the new government asserted control.
The practices it documented included beating prisoners with rifle butts, sticks, pipes, bars and cables; the use of electric shocks and other forms of torture; mock executions; and sexual violence.
Syrians for Truth and Justice, a human rights organisation that tracks abuses, in a report published earlier this month said that "severe beatings, electric shocks, humiliation, threats, deprivation of basic necessities, and deaths in custody continue to be common practices at the hands of multiple security and military actors."
The group concluded that the incidents were too widespread to treat as isolated incidents but that there was not evidence of a "single centralised system equivalent in structure and direction to the torture apparatus entrenched by the Assad regime."
"It is somehow widespread, but it’s not structured," Bassam Alahmad, the group’s executive director, told The Associated Press. "For us, there is no evidence that these orders came from the commanders to torture people, but still (the authorities) have a responsibility to stop this behavior."
Syrians whose loved ones disappeared or died in detention centers during Assad's rule said they were disturbed to see the patterns being repeated under the new government.
Families for Freedom, a group representing relatives of detainees, said in a statement, "What happened to Mohammed reopens the wounds of torture and death in detention for thousands of Syrian families—practices Syrians have struggled for years to end, and the recurrence of which cannot be accepted today."

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,469,970 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:04:30 UTC
16:04:30 KST

Russia has lost around 1,469,970 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 18.
The figure includes 1,210 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,274 tanks, 25,162 armored combat vehicles, 135,891 vehicles and fuel tanks, 48,155 artillery systems, 2,040 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,577 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 467,459 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,292 unmanned ground systems, 5,010 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs). The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Oil prices have risen again after the two-month window to negotiate a peace deal in the US-Israel war on Iran expired on Monday with no end to the conflict in sight.
Iran said on Monday that it would take a more aggressive stance if talks with the US failed, while Donald Trump demanded Tehran “put up the white flag of surrender” in an interview with Fox News.
Trump also threatened to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of his effort to end the war, the second time he has directed such a threat at the longtime US strategic partner. “If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them,” Trump told Fox News on Monday.
Brent crude rose above $90 a barrel for the first time since 30 July, and was trading at $91.63 on Tuesday morning.
Angeline Ong, a senior technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Trump’s threat to bomb Oman could be the moment the oil market shifts from pricing a temporary disruption to pricing a prolonged one.
“If Muscat pulls back from talks with Tehran, the diplomatic route to restoring normal flows through Hormuz narrows considerably. That would be a signal to add to energy longs rather than fade the rally – with roughly a quarter of global seaborne oil normally passing through the strait, even a small reduction in the probability of reopening warrants a higher geopolitical premium in crude.”
A cargo ship was attacked while travelling through the strait early on Tuesday, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency, after an Iranian official told Reuters that it would shift to a “fully offensive” military stance.
Fox News reported on Tuesday that the Iranian military spokesperson Ebrahim Zolfaghari said vessels attempting to pass through the strait would “find several beautiful holes in their hulls”.
Just six commodity ships travelled through the waterway on Monday, according to Kpler, a ship tracking company. That was slightly up compared with the weekend, when five ships transited on Saturday and Sunday combined.
Analysts at Deutsche Bank wrote on Tuesday that the rising oil prices were a sign of investors pricing in “a more extended closure” of the strait.
Trump made the threat against Oman as he struggles to draw the conflict to a close almost six months after it began. But the US president also claimed during Monday’s interview that he was “not in a hurry” to reach a deal.
He has repeatedly claimed the war would end “soon”, and talked up the prospect of a lasting peace deal in recent months, without such a breakthrough materialising. Trump said he would not impose a fresh deadline on Iran, adding: “I have no time schedule. I’m not in a hurry.”
Dan Alamariu, the chief geopolitical strategist at the research company Alpine Macro, warned that if there was no end to the fighting in the Middle East, energy prices could see a “double whammy” from that combined with Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine.
He said: “Escalation from September through November is likely and could deliver a double shock … even if a bigger two-war convergence remains just a tail risk.
“Energy market risks will persist, and oil and gas prices and volatility would spike with another bout of sustained, intense conflict, especially in the Gulf.”

Russian businesses transfer hundreds of billions of roubles to treasury at Putin's request
Major Russian businessmen have transferred hundreds of billions of roubles to the federal budget after Russian leader Vladimir Putin called on them to make voluntary contributions to the state treasury.
Source: The Moscow Times
Details: Putin called for voluntary contributions amid a record deficit, the publication recalls. As of mid-August, according to the Electronic Budget system, such contributions had already totalled RUB 383.69 billion (approx. US$4.5 billion).
Before Putin's meeting with business representatives in March, at which he proposed that entrepreneurs help the budget according to The Bell's sources, contributions to the treasury from non-state organisations amounted to RUB 15.6 billion (US$184 million), the publication states.
Over the following month, the sum of donations increased tenfold, to RUB 159.7 billion (US$1.8 billion). In May, according to the Russian publication Vedomosti, it grew by 45.5%, in June by 27%, and over July and the first half of August by a further 30%.
"The fact that Russian business is helping the budget is a fact," said Aleksandr Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs. According to him, businessmen transferred funds not only from corporate but also from family foundations.
Sources of the Expert magazine reported that the government expects to receive approximately RUB 300 billion (US$3.5 billion) in voluntary contributions from businesses by the end of the year.
Background:
- It was previously reported that the Kremlin wants to improve Russia's financial situation through voluntary contributions from oligarchs, and some of them have already agreed, considering it a "debt for the 90s", when they launched their businesses.
- The Kremlin leader signed a decree allowing companies that fail to fulfil state orders during martial law to be placed under external administration.
- Putin said that companies which "slammed the door defiantly" and left the Russian market would not be allowed to buy back their assets at low prices or reclaim their former market positions.
- It was also reported that several of Russia's wealthiest individuals, including those close to Putin, have transferred billions of dollars abroad over the past year, as they grow increasingly concerned about the state of the country's economy and the state budget.

The unpopular populist: Why Nigel Farage’s Reform UK is losing support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:03:30 UTC
16:03:30 KST

Right-wing British populist Nigel Farage has returned to Parliament as planned, but the event can hardly be called a triumph. His Reform UK party, which until recently dreamed of definitively replacing the Conservatives, has faced falling poll numbers, investigations into suspicious donations, and its own institutional weakness. Now its leader must prove that his creation is not merely a temporary home for protest voters (or a one-man party built around a single scandal-prone politician), but a real political force.
Nigel Farage's the right-wing populist party, Reform UK, is at a make-or-break moment. It will either replace the Tories as the country's main political force on the right, or it will continue to be a marginal movement with no real hope of taking power. The populists face three fundamental barriers on the road to success: high unfavorable ratings outside their electoral base, an electoral platform that essentially promises to dismantle the government structures is seeks to lead, and a lack of “institutional depth” — i.e., a history, a developed organization, and a firm place in voters’ political memory.
What Reform UK does have in abundance, however, is dependence on its leader.
The Battle of Clowns in Clacton
Financing is often a weak spot for right-wing populists. Nigel Farage likes to talk about how he was given millions of pounds without being asked for anything in return, arguing that his finances are being investigated by British authorities only because the establishment cannot defeat him in a fair political fight. “Let ordinary voters judge me,” he said: “If I win, you win, because if I lose, they win.” This was the main message of Farage’s speech this past July 7, when he announced that he would stand again in an early election in his Clacton constituency. His slogan for that campaign: “The People versus the Establishment.”
The comedy began the very next day. All parties with any meaningful support – Labour, the Tories, the Liberal Democrats, the Greens, and Restore Britain (Farage’s rival on the right) – declined to field candidates. Thus, Farage’s main opponent was Count Binface (literally a man with a garbage bin on his head), along with three representatives of the Official Monster Raving Loony Party, several other novelty candidates, and a couple of dozen independents. A record 34 candidates in all joined the field.
Farage, of course, won. From the outset, around 70% of the constituency’s voters were ready to support him, compared with roughly 20% for Count Binface, and in the end the Reform UK head claimed 63% (then declined to attend the official announcement of the results). More importantly though, at the national level, 73% of Britons believe the investigation into Farage's finances should continue, no matter what the voters of Clacton may have said.
Political resilience
Farage is one of the most consistent and persistent politicians in modern Britain. For more than 30 years, he has built his political career around a single idea: I am on the side of the people in their struggle against a political class that betrays the will of ordinary Britons, and I will restore the country’s national sovereignty and control over its borders. The names and party labels change, but Farage and his basic message remain.
In 1989, Farage, still a Tory at the time, voted for the Green Party, reportedly because it was then seen as Euroskeptic. Three years later, in protest against the signing of the Maastricht Treaty (which created the European Union), he left the Conservative Party and joined the Anti-Federalist League, which soon became the United Kingdom Independence Party (UKIP). He led UKIP from 2006 to 2016 before taking over the newly established Brexit Party in 2019. In 2021, the party was renamed Reform UK, and Farage announced his retirement from politics. But ahead of the 2024 general election, he unexpectedly returned and, on his eighth attempt, was elected to the House of Commons.
Farage likes to portray himself as an outsider who can bring about the political revolution Britain so badly needs
Farage likes to portray himself as an outsider who can bring about a political revolution Britain supposedly so badly needs. The son of a trader, he attended a private school and then followed in his father's footsteps, becoming a trader in non-ferrous metals in the City of London. He made his way into politics thanks to an obvious talent for working with the media and a skillfully crafted political narrative that was very simple – and, therefore, persuasive.
The narrative works
Immigration and sovereignty remain at the core of Farage’s political program – in other words, his main political tool remains emotion. Farage's positions on “secondary” issues, especially economic ones, can change, sometimes radically, and his critics' charge that Farage offers slogans rather than plans are indeed consistent with reality. Unsurprisingly, 86% of Reform supporters consider immigration to be the country's most important political issue, compared with 42% of Britons overall. (The cost of living comes second, at 38%.)
In the worldview Farage offers, the topics of immigration, Brexit, economic problems, the declining quality of public services, and distrust in government institutions have become intertwined. The conclusion – that Britain is “broken” – is often expressed in forceful, militaristic rhetoric, with words such as “betrayal,” “war,” and “invasion.” The changes proposed are sometimes even given the names of military campaigns, such as “Operation Restore Justice.”
Channeling these emotions has proven effective. By summer 2026, 61% of Britons surveyed considered Reform to be one of the “major parties,” compared with just 19% two years earlier. In the 2025 and 2026 local elections, hundreds of the party’s candidates were elected as local councilors, and Reform now controls dozens of local authorities. It has become a real political force.
Something went wrong
Until early fall 2025, the average of the seven most recent polls conducted by different firms showed a steady rise in support for Reform, reaching around 32%. For comparison, Labour, now the governing party, won more than 400 of the 650 seats in 2024 with a comparable share of the vote.
But then came an equally steady decline. As of Aug. 5, support for Reform UK was back down to 24.0%, coming in behind Labour at 25.9%, with the Conservatives, Greens, and Liberal Democrats attracting 19.4%, 11.1%, and 10.7% support, respectively).
Reform’s growing prominence probably brought greater scrutiny of its plans, revealing that many people either saw the party’s proposals as eye-catching wish lists without realistic plans behind them (such as its call to invade France) or simply did not approve of them. For example, critics described as unfair and “un-British” the proposal to force people who had legally settled in Britain years or even decades ago to prove their right to remain all over again.
Another possible reason for Reform’s deteriorating position in the polls is the gradual recovery of the Conservative Party, which Farage has publicly vowed to displace. The Tories' current leader, Kemi Badenoch, has seen her popularity rise since September 2025.
Finally, a string of new scandals and reports of parliamentary and police investigations into the financial dealings of Farage and Reform, which began in spring 2026, may also have played a role. Not the main one, since Reform’s decline in the polls began long before the first reports of possible financial irregularities. Nevertheless, the allegations could ultimately cost Farage his seat in Parliament.
Is there life after Farage
The facts and suspicions described above – million-pound gifts, transfers sent through complicated channels, questions about financial disclosures, and ongoing investigations – look like a pattern of behavior when taken together, even if all of the allegations are yet to be proven. As a result, Farage's rhetoric of being with the people and against the elites is beginning to sound less convincing.
Traditionally, Farage is seen as the party’s main asset – he is still better than anyone else in Britain at using the media, and the loyalty of Reform UK supporters is centered on him. As many as 91% of those who back the party view him positively, with 49% viewing him very positively. Among the electorate as a whole, however, the picture is radically different. When More in Common asked Britons “Who do you trust more, the leader or the party?”, 7% chose Farage, while 17% chose Reform UK. Under the circumstances, breaking with Farage might actually benefit the party: while the leader once pulled the party upward, his high personal unfavorable ratings and financial scandals could now drag it down. For now, however, Reform UK is, in essence, Nigel Farage himself.
In the More in Common poll, when asked “Who do you trust more, the leader or the party?”, 7% chose Farage, while 17% chose Reform UK
Major internal party disagreements are usually resolved through Farage’s personal intervention. That was the case, for example, in June 2025, when party official Zia Yusuf announced his resignation. However, after speaking with Farage, who publicly said he had “forgiven” Yusuf, he returned 48 hours later. The same applies to tensions between Reform UK’s old core and the Conservatives who have joined the party – above all Robert Jenrick. For now, these tensions are largely being managed from above by Farage.
Or take the procedure for selecting parliamentary candidates. As of early August, the party’s Parliamentary candidates portal promised to “publish in due course” the rules for selecting them – this despite the fact that the party has existed for more than seven years, participated with some success in a general election two years ago, and intends to win a parliamentary majority in 2029. Somehow though, there are still no clear rules beyond the discretionary decisions of the party leadership.
The same story is playing out at the local level. In the absence of an established procedure, Reform UK can end up with candidates like Linden Kemkaran, who became leader of Kent County Council after the party won a majority there in 2025. So far, under her leadership, the local administration has been known largely for the advice its new leader gave to dissenting fellow party members: “fucking suck it up.”
That is precisely why bringing in experienced politicians and administrators is so important for Reform UK, as demonstrated by the example of North Northamptonshire Council, which is successfully led by a former Tory. Once in power, the rhetoric of revolution runs up against the mundane realities of everyday work like drawing up budgets and dealing with the rest of the administrative grind.
To become a successful, long-lived political force, Reform UK will have to develop mechanisms and procedures for the party’s internal life: how to resolve conflicts, how to constrain the leader’s arbitrary power, how to select high-quality candidates, and what a party member can do if they disagree with a decision. It is precisely the existence of such mechanisms that allows Labour and the Conservatives to survive instability at the top. With the “Faragists,” it is the other way around – stability at the very top and chaos below.
Obstacles from the right as well
In addition to internal professionalization, Reform UK’s future also depends on what happens to the Conservative Party over the next few years. The two right-of-center political groupings face different challenges. For Reform to win in the long run, it is not enough to be incrementally more popular; instead, it needs to prove that the Conservatives are finished as a serious electoral player.
This will not be easy. The growing personal popularity of Tory leader Kemi Badenoch represents a real threat to Reform UK. Among Reform supporters, 56% have a positive view of her, up from 37% a year earlier, and 40% say they would consider voting for her party. Among those who voted Conservative in 2024 but later switched to Reform, her net favorability rating has risen from +20 to +58, and 73% of this group say they could return to the Conservatives.
In short, the Conservatives are showing true signs of life. The results of the 2026 local elections were not as bad as expected, and they looked poor in part because they were being compared with unusually strong results in the previous electoral cycle. The Tories won the Aberdeen South parliamentary by-election with 49.5% of the vote, leaving Reform in third place with 8.6% – several times lower than its nationwide polling numbers. Moreover, this was the first Scottish by-election won by the Conservatives in half a century.
This was the first Scottish by-election won by the Conservatives in half a century
The Tories’ long-term prospects are impossible to predict. They may gradually recover under the firm hand of Badenoch, but it may also turn out that what we took for signs of life were merely bumps that made the corpse jolt.
Reform also has a more radical rival on the right – Restore Britain, founded by former Reform member Rupert Lowe. Like Reform, Restore too is “viciously attacked by the establishment.” It has also been publicly endorsed by Elon Musk and has already won 7–9% in several elections.
Lowe is popular among Reform supporters, particularly those who voted for the party in 2024 but do not see Farage as being radical enough. However, if Reform drifts to the right under the influence of this faction, it will ultimately lose the center, where elections are still won.
The electoral pen
Institutional weakness, an incomplete program, and high unfavorability ratings could trap Reform in a kind of electoral pen. Its outer boundary is made up of the many voters who find Farage and his party unacceptable, as even some people who are planning to vote for Reform sometimes say in focus groups that they will do so while holding their noses. Its inner boundary consists of the most radical supporters, who are ready to switch to Restore if Reform tries to become more moderate – for example, if it refuses to hold the referendum on restoring the death penalty as demanded by Lowe.
Institutional weakness could prevent Reform UK from convincing voters that it is capable of governing effectively. There is a gap between support for the party and perceptions of its readiness for exercising power — an Ipsos poll conducted in late June 2026 showed that support for Reform was significantly higher than the number of people prepared to trust it to form a government (and the latter figure fell from 29% last September to 21% earlier this summer). With Reform and Labour hovering around comparable polling numbers, 30% overall still preferred to see Andy Burnham as prime minister, while only 16% chose Farage.
Looking competent is especially important for a party that is deeply unpopular beyond outside its base of loyal supporters. This is a feature of the first-past-the-post system: whatever your overall polling numbers, what matters is beating your opponent by a single vote in a given constituency. As tactical voting becomes more popular, some voters cast their ballots for the party that can stop a candidate they dislike.
Here Reform is at a real disadvantage. A YouGov poll published in early July 2026 shows that around 62–63% of Britons have a negative view of Farage's party. When compared with the Conservative Party the overall figure for support is comparable, but 39% viewed the Tories “very negatively,” as opposed to 53% in the case of Reform – this a mere two years after the Tories suffered their worst electoral defeat in history.
Farage himself is doing no better. According to Pollcheck, as of Aug. 1 he ranked last among party leaders, with a net favorability rating of –22.3%, while his main rival on the right, the Conservatives' Badenoch, stood at +1.7%.
How the story ends
Forecasting at a point of bifurcation is a thankless task. Broadly speaking, two medium-term scenarios are emerging: Reform could replace the Tories as the main party on the right, or it could end up in its own electoral pen, expansive but with no way out.
For Farage’s party to succeed, it needs to halt its decline in the polls, become a professional political institution, and establish itself in the eyes of right-wing voters as the main means of removing Labour from power – and it needs to do so before investigations and internal infighting undermine voters' confidence in Farage and his movement. If Reform succeeds, it would attract not only tactical voters (for whom defeating the “left” is the overriding priority), but also higher-caliber candidates and staff.
Reform UK could replace the Tories as the main party on the right or end up in its own electoral pen, expansive but with no way out
But the opposite outcome is entirely possible: the party could retain its high unfavorable rating and remain unable to move beyond its current base, while also failing to professionalize. Meanwhile, the “revived” Conservatives could win back some of their erstwhile supporters who are currently holding their noses while voting for Reform.
In short, the populist tactics that enabled Reform to grow so quickly are now holding it back, making it harder to turn a “party of the aggrieved” into a party of government.
And of course, there is the separate question of what will happen with Farage himself. He has already shown that he can pursue his goal for decades and get back on his feet after defeats. But he has now set himself a new task – to create a party capable of crushing or absorbing one of the oldest political institutions in history. The Conservatives need only avoid losing, while Farage needs to win. The moment of truth is approaching for Farage and Reform UK.

An unenlightened traveller’s guide to Pride
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:01:21 UTC
16:01:21 KST

“But you aren’t gay?”
A family member said, raising her eyebrows, after I mentioned, between bites of a breakfast roll, that I was thinking about going to Copenhagen Pride.
She said it as if I’d be denied entry unless I could document my same-sex body count.
Later that week, I was in a bar with a friend drinking beers as if they were going to ask for them back.
“I’m thinking about going to Pride,” I said during my fifth beer.
He put down his glass but raised his eyebrows. “Is there something you want to tell me?”
According to the eyebrow raisers, Pride was for them, not for us. You had to be gay—or at least considering it—to think about going. I found that odd. Had I told them I was going to a food festival, nobody would have worried I’d quit my job to become a chef.
The concept of Pride began to gnaw inside of me. Were they right? Did I have to be gay? Could I pull off a netted vest? Would I trigger a gaydar? What is a gaydar?
It was settled; I would set out to be an unenlightened traveller. A goldfish being carried towards an unfamiliar aquarium in a plastic bag.
On P day, I donned my rainbow bucket hat and matching bracelets and burst out onto the streets, where I was immediately met with jeers from a group of lads in a passing car. When in a provincial town, this is the best indication that my outfit was spot on.
On the delayed train, an elderly man gestured to his wife. She glanced at me and whispered, as elderly people do, loudly.
“Pride.”
He tutted.
Stepping out of Copenhagen station, there was no doubt Pride had begun without me. Music reverberated through the busy streets. I dashed towards the thumping beat.
The parade had come to a halt, forcing the pink fairies, sequined cowboys and other colourful characters to wait like race car drivers for the green flag. Around them, soundboxes fought for supremacy with pop jams from every decade.
Kids chased confetti, gathering it in handfuls to toss back into the air over the paradees, who passed the wait with ecstatic dancing and euphoric kissing.
As the wheels of the parade started to turn, I snapped pictures with my camera and waved like a madman at anyone who looked in my direction.
The atmosphere was intoxicating. I needed to join in. When I saw an opening, I slipped into the parade’s ranks.
Feeling naughty, I went rigid, trying not to be detected, but as we progressed through the streets, my fellow paraders relaxed me. Soon I was moving to the tunes vibrating off the surrounding buildings. I caught the eye of a woman parading next to me who cheered me on, which spurred me into a full-on dance.
The route took us towards Rådhuspladsen. I jumped out of the parade and browsed the merchandise. If they can put a flag on it, they will.
Crowds flowed like a lazy river. I merged with one, allowing myself to drift with the current.
On route, I saw more leather than a shift manager at a tannery. And enough bulging abs to put most of the marble statues in Glyptoteket to shame.
Answering one of my questions, no, I most definitely couldn’t pull off a netted vest. I’d look like a Christmas ham, with the pork poking through the netting.
Sunlight was fading, and I was nowhere near to figuring out Pride. But I soon found that when the sun goes down, the volume of Pride cranks up.
That night, Copenhagen stood in stark contrast to the black night sky. I moved from street party to street party. Lights draped the old buildings in twinkling colours, refracted off the discoballs that spun over DJs banging out everything from Aqua, Cher and even Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas.”
At Slutterigade, the junction in front of the archway was clogged with people. With every step, I kicked glasses and shot tubes. When I reached the epicentre of the crowd, residue from hundreds of dropped drinks made my canvas sneakers stick to the cobbles. Even without the alcoholic glue, I couldn’t move. I was wedged amongst hundreds of people. I stood there and felt the crowd. Hundreds of people merged into one body, moving together to the greatest power women in music history. Every bump of a shoulder, every brush of bare, sweaty skin against my face seemed to connect me to it, and I realised I had become a small part of the party.
I’m not claiming Pride as my own. I can’t and probably never will understand the struggle of the majority of those on that street. But in that pulsating crowd on Slutterigade, I came to the realisation that the LGBTQ community were the hosts. I was a guest. And they seemed remarkably happy to let me dance in their living room.
There on the packed cobbles of Copenhagen, people expressed themselves and their love openly, turning the city into a bowl of pick ‘n’ mix where everyone was welcome to have a taste.
After unsticking my shoes from the pavement and bidding the hosts goodnight, I thought about all those eyebrow raisers who think Pride is just for the LGBTQ community. They are missing out on one hell of a party. I’d take power women and sweaty abs over standing on the outside tutting any day of the week.
Back at the station, my train was late again. And just as I thought Pride was coming to an end for me, there was one last surprise. The contrast between sky and street was broken as fireworks leapt into the black night sky, painting it with all the colours of a rainbow.
By then, feet were aching and my legs and shoes were sticky. But I found myself singing power woman Kylie Minogue’s “I Can’t Get You Out of My Head.”
And Pride, I’m sure you’ll be in there for some time.
